statement: Software architecture consists of four parts: the structure of the system, the architecture characteristics it must support, the architecture decisions, and the design principles.
Describing a system only by its structure (its architecture style) does not fully define its architecture; the characteristics, decisions, and design principles are also needed.
Architecture characteristics (the -ilities) define the success criteria of a system and are generally orthogonal to the system's functionality.
Architecture decisions define the rules for how a system is constructed and form the constraints that direct development teams on what is and is not allowed.

When an architecture decision cannot be implemented in part of the system, it may be broken through a formal variance that an architecture review board or chief architect approves or denies based on justifications and trade-offs.
condition: a decision cannot be implemented in one part of the system due to a condition or constraint

statement: A design principle is a guideline rather than a hard-and-fast rule: it states a preferred approach while leaving the developer room to choose appropriately for a specific circumstance.
Express guidance as a design principle rather than a rigid rule when no single rule can cover every condition and option.
condition: no single rule can cover every condition and option

statement: An architect should guide technology choices rather than specify them, instructing teams toward a category of technology rather than naming a single product.
exception: an architect may specify a particular technology when it is necessary to preserve an architecture characteristic such as scalability, performance, or availability

statement: There are eight core expectations of a software architect regardless of role or title: make architecture decisions, continually analyze the architecture, keep current with trends, ensure compliance with decisions, have diverse exposure and experience, have business domain knowledge, possess interpersonal skills, and understand and navigate politics.
An architect should continually analyze the architecture and current technology environment and recommend improvements, because most architectures suffer structural decay when this is neglected.
Structural decay occurs when developers make coding or design changes that impact required architecture characteristics such as performance, availability, and scalability.
Agility in code modification does not deliver overall architectural agility if testing takes weeks and releases take months; testing and release environments must also be agile.
condition: testing takes weeks and releases take months

statement: An architect should keep current with the latest technology and industry trends because architectural decisions tend to be long-lasting and difficult to change.

Ensuring compliance means the architect continually verifies that development teams follow the documented and communicated architecture decisions and design principles, since uncontrolled violations cause the system to miss its required characteristics.
Restricting (closing) database access to only the business and services layers lets database changes be made without impacting the presentation layer, which controls change.
For an architect, technical breadth (familiarity with many technologies and their trade-offs) is more valuable than technical depth (expertise in a single one).
An architect needs a level of business domain knowledge, without which it is difficult to understand the business problem and to communicate credibly with stakeholders and business users.
The most successful architects combine broad hands-on technical knowledge with strong knowledge of a particular business domain.
Leadership and interpersonal skills account for at least half of what it takes to become an effective software architect, regardless of role or title.

Almost every decision an architect makes will be challenged by product owners, project managers, business stakeholders, or developers, so an architect must apply negotiation skills to get decisions approved.
The scope of the software architect role has expanded over the past decade beyond purely technical concerns to encompass operations, process, data, and security.

Software engineering practices are process-agnostic practices with demonstrated, repeatable benefit (such as continuous integration), distinct from process, which concerns how teams are formed, managed, and how they interact.

A given architectural style and the team's engineering practices must form a symbiotic mesh; for example, microservices assumes automated provisioning, testing, and deployment, and building it with manual processes and little testing creates tremendous friction.
All architectures become iterative because of unknown unknowns; Agile simply recognizes this and starts iterating sooner.
Architects cannot design for unknown unknowns, which is why Big Design Up Front software efforts suffer.

An iterative (Agile) process fits the nature of software architecture better than planning-heavy processes such as Waterfall, partly because of its tighter feedback loop and support for techniques like the Strangler pattern and feature toggles.

An architectural fitness function is an objective integrity assessment of one or more architecture characteristics, implemented with mechanisms such as metrics, unit tests, monitors, and chaos engineering, and run continuously to govern those characteristics as the system changes.

Adopting Agile engineering practices such as continuous integration and automated machine provisioning makes building resilient architectures easier, and there is a correlation between how often fitness functions execute and the feedback they provide.

Some operational concerns such as elastic scale are better handled by operations; creating a liaison between architecture and operations (as microservices does) lets architects simplify the design instead of building those capabilities defensively into the architecture.
Building operational concerns defensively into the architecture (as ESB-driven SOA did for elastic scale) creates accidental complexity and a vastly more complex architecture.
The software development process a team uses has a real impact on many facets of software architecture, contradicting the older axiom that process and architecture are orthogonal.
Code and data have a symbiotic relationship in which neither is useful without the other, so architecture must account for external data storage rather than ignoring it.
The First Law of Software Architecture is that everything in software architecture is a trade-off, so every decision must weigh many opposing factors.
If an architect thinks they have found something that is not a trade-off, more likely they simply have not identified the trade-off yet.
Architects should soberly analyze the trade-offs of every choice rather than becoming enamored with a technology, because virtually nothing in the real world offers a convenient binary choice.
The Second Law of Software Architecture is that why is more important than how.
Architects should capture why decisions were made, not only how the topology was built, for example by recording Architecture Decision Records.

Architects should regularly question fundamental axioms inherited from earlier eras, because improved engineering practices, operational ecosystems, and development processes continually change the assumptions earlier writing relied on.
All architectures are a product of their context, and architectural decisions can only be understood in the context of the environment in which they were made.
Because no concise universal definition of the software architect role exists, it is more useful to focus on the expectations placed on an architect than to try to define the role.

Architectural thinking has four aspects: knowing the difference between architecture and design and collaborating with teams, having technical breadth with some depth, analyzing and reconciling trade-offs, and understanding how business drivers translate to architectural concerns.

To make architecture work, the physical and virtual barriers between architects and developers must be broken down to form a strong bidirectional relationship in which they operate as one virtual team.

The traditional unidirectional handoff model, in which an architect passes artifacts across a barrier to developers, is a primary reason architecture rarely works, because architect decisions fail to reach teams and team changes fail to return to the architect.
In modern systems, architecture changes and evolves every iteration or phase, so architecture and design are not separate phases and must be kept continuously synchronized.

The microservices style treats change as a first-class design consideration, so making structural changes is no longer necessarily expensive, though this capability trades off against other concerns such as coupling.
exception: this capability incurs trade-offs with other concerns such as coupling

statement: A developer needs significant technical depth to do their job, whereas a software architect needs significant technical breadth to think with an architectural point of view.
Any individual's knowledge partitions into three parts: stuff you know, stuff you know you don't know, and stuff you don't know you don't know, the last being the largest.
The stuff you know is also the stuff you must maintain: technical depth requires continual time investment or the expertise decays.
For an architect, breadth is more important than depth, so the wise course is to sacrifice some hard-won expertise and reinvest that time in broadening the technology portfolio.
Trying to maintain deep expertise across a wide variety of areas is a dysfunction: the architect succeeds in none of them and works themselves ragged.

Stale expertise, the mistaken sensation that outdated information is still cutting edge, is a common architect dysfunction, often seen in founders who moved into leadership yet decide using ancient criteria.
In the Frozen Caveman anti-pattern an architect repeatedly reverts to a pet irrational concern, usually after being burned by a past decision, producing unrealistic risk assessments.
Architects should distinguish genuine technical risk from perceived technical risk and keep risk assessment realistic.

The honest answer to most architecture questions is it depends, because the right choice depends on the deployment environment, business drivers, company culture, budgets, timeframes, developer skill set, and many other factors.
There are no right or wrong answers in architecture, only trade-offs.

Architectural thinking means analyzing both the benefits and the negatives of a solution; programmers tend to know the benefits of everything and the trade-offs of nothing, while architects need to understand both.

Publish-subscribe topic messaging makes the producer more decoupled and the system more extensible because new consumers can subscribe with no change to existing services, but it exposes the data to any subscriber, supports only homogeneous contracts, and limits per-consumer monitoring and auto-scaling.

Point-to-point queue messaging gives each consumer its own contract, better data security, and individual monitoring and scaling, but couples the producer to its consumers and requires changing the producer to add a new consumer.
Every option in software architecture has both an advantage and a disadvantage, so the architect's job is to analyze the trade-offs and ask which quality matters more in the specific context.

Thinking like an architect includes understanding business drivers and translating them into architecture characteristics such as scalability, performance, and availability, which requires domain knowledge and collaborative relationships with stakeholders.
Every architect should still code and maintain a certain level of technical depth.
The bottleneck trap occurs when an architect takes ownership of code in the critical path (usually framework code) and becomes a bottleneck, because they cannot be a full-time developer.

To avoid the bottleneck trap, the architect should delegate the critical-path and framework code to the development team and instead build a piece of business functionality one to three iterations down the road.

An architect who cannot develop alongside the team can still remain hands-on through frequent proof-of-concepts, tackling technical-debt or architecture stories, fixing bugs, building automation and fitness functions, and doing frequent code reviews.
condition: the architect cannot develop code directly with the development team

statement: When doing proof-of-concept work an architect should write the best production-quality code they can, because throwaway POC code often becomes the reference example others follow and because it keeps the architect's coding skills sharp.

Modularity is an organizing principle, and because software systems tend toward entropy, architects must constantly expend energy to ensure good structural soundness, which will not happen by accident.
Good modularity is an implicit architecture characteristic: virtually no project states it as a requirement, yet sustainable code bases require order and consistency.

Modularity denotes a logical grouping of related code, which is distinct from physical separation; loose physical partitioning encourages coupling that later becomes an impediment to breaking a monolith apart.
Three key language-agnostic measures of modularity are cohesion, coupling, and connascence.
Cohesion measures how related the parts of a module are; an ideally cohesive module would only gain increased coupling and decreased readability if it were divided.
Cohesion measures rank from best to worst as functional, sequential, communicational, procedural, temporal, logical, and coincidental cohesion.
Cohesion is a less precise metric than coupling, and a module's degree of cohesiveness is often at the discretion of the particular architect.

The Lack of Cohesion in Methods (LCOM) metric measures structural lack of cohesion and exposes incidental coupling, helping architects find classes that should never have been one class, but it can find only structural, not logical, lack of cohesion.
exception: it cannot determine whether pieces logically fit together

statement: Afferent coupling measures the number of incoming connections to a code artifact, and efferent coupling measures the number of outgoing connections to other artifacts.
Abstractness is the ratio of abstract artifacts to concrete artifacts, and instability is the ratio of efferent coupling to the sum of efferent and afferent coupling.

A code base with high instability breaks more easily when changed because of its high efferent coupling: a class that delegates to many others is highly susceptible to breakage when any of them changes.
Distance from the main sequence (D = A + I minus 1) is one of the few holistic structural metrics: classes near the idealized line exhibit a healthy balance of abstractness and instability.

Code that is too abstract falls into the zone of uselessness (hard to use), while code with too much implementation and too little abstraction falls into the zone of pain (brittle and hard to maintain).

Code-level metrics are blunt and require interpretation; for example, cyclomatic complexity measures complexity but cannot by itself distinguish essential complexity from accidental complexity, so architects should establish baselines.
Two components are connascent if a change in one would require the other to be modified to maintain the overall correctness of the system.
Static connascence is source-code-level coupling and includes connascence of name, type, meaning/convention, position, and algorithm.
Dynamic connascence analyzes runtime calls and includes connascence of execution (order), timing, values, and identity.
Architects should prefer static connascence to dynamic connascence, because static connascence can be found by simple source-code analysis and modern tools make it trivial to improve.
Connascence has three properties that guide its use: strength, locality, and degree.
The strength of connascence is determined by how easily the coupling can be refactored, and architects can improve a code base by refactoring toward weaker, more desirable forms of connascence.
By the locality property, stronger connascence within the same module represents less of a code smell than the same form spread across modules, so strength and locality must be considered together.
The degree of connascence relates to the size of its impact; lower-degree connascence damages a code base less, but because code bases tend to grow, small connascence problems tend to become bigger.

Page-Jones offers three guidelines for using connascence: minimize overall connascence by breaking the system into encapsulated elements, minimize remaining connascence that crosses encapsulation boundaries, and maximize connascence within encapsulation boundaries.

Weirich's two rules of connascence are the Rule of Degree (convert strong forms into weaker forms) and the Rule of Locality (as the distance between software elements increases, use weaker forms of connascence).

Architects tend to care more about how modules are coupled (such as synchronous versus asynchronous communication) than about the raw degree of coupling, and 1990s connascence focuses on low-level code hygiene without resolving the synchronous-versus-asynchronous decision in distributed architectures.

An architecture characteristic meets three criteria: it specifies a nondomain design consideration, it influences some structural aspect of the design, and it is critical or important to application success.

Prefer the term architecture characteristics over nonfunctional requirements or quality attributes, because nonfunctional is self-denigrating and quality attributes implies after-the-fact assessment rather than design.

A concern rises to the level of an architecture characteristic only when it requires special structural consideration: in-application payment processing may need a structurally isolated module, whereas a third-party payment processor needs only standard security hygiene.
condition: the concern requires special structural consideration to succeed

statement: Each supported architecture characteristic adds complexity to the design, so a critical job for architects is to choose the fewest architecture characteristics rather than the most possible.

Implicit architecture characteristics such as availability, reliability, and security rarely appear in requirements yet are necessary for success, so architects must use problem-domain knowledge to uncover them during analysis.
Explicit architecture characteristics are those that appear in requirements documents or other specific instructions.

Architecture characteristics interact, so improving one often degrades another (for example, improving security almost certainly degrades performance), making characteristic selection a balancing exercise.
Architects should never shoot for the best architecture but rather the least worst architecture, because it is rarely possible to maximize every architecture characteristic.
Supporting too many architecture characteristics leads to generic solutions that try to solve every business problem, and those architectures rarely work because the design becomes unwieldy.
Architects should strive to design architecture to be as iterative as possible, because if changes are easy to make there is less pressure to discover the exact correct design on the first attempt.
To reduce term-based misunderstandings, architects should follow domain-driven design's advice to establish and use a ubiquitous language among colleagues.
An architect uncovers architecture characteristics in at least three ways: by extracting them from domain concerns, from requirements, and from implicit domain knowledge.

When collaborating with domain stakeholders, keep the final list of driving architecture characteristics as short as possible, because designing a generic architecture that supports all characteristics is a common anti-pattern.

Rather than ranking every architecture characteristic, have the domain stakeholders select the top three most important ones in any order, which is easier to reach consensus on and fosters trade-off discussion.

The Vasa warship, over-specified to be both troop transport and gunship with twice the decks and cannons, became top-heavy and capsized, illustrating that over-specifying architecture characteristics can kill a project.
Architects and domain stakeholders speak different languages, creating a lost-in-translation problem, but a translation usually exists from domain concerns to architecture characteristics.
The domain concern of time to market does not equal agility alone; it is agility plus testability plus deployability, and focusing on only one ingredient is a common translation trap.

Some architecture characteristics come from explicit statements in requirements, while others come from the architect's inherent domain knowledge, such as anticipating that university students will all register at the last minute.

Architecture katas, which present a domain problem with additional context for small teams to design in a timebox, give aspiring architects practice deriving architecture characteristics, on the principle that great designers are made by designing.

Scalability (handling many concurrent users without serious performance degradation) and elasticity (handling bursts of requests) are distinct characteristics with different constraints; a system can be scalable but not elastic, and elastic systems often also need scalability.
Architects must often decode domain language into engineering equivalents, for example translating an expected number of users into the architecture characteristic of scalability.

Architects should guard against building unnecessary brittleness or fragility into designs; for example, when an external service is unavailable the system should offer slightly reduced function rather than fail entirely.
condition: a depended-on external service can become unavailable

statement: Over-specifying architecture characteristics is just as damaging as under-specifying them, because it overcomplicates the system design.
There are no wrong answers in architecture, only expensive ones.

Architecture implies a structural component while design resides within the architecture, so whether to support a capability with a structural architecture choice or with a design pattern is itself a trade-off decision.

No architecture decision should be made in isolation from the implementation team, since doing so leads to the Ivory Tower Architect anti-pattern; architects must collaborate with developers, project managers, operations, and domain analysts.
There is no best design in architecture, only a least worst collection of trade-offs.

A useful prioritization exercise is to identify the least important architecture characteristic to eliminate; architects are more likely to cull explicit characteristics because many implicit ones underpin general success.

Three common problems plague the definition of architecture characteristics: they are not physics (vague meanings), they have wildly varying definitions even within one organization, and many are too composite; agreeing organization-wide on objective definitions creates a ubiquitous language and lets teams decompose composite characteristics into measurable ones.
When measuring an operational characteristic such as response time, teams should measure the maximum, not only the average, because averaging hides boundary-condition outliers.

High-functioning teams set performance budgets (such as a first-page-render target or a K-weight byte budget for page downloads) and base characteristic definitions on statistical models that raise alarms when real-time metrics fall outside the predictions.

Cyclomatic complexity, developed by Thomas McCabe in 1976, is a code-level metric computed as CC = E minus N plus 2P (E edges or decision points, N nodes, P connected components) that objectively measures the number of execution paths in code.

Overly complex code is a code smell that harms nearly every desirable characteristic of a code base (modularity, testability, deployability), and if teams do not watch gradually growing complexity it will come to dominate the code base.

Industry thresholds suggest a cyclomatic complexity under 10 is acceptable, but the authors prefer code to fall under 5, indicating cohesive, well-factored code, unless the problem domain is genuinely complex.
exception: the problem domain is algorithmically complex, which legitimately yields complex functions

statement: Test-driven development has the side effect of generating smaller, less complex, more cohesive methods with lower cyclomatic complexity, because developers write the smallest code to pass each discrete test.

Agility is a composite architecture characteristic decomposable into testability and deployability; testability is measurable via code coverage tools, but coverage cannot replace intent because a code base can have 100 percent coverage yet poor assertions.
exception: high code coverage with poor assertions does not provide confidence in correctness

statement: Governance (from the Greek for to steer) is a core responsibility of the architect, covering any aspect of the development process the architect wants to influence, such as ensuring software quality.

An architecture fitness function is any mechanism that provides an objective integrity assessment of one or more architecture characteristics; it is a new perspective on existing tools (metrics, monitors, unit-test libraries, chaos engineering) rather than a new framework to download.

Cyclic dependencies between components damage modularity because a developer cannot reuse one component without bringing the others along, pushing the architecture toward the Big Ball of Mud anti-pattern.

Code reviews happen too late in the cycle to govern accidental coupling effectively, so architects should encode such governance as a fitness function (for example a JDepend cycle test) wired into the continuous build to guard important-but-not-urgent practices.
Architects must ensure that developers understand the purpose of a fitness function before imposing it on them, rather than developing esoteric governance from an ivory tower.
Chaos engineering reframes failure as a matter of when, not if, something will break, and anticipating breakages with tests to prevent them makes systems much more robust.

Like the checklists used by pilots and surgeons, fitness functions let architects codify important governance checks into the substrate of the architecture so that priorities are not lost among the many competing demands on busy developers.

The scope of architecture characteristics has narrowed from the system level to a smaller scope with modern styles such as microservices, so the older axiom that characteristics are evaluated system-wide is increasingly outdated.
An architecture quantum is an independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion and synchronous connascence.

A dependent component outside the code base, such as a database, is part of the architecture quantum because the system cannot function without it, so a legacy single-database system is a quantum of one while each microservice with its own database forms a separate quantum.
Synchronous calls between distributed services create dynamic connascence for the duration of the call, so the caller and callee must have similar operational architecture characteristics.
condition: two services communicate synchronously
exception: if the caller is far more scalable than the callee, timeouts and other reliability concerns occur

statement: Asynchronous communication, such as a message queue that buffers timing differences, creates a more flexible architecture by decoupling the operational characteristics of the communicating services.

Domain-driven design's bounded context makes everything related to a domain visible internally but opaque to other contexts; because holistically shared entities cause coupling, harder coordination, and complexity, each context should keep its own model and reconcile differences at integration points.

In modern systems architects should define architecture characteristics at the quantum level rather than the system level, which surfaces architectural challenges and hybrid-architecture needs earlier.

A litmus test distinguishes a domain concern from an architecture characteristic: if implementing it requires domain knowledge it is a domain concern, whereas if it can be described abstractly across any kind of application it is an architecture characteristic.

A component is the physical manifestation (packaging) of a module; a library runs in the caller's memory as a compile-time dependency, while a service runs in its own address space and communicates via networking protocols.

The component is generally the lowest level of the system an architect interacts with directly; class and function design belongs mostly to tech leads and developers, and architects should avoid micromanaging it so that the organization can empower the next generation of architects.

One of the first and most fundamental decisions an architect makes is the top-level partitioning of components: technical partitioning (separation of technical concerns, as in a layered monolith) versus domain partitioning (as in a modular monolith or microservices).

Technical partitioning lets developers find code by capability and decouples layers but smears each domain workflow across all layers, while domain partitioning aligns components with the business and eases migration to distributed systems but spreads customization code across multiple components.
The authors observe an industry trend over recent years toward domain partitioning for both monolithic and distributed architectures.

Conway's law states that organizations are constrained to produce designs that copy their communication structures, and the Inverse Conway Maneuver evolves team and organizational structure together to promote the desired architecture.
Developers should treat an architect's initial component design as a first draft and iterate on it, because implementation reveals more details and refinements.

Component identification works best as an iterative cycle: identify initial components, assign requirements to them, analyze roles and responsibilities, analyze architecture characteristics, then restructure components based on feedback.

Finding the proper component granularity is one of the hardest architect tasks: too fine-grained components require too much inter-component communication, while too coarse-grained components cause high internal coupling that hurts deployability, testability, and modularity.

The entity trap anti-pattern creates one Manager component per database entity, producing an object-relational mapping rather than an architecture; such components are too coarse-grained and signal a lack of thought about the application's actual workflows.

If the need is merely a simple mapping from a database to a user interface, a full-blown architecture is unnecessary and a CRUD or scaffolding framework such as Naked Objects or Rails scaffolding will suffice.
condition: the requirement is only simple database CRUD with a default user interface

statement: Component-discovery techniques (actor/actions, event storming, and the workflow approach) are not superior to one another; choose based on the team's process, using actor/actions for general or waterfall projects and event storming for DDD and microservices.

Architects should not obsess over finding the one true design; because many designs will suffice, they should objectively assess the trade-offs and choose the design with the least worst set of trade-offs.

The number of quanta discovered during design drives the monolith-versus-distributed decision: a single quantum (one set of architecture characteristics) favors a monolith, while components requiring different architecture characteristics require a distributed architecture.

An architecture style is the overarching structure of how the user interface and backend code are organized and how they interact with a datastore, whereas an architecture pattern is a lower-level design structure that forms a specific solution within a style.

Each architecture style embodies a well-known set of trade-offs and default architecture characteristics, so the style's name acts as shorthand among experienced architects for its topology, data strategies, and its beneficial and detrimental characteristics.

A Big Ball of Mud is an architecture with no discernible structure in which information is shared promiscuously until nearly everything is global or duplicated; architects should avoid it at all costs because its lack of structure makes change difficult and harms deployability, testability, scalability, and performance.
A Big Ball of Mud is rarely created intentionally; projects drift into it through a lack of governance around code quality and structure.

Architects should favor simple designs as a defense against the hard-to-predict long-term consequences of design decisions, as illustrated by Java baking serialization into the language for a three-tier era that later passed.
Architecture styles fall into two main types: monolithic, a single deployment unit of all code, and distributed, multiple deployment units connected through remote access protocols.

Distributed architectures are more powerful than monolithic ones in performance, scalability, and availability, but they incur significant trade-offs, beginning with the eight fallacies of distributed computing and other challenges absent from monoliths.

The eight fallacies of distributed computing, first coined by L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems in 1994, are assumptions believed true but false, and all eight still apply to distributed architectures today.

It is a fallacy that the network is reliable: networks remain generally unreliable, so distributed services need timeouts and circuit breakers, and the more a system relies on the network the potentially less reliable it becomes.

It is a fallacy that latency is zero: a remote call (milliseconds) is always slower than a local call (nanoseconds), so architects using a distributed architecture must know both the average latency and the 95th-to-99th percentile, since long-tail latency is what usually kills distributed performance.

It is a fallacy that bandwidth is infinite: stamp coupling (returning far more data than the caller needs) consumes large amounts of bandwidth, so architects should pass the minimal data between services using techniques such as field selectors, GraphQL, or consumer-driven contracts.

It is a fallacy that the network is secure: moving from monolithic to distributed magnifies the attack surface, so every endpoint including interservice communication must be secured, which also slows synchronous highly-distributed architectures.

It is a fallacy that the topology never changes: the network topology changes constantly and can silently invalidate latency assumptions, so architects must stay in constant communication with operations and network administrators.

It is a fallacy that there is only one administrator: a typical large company has dozens of network administrators, which raises the coordination cost and complexity of distributed architectures relative to monoliths.

It is a fallacy that transport cost is zero: distributed architectures cost significantly more than monolithic ones because of additional hardware, servers, gateways, firewalls, and proxies, so architects should analyze current capacity, bandwidth, latency, and security zones before going distributed.

It is a fallacy that the network is homogeneous: most companies use multiple network hardware vendors that do not always integrate seamlessly, causing occasional lost packets that feed back into the reliability, latency, and bandwidth fallacies.

Distributed architectures generally replace ACID transactions with eventual consistency (BASE: basic availability, soft state, eventual consistency), trading data consistency and integrity for scalability, performance, and availability, and use transactional sagas to manage distributed transactions.
condition: the operation spans separate deployment units or databases

statement: Distributed logging and contract maintenance and versioning are significantly harder in distributed than in monolithic architectures, because logs are scattered across many systems in different formats and contracts are owned by different teams.

The layered (n-tier) architecture is the de facto standard for most applications because of its simplicity, familiarity, and low cost, and it is a natural consequence of Conway's law since organizational roles map onto its tiers.

If a team is unsure which architecture style they are using, or an Agile team just starts coding, they are most likely building a layered architecture, an instance of the architecture-by-implication and accidental-architecture anti-patterns.

The layered architecture is technically partitioned, organizing components by technical role for separation of concerns, which spreads each business domain across all layers and makes a domain-driven design approach fit poorly.

By the layers-of-isolation concept, with closed layers a change in one layer does not affect other layers as long as the contracts between them are unchanged, allowing any layer to be replaced; layers in the major request flow must therefore be closed to preserve isolation.
condition: the contracts between layers remain unchanged

statement: The architecture sinkhole anti-pattern occurs when requests pass through layers with no business logic performed; apply the 80-20 rule, where about 20 percent sinkhole requests is acceptable but about 80 percent indicates the layered style is wrong for the problem domain.

The layered architecture is a good low-cost starting point for small or simple applications, and when the eventual style is still unknown, but its maintainability, agility, testability, and deployability are adversely affected as the application grows.

The layered architecture rates strong on cost and simplicity but low on deployability, testability, elasticity, scalability, and fault tolerance, because it is a monolithic single quantum with a high mean time to recovery.

In the pipeline architecture, pipes are unidirectional point-to-point communication channels and filters are self-contained, stateless, and each perform only one task, with composite work handled by a sequence of filters rather than a single filter.

The pipeline architecture has four filter types: producer (the source), transformer (map), tester (reduce), and consumer (the termination point), and the unidirectional simplicity of pipes and filters encourages compositional reuse.

The pipeline architecture is technically partitioned and, being monolithic, is always a single quantum; its strengths are cost, simplicity, and modularity (any filter can be changed or replaced independently), while elasticity, scalability, and fault tolerance are weak.

The microkernel (plug-in) architecture consists of a core system (the minimal functionality, or happy path) plus independent plug-in components, providing extensibility, adaptability, and isolation of custom or highly volatile logic.
Plug-in components should ideally be independent of each other with no dependencies between them, so that adding a capability is simply a matter of adding a new plug-in and updating the registry.
Moving custom or volatile rules out of the core system and into separate plug-in components removes cyclomatic complexity from the core and improves extensibility, maintainability, and testability.

Plug-in components can be compile-based, which are simpler but require redeploying the whole monolithic application when changed, or runtime-based, which can be added or removed at runtime without redeploying via frameworks such as OSGi, Jigsaw, or Prism.

The core system should locate plug-ins through a registry holding each plug-in's name, data contract, and access protocol, and when a third party controls a plug-in's contract the team should create an adapter so the core needs no specialized per-plug-in code.

Plug-in components should not connect directly to a centrally shared database; the core system owns shared data access so that a database change impacts only the core, though a plug-in may own its own private data store.
exception: a plug-in may have its own separate data store accessible only to that plug-in

statement: Making plug-in access remote turns the microkernel into a distributed architecture, gaining decoupling, scalability, and asynchronous communication but adding complexity, cost, and a new failure mode where an unresponsive plug-in fails the request, so the point-to-point-versus-remote choice requires trade-off analysis.
exception: with a monolithic point-to-point deployment an unresponsive plug-in would not fail the whole request

statement: The microkernel is the only architecture style that can be both domain-partitioned and technically partitioned, and it fits products that emphasize user customization and feature extensibility or that need different configurations per client or location.

Service-based architecture is a distributed hybrid of microservices and one of the most pragmatic styles, because it offers distributed flexibility without the full complexity and cost of microservices or event-driven architecture.

Service-based architecture is a distributed macro-layered structure with a separately deployed user interface, separately deployed coarse-grained domain services, and a typically shared monolithic database, usually comprising 4 to 12 services (about 7 on average).

In service-based architecture, interservice communication between domain services should be avoided, and when splitting the shared database the architect must ensure each database's data is not needed by another domain service.

Coarse-grained domain services allow regular ACID transactions and better data integrity within a single service, whereas fine-grained microservices rely on BASE eventual consistency and do not provide the same level of data integrity.

The coarse-grained service of service-based architecture carries a trade-off: a change requires testing and redeploying the whole service (more risk), whereas a single-responsibility microservice isolates the change to a small service.

To control database change in service-based architecture, logically partition the shared database and mirror the partitions with federated shared libraries of entity objects, keeping the partitioning as fine-grained as possible while maintaining well-defined data domains and locking common entity objects to the database team.

Orchestration coordinates multiple services through a separate central mediator that controls the workflow, while choreography coordinates services that talk to one another with no central mediator; both become necessary as services grow more fine-grained.

Service-based architecture preserves ACID transactions better than any other distributed architecture because of its coarse-grained domain services, so most transactions stay within one service and use ordinary commit and rollback.
exception: when a user interface or API gateway orchestrates two or more domain services, the transaction must rely on sagas and BASE

statement: Service-based architecture is a good way to achieve architectural modularity without the granularity pitfalls of finer-grained services, because coarse-grained services require far less orchestration and choreography.

In a service-based architecture the number of quanta is greater than or equal to one: services sharing a single database and user interface form one quantum, while federating the user interface and database yields multiple quanta.

In the request-based model a request orchestrator deterministically and synchronously directs data-driven requests to request processors, whereas in the event-based model the system reacts to a situation and takes action based on that event.

Choose the request-based model for well-structured, data-driven requests where certainty and control over the workflow are needed, and choose the event-based model for flexible, action-based events that require high responsiveness and scale with complex, dynamic processing.

The broker topology of event-driven architecture has no central mediator: events flow chain-like through a lightweight broker using publish-subscribe topics, making event processors highly decoupled, scalable, responsive, performant, and fault-tolerant.

In the broker topology each event processor should advertise what it did to the rest of the system regardless of whether any processor is currently listening, which provides architectural extensibility because new processors can later tap that event feed without changing existing processors or infrastructure.

The broker topology's weaknesses are lack of workflow control, difficult error handling, no recoverability or restart, and data inconsistency, because no component owns the state of the original business transaction.

The mediator topology of event-driven architecture uses a central event mediator that knows and controls the workflow, generating processing events to dedicated queues, and its event processors do not advertise what they did to the rest of the system.

Because the mediator maintains event state, the mediator topology supports workflow control, error handling, recoverability, restart, and better data consistency, at the cost of more coupling among event processors, lower scalability, lower performance, lower fault tolerance, and difficulty modeling complex workflows.

In the broker topology processing occurrences are events (things that have already happened and can be ignored), whereas in the mediator topology they are commands (things that need to happen and must be processed).
Choosing between the broker and mediator topologies comes down to a trade-off between workflow control and error-handling capability versus higher performance and scalability.

Because events rarely share one class of complexity, classify events as simple, hard, or complex and route every event through a simple mediator that either handles it or forwards it to a more complex mediator (the mediator delegation model).

Choose the event-mediator implementation by event complexity: a simple integration hub such as Apache Camel for simple flows, BPEL for complex dynamic workflows, and a BPM engine such as jBPM for long-running flows that require human intervention, because mismatching the engine to the event wastes large amounts of effort.

Responsiveness and performance are different: responsiveness notifies the user that an action is accepted and will be processed (achievable with asynchronous communication), while performance makes the end-to-end process faster; improving one does not necessarily improve the other.

The main drawback of asynchronous communication is error handling, because a significantly improved responsiveness comes with the difficulty of addressing error conditions when there is no synchronous caller to respond to.

The workflow event pattern of reactive architecture handles asynchronous errors through delegation, containment, and repair: the event consumer immediately delegates an error to a workflow processor and moves to the next message, preserving responsiveness, and messages that cannot be repaired automatically go to a dashboard for manual fixing and resubmission.

A consequence of the workflow event pattern is that repaired messages are reprocessed out of sequence, so preserving message order within a context requires extra work such as queueing same-context messages until the errored one is fixed.
condition: the order of messages within a given context matters

statement: The three data-loss points in asynchronous messaging are mitigated by persistent queues plus synchronous send (producer to queue), client acknowledge mode (queue to a crashing consumer), and an ACID database commit plus last participant support (consumer to database).

Broadcasting is the highest level of decoupling between event processors because the producer publishes a message with no knowledge of which processors receive it or what they do, and it underpins patterns for eventual consistency and complex event processing.

When synchronous communication is needed in event-driven architecture, use request-reply (pseudosynchronous) messaging with a request queue and a reply queue, implemented with a correlation ID (preferred) or a temporary reply queue (simpler but able to slow the broker at high volume).

Event-driven architecture is primarily technically partitioned because a domain is spread across many event processors, and its quanta range from one to many depending on shared databases and synchronous request-reply ties, since a needed immediate reply binds two event processors into the same quantum.

Event-driven architecture rates highest for performance, scalability, and fault tolerance (through asynchronous parallel processing, competing consumers, and eventual consistency) and is highly evolutionary, but rates low on simplicity and testability because of its nondeterministic, dynamic event flows.

Space-based architecture removes the central database as a synchronous constraint by keeping application data in replicated in-memory data grids and persisting asynchronously through data pumps, achieving high scalability, elasticity, and concurrency for variable, unpredictable user volumes.

In a traditional web topology, scaling out one tier usually just moves the bottleneck down to the next tier, and the database is the hardest and most expensive to scale and the final limiting factor under high concurrency.

Space-based architecture comprises a processing unit (application logic plus an in-memory data grid and replication engine), virtualized middleware (messaging grid, data grid, processing grid, and deployment manager), data pumps, data writers, and data readers.
The deployment manager achieves variable scalability (elasticity) by continually monitoring response times and user load and dynamically starting up and shutting down processing-unit instances.

Data pumps in space-based architecture are always asynchronous, usually messaging with guaranteed delivery and FIFO order, giving eventual consistency between the in-memory cache and the database and decoupling the processing unit from the data writer so processing continues even if the writer is unavailable.

Space-based architecture generally relies on a data abstraction layer rather than a data access layer, decoupling processing units from the database table structures via contracts so the cache schema can differ from the database and the database can change incrementally without impacting the processing units.

Replicated active/active caching risks data collisions caused by replication latency, where the collision rate rises with the number of instances and the update rate and falls with lower replication latency and larger cache size, so the rate should be computed to judge whether replicated caching is feasible.

A powerful option unique to space-based architecture is deploying processing units and virtualized middleware in elastic cloud environments while keeping the physical database on-premises, made possible by the asynchronous data pumps and eventual-consistency model.

Replicated caching gives each processing unit its own in-memory data grid kept in sync across units, offering high speed and fault tolerance with no single point of failure, whereas distributed caching uses an external central cache server, offering better data consistency but lower performance and a single point of failure.

Replicated caching cannot be used when the cache is too large (internal caches over about 100 MB strain elasticity and scalability) or the update rate is too high for the replication engine to keep consistent; in those situations distributed caching should be used.
condition: the cache exceeds roughly 100 MB or the update rate is too high for the replication engine

statement: When cache size and update rate are manageable, the choice between replicated and distributed caching is data consistency versus performance and fault tolerance; both models are usually applicable in one application, so use a distributed cache for highly dynamic, consistency-critical data and a replicated cache for relatively static reference data.

The authors do not recommend the near-cache model for space-based architecture, because the per-processing-unit front caches are not synchronized with each other, creating inconsistencies in data and responsiveness between processing units.

Space-based architecture is well suited to applications with high, variable, and unpredictable load spikes and throughput in excess of about 10,000 concurrent users, such as online concert ticketing and online auction systems.

Space-based architecture maximizes elasticity, scalability, and performance by using in-memory caching to remove the database constraint, but trades off simplicity and testability and is relatively expensive, and its extreme-load testing is so difficult that it often must happen in production.

In space-based architecture the database is not part of the quantum equation because processing units do not communicate synchronously with it; quanta are delineated by the association between user interfaces and synchronously communicating processing units.

Orchestration-driven service-oriented architecture centered on enterprise-level reuse and pushed technical partitioning to an extreme, with a taxonomy of business, enterprise, application, and infrastructure services stitched together by a central orchestration engine.

Building a system primarily around reuse incurs heavy coupling, so a change to a shared canonical service such as a single Customer service ripples out to all consumers, making incremental change risky and forcing coordinated deployments and holistic testing.

Consolidating all behavior into a single canonical service forces every consumer to carry details it does not need, such as a single Customer service exposing driver's-license data that the disability-insurance division cares nothing about, adding unnecessary complexity.

In orchestration-driven SOA the orchestration engine is a giant coupling point that prevents any part from having different architecture characteristics, and Conway's law predicts its integration-architect team becomes a bureaucratic bottleneck, so the style ends up combining the disadvantages of both monolithic and distributed architectures.

Orchestration-driven SOA taught architects how difficult distributed transactions are in practice and the practical limits of technical partitioning, and the backlash against it led to more modern architectures such as microservices.

Microservices is heavily inspired by domain-driven design's bounded context: a context's internal code and data schemas are coupled together internally but never coupled to anything outside the context, so each context defines only what it needs rather than accommodating other constituents.

Reuse and decoupling are opposing forces, so favoring reuse also favors coupling through inheritance or composition; when the goal is high decoupling, favor duplication over reuse, which is why the primary goal of microservices is high decoupling.

Microservices is a distributed architecture in which each service runs in its own process, VM, or container, so performance is a common negative side effect because network calls and per-endpoint security checks add overhead, making service granularity the key to success.
The term microservice is a label, not a description, so architects often make services too fine-grained, which forces them to build communication links back between the services to do useful work.

Find microservice boundaries by purpose (one functionally cohesive behavior), by transactions (entities that must cooperate in a transaction suggest a boundary, and designing to avoid distributed transactions yields better designs), and by choreography (bundle services back together if they require extensive communication); iteration is the only way to ensure good service design.

Microservices requires data isolation: avoid shared schemas and databases used as integration points, give each service its own database, and choose a single source of truth or use replication and caching, which also lets each service select the most appropriate database for its needs.

A microservices API layer is optional and should not be used as a mediator or orchestration tool, because all interesting logic should occur inside a bounded context; mediators belong to technically partitioned architectures, whereas microservices is firmly domain partitioned.

Microservices separates domain reuse from operational reuse: the sidecar pattern places shared operational concerns such as monitoring, logging, and circuit breakers into each service, the connected sidecars form a service mesh for unified operational control, and service discovery provides elasticity.

Microservices communication is either synchronous or asynchronous, and services typically use protocol-aware heterogeneous interoperability where each service knows or discovers the protocol to call others and the architecture supports polyglot technology stacks, so mandating different stacks can even be used to enforce decoupling.

In microservices the broker and mediator event-driven patterns appear as choreography (no central coordinator, preserving the bounded-context decoupling) and orchestration (a localized mediator); choreography reaps the style's benefits but makes error handling and coordination more complex.

Domain/architecture isomorphism describes how the shape of a problem maps onto an architecture style, and because microservices favors decoupling its shape resembles broker event-driven architecture, making those two patterns symbiotic.

When a choreographed service must coordinate across many others it becomes a de facto mediator (the front controller pattern), adding complexity, whereas orchestration concentrates coordination in a single mediator service at the cost of coupling.

Architects should not build transactions across microservice boundaries, because doing so violates the decoupling principle and creates connascence of value (the worst dynamic connascence); fix the service granularity instead, since transaction boundaries indicate granularity.
exception: occasionally two services need vastly different architecture characteristics yet still need transactional coordination, where saga-style patterns apply with serious trade-offs

statement: The saga pattern coordinates a distributed transaction through a mediator using compensating transactions that undo successful steps when a later step fails, but it is complex, so it should be used sparingly: a few cross-service transactions can be necessary, but if they dominate the architecture, the granularity was wrong.

Microservices rates highest for scalability, elasticity, and evolutionary change and depends on the DevOps revolution and automation; performance is often an issue because of network calls and per-endpoint security, and fault tolerance is high for single-purpose services under normal conditions but degrades with excessive interservice communication.
Microservices has the most distinct quanta of any modern architecture and exemplifies the quantum measure, because each service boundary should correspond to a domain.

There is no universally correct architecture style; the choice is highly contextual, and preferred styles shift over time due to past observations, ecosystem and domain and technology changes, new capabilities, acceleration, and external factors, so architects must understand industry trends to know when to follow and when to make exceptions.

When choosing an architecture style an architect should understand the domain, the architecture characteristics that impact structure, the data architecture, organizational factors, the process/team/operational context, and domain/architecture isomorphism.

The core determinations when choosing a style are monolith versus distributed (a single set of architecture characteristics implies a monolith, while differing characteristics imply a distributed architecture), where data should live, and synchronous versus asynchronous communication.

Architects should default to synchronous communication and use asynchronous only when necessary, because synchronous presents fewer design, implementation, and debugging challenges, whereas asynchronous brings data synchronization, deadlocks, race conditions, and debugging headaches.

Performing quantum analysis at the component-design stage lets an architect identify service, data, and communication boundaries earlier, as in the Going, Going, Gone case study which resolved to five quanta with the least worst set of trade-offs.

A good architecture decision is one that helps guide development teams toward the right technical choice, and making it involves gathering enough relevant information, justifying the decision, documenting it, and effectively communicating it to the right stakeholders.

The Covering Your Assets anti-pattern is avoiding or deferring an architecture decision out of fear of being wrong; overcome it by deciding at the last responsible moment and by continually collaborating with development teams so a flawed decision can be adjusted quickly.

The Groundhog Day anti-pattern is re-discussing a decision repeatedly because no one knows why it was made; overcome it by providing both a technical and a business justification, since whether a decision has business value is also a litmus test for whether it should be made.

The Email-Driven Architecture anti-pattern is decisions being lost, forgotten, or unknown; avoid it by not placing the decision in an email body but linking to a single system of record, and notifying only the stakeholders the decision directly impacts.

An architecturally significant decision, in Michael Nygard's term, is one that affects the structure, nonfunctional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques, so a technology choice becomes an architecture decision when it supports an important architecture characteristic.

An Architecture Decision Record is a short one-to-two-page text file with the sections Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences (often plus Compliance and Notes); its Status is Proposed, Accepted, or Superseded, and the Superseded status with a bidirectional link trail preserves a historical record of why a decision changed.

Use a Request for Comments (RFC) ADR status with a stated deadline to gather stakeholder input on a draft decision, which avoids the Analysis Paralysis anti-pattern of a decision being discussed forever but never made.

Establish and document explicit criteria for when an architect may self-approve a decision versus escalate it, with cost, cross-team impact, and security as a good starting set; decisions that impact other teams or systems or have security implications cannot be self-approved.
The Context section of an ADR states the forces at play (the situation forcing the decision) and concisely documents the relevant area of the architecture and the alternatives considered.

State the ADR Decision in an affirmative, commanding voice (we will) rather than a passive one, and use the section to emphasize why the decision was made over how it works, because understanding the why prevents costly mistaken refactorings later.
The Consequences section of an ADR documents the overall impact of the decision and its trade-off analysis, forcing the architect to weigh whether the impacts outweigh the benefits.
Add a Compliance section to each ADR that specifies how the decision will be measured and governed, deciding whether the compliance check must be manual or can be automated with a fitness function.

Store each ADR in its own file or wiki page, and for larger organizations prefer a wiki or shared file server over the source-code Git repository, because not everyone has repo access and some decisions (integration or enterprise) are outside the application's context.

ADRs are an effective way to document both architecture and standards because the Decision section records why; if an architect cannot justify a standard then it probably should not exist, and developers who understand why a standard exists are more likely to follow it.
Every architecture decision made in a system, no matter how obvious, should be documented and justified.

Qualify architecture risk with a risk matrix that multiplies impact (low 1, medium 2, high 3) by likelihood (1 to 3), giving 1-2 low, 3-4 medium, and 6-9 high risk, and consider the impact dimension first and the likelihood dimension second.

A risk assessment summarizes architecture risk by assessment criteria and domain area; filter it to the message relevant for the audience and show the direction of risk (for example with plus and minus signs), which can be derived from continuous fitness-function measurements.

Risk storming is a collaborative exercise in which participants first identify risk individually and noncollaboratively (so they do not influence one another) using the risk matrix, then collaborate to reach consensus and mitigate, ideally restricted to a single risk dimension per session.

Include senior developers and tech leads in risk storming, not just architects, because they add an implementation perspective and learn the architecture, and a developer's unfamiliarity with a technology is itself valuable information about risk.
Always assign the highest risk rating to any unproven or unknown technology, because the impact-times-likelihood risk matrix cannot be applied to that dimension.

Risk mitigation usually incurs additional cost, so key stakeholders must decide whether the cost outweighs the risk, and risk storming is a continuous process repeated through a system's life (for example after a major feature or at the end of each iteration), not a one-time exercise.

The risk matrix also applies to Agile story risk: rate the impact of a story not being completed in the iteration against the likelihood it will not be completed, to identify, track, and prioritize high-risk stories.

Representational consistency is the practice of always showing the relationship of a part to the overall architecture before drilling into that part, in both diagrams and presentations, to eliminate a common source of viewer confusion.

Use low-fidelity, ephemeral artifacts early in design to avoid the Irrational Artifact Attachment anti-pattern (attachment proportional to the time invested in an artifact), and move to a polished diagramming tool only after the design has iterated enough.

UML class and sequence diagrams remain useful while most other UML diagram types have fallen into disuse; C4 (context, container, component, class) is a good diagramming standard best suited to monolithic architectures and less suited to distributed ones; ArchiMate is a deliberately lightweight enterprise modeling language.

A near-universal diagram convention is that solid lines indicate synchronous communication and dotted lines indicate asynchronous communication, and diagrams should also use clear titles, labels, consistent shapes, judicious color, and a key whenever shapes are ambiguous.

Because in a presentation the presenter (not the reader) controls the pace, architects should manipulate time using transitions and animations and use incremental builds to reveal information as needed, avoiding the Bullet-Riddled Corpse anti-pattern of slides that are just projected speaker notes.

A presenter has two information channels, verbal and visual, so overloading the visual channel with text that the speaker then repeats starves the verbal channel, and the Invisibility pattern (a blank slide) refocuses all attention on the speaker.
Slides are only half of a presentation, the other half being the speaker, so a deck comprehensive enough to stand alone is an infodeck meant to be read rather than presented.

An architect is responsible for guiding the development team through implementing the architecture rather than handing off a siloed design, and being able to make teams productive is a key way effective architects differentiate themselves.

An architect creates the constraints (the box) within which developers implement the architecture; boundaries that are too tight or too loose both harm the team, and an effective architect provides just the right level of guidance and constraints.

Three architect personalities map to boundary types: the control freak architect creates tight boundaries by micromanaging class design and patterns and stealing the art of programming, the armchair architect creates loose boundaries by being disconnected and too high-level, and the effective architect creates just-right boundaries.

The architect's role is to define components and the interactions between them, while determining a component's internal class design and design patterns is the developer's role, which the architect should not usurp.

How much control an architect should exert (Elastic Leadership) depends on five factors, team familiarity, team size, overall experience, project complexity, and project duration, and these should be reassessed continually throughout the project's life cycle.

A shorter project duration calls for less architect control and a longer duration for more, because a short project already carries urgency that a control freak would only delay, while a long project's relaxed pace needs more guidance to keep moving.

Three warning signs indicate a development team is too large: process loss (Brooks's law, where adding people increases time and frequent merge conflicts are a symptom, mitigated by parallelizing work), pluralistic ignorance (members publicly agree to but privately reject a norm, which the architect should surface), and diffusion of responsibility (responsibilities get dropped as the team grows).

Checklists demonstrably work, as shown by The Checklist Manifesto where surgical checklists drove hospital staph-infection rates to near zero, so software teams should leverage them, but selectively rather than for everything.

Good checklist candidates are processes with no procedural order or dependent tasks that are error-prone or have frequently missed steps, whereas processes with a procedural flow of dependent tasks and simple, frequent, error-free processes are bad candidates.
Keep checklists as small as possible and remove items that can be automated, because making too many or too-large checklists invokes the law of diminishing returns and developers stop following them.
Do not omit the obvious from a checklist, because it is the obvious steps that are usually the ones skipped or missed.

The Hawthorne effect, where people change behavior when they know they are being observed, can be used to govern checklist use: tell the team checklists will be verified while in practice only occasionally spot-checking them.

Three high-value checklists are the developer code-completion checklist (which defines done), the unit-and-functional-testing checklist (covering edge cases and growing with every QA-found defect), and the software-release checklist (covering the most error-prone phase and growing with the root cause of each failed deployment).

An architect provides guidance through design principles that form the box developers work in; for a proposed third-party library the developer should be required to analyze overlap with existing functionality and to provide both a technical and a business justification.

Requiring a business justification, not just a technical one, for a desired technology is a powerful technique that creates awareness and can transform disruptive behavior, as when a developer pushing to adopt Scala realized it offered no business value in cost, budget, or timeline and became a productive team member.

Give developers tiered decision authority by library category, for example letting them decide special-purpose libraries themselves, recommend general-purpose libraries with overlap analysis subject to architect approval, and leaving highly invasive framework libraries as an architect decision.

Making development teams effective is genuinely the software architect's responsibility, not only the development or project manager's, and it is what differentiates a merely technical architect from an effective one.

Leverage grammar and buzzwords in a negotiation to uncover the stakeholder's real concern, since phrases like zero downtime indicate that availability matters and I needed it yesterday indicates that time to market matters.

Gather as much information as possible before a negotiation and translate vague vernacular into concrete terms (for example expressing nines of availability as actual hours and seconds of downtime), reserving cost and time as a last-resort argument rather than an opening one.
Use divide and conquer in a negotiation by qualifying which specific part of the system truly needs a costly requirement, which reduces the scope of the difficult demand and of the negotiation.

When negotiating with another architect, remember that demonstration defeats discussion: run a comparison in a production-like environment rather than arguing, because every environment differs, and avoid letting the exchange become personal, since calm leadership with clear, concise reasoning wins.

When negotiating with developers, do not leverage the architect title (the Ivory Tower anti-pattern) but provide the justification first, before the listener stops listening, and phrase requests as statements of fact rather than as you must commands.

When a developer disagrees with a decision, have them try to demonstrate their alternative themselves: either they fail and gain firsthand buy-in for the original decision, or they succeed and reveal a better option, making it a win either way.
About half of being an effective software architect is people, facilitation, and leadership skills rather than technical knowledge.

Architects should avoid accidental complexity (making a problem hard) as distinct from essential complexity (having a hard problem) by applying the 4 C's of architecture: communication, collaboration, clarity, and conciseness.

An effective software architect must be pragmatic yet visionary, balancing imagination and wisdom about the future with practical constraints such as budget, time, team skill, trade-offs, and technical limitations.
Effective architects lead by example rather than by title to gain respect, recognizing that no matter what the problem is, it is ultimately a people problem.

Use collaborative grammar such as have you considered or what about instead of commanding grammar such as you must or what you need to do in order to keep collaboration open, and use people's names to build familiarity and respect.

Turning a request into a personal favor, by admitting a bind and asking for help, often succeeds where a direct demand fails, because people dislike being told what to do but generally want to help others.

An architect should become the go-to person on the team by taking initiative to help with technical and personal struggles and by hosting periodic brown-bag lunches to mentor and demonstrate expertise.

An architect should control meetings to make more time for the team: for imposed-upon meetings ask why attendance is needed and request the agenda in advance, and for meetings they call, keep them minimal, set an agenda, and respect developer flow by scheduling them at the start of the day, after lunch, or at the end rather than mid-day.

An architect should physically integrate with the development team by sitting with them, or at least walking around and being seen, because isolation in a separate office or cubicle prevents guiding and mentoring the team.

An architect must keep learning continuously because technology changes at a rapid pace, and being heavily invested in a single technology creates a dangerous memetic bubble and echo chamber that collapses without warning from the inside.

Apply the 20-minute rule by spending at least 20 minutes a day developing technical breadth, ideally first thing in the morning before checking email, because lunch and evening attempts rarely actually happen.

An architect should maintain a personal technology radar, a living document with four quadrants (tools, languages and frameworks, techniques, platforms) and four rings (hold, assess, trial, adopt), to formalize and structure technology assessment.

Treat a technology portfolio like a financial portfolio and diversify it, tracking widely in-demand skills while also trying technology gambits such as open source or mobile, reinforcing the value of breadth over depth.

A person's next job is more likely to come from a weak link than a strong one, so architects should follow respected technologists on social media to feed the assess ring of their radar with ideas from outside their normal experience.
Practice is the proven way to build architecture skill, and there is no answer key for architecture katas because there are no right or wrong answers in architecture, only trade-offs.
The goal of software architecture is to minimize the human resources required to build and maintain the required system.
There is no meaningful distinction between design and architecture; low-level details and high-level structure form one continuum of decisions.
Design quality is measured by the effort required to meet customer needs: the design is good if that effort stays low across the system lifetime, and bad if it grows with each release.
When code cleanliness and design structure are neglected, developer productivity declines release over release toward zero while cost per line of code rises sharply.
condition: systems are thrown together in a hurry and headcount is the sole driver of output

statement: Developers should take responsibility for software-architecture quality continuously rather than relying on a later cleanup, because the promised cleanup never arrives under sustained market pressure.
Making messes is always slower than staying clean, on every time scale.

In Jason Gorman's six-day controlled experiment, the test-driven-development days completed roughly 10% faster than the non-TDD days, and even the slowest TDD day was faster than the fastest non-TDD day.
A from-scratch redesign undertaken by the same overconfident team reproduces the original mess rather than escaping it.
The only way to go fast is to go well.
Every software system delivers two distinct values to stakeholders: its behavior and its structure (architecture).

Architecture (the ability to change the system) is the greater long-term value: a program that works but cannot change becomes useless once requirements change, whereas a program that does not yet work but is easy to change can be made to work and kept working.
Software must remain soft: the difficulty of a change should be proportional only to the scope of the change, not to its shape.
