The more an architecture prefers one shape of change over another, the harder new features become to fit into that structure.
condition: the architecture favors one shape of change over others

statement: Architectures should be kept as shape-agnostic as is practical.
Behavior is urgent but not always important, while architecture is important but never urgent (Eisenhower's importance-versus-urgency distinction).

The software development team is responsible for asserting the importance of architecture over the urgency of features, because business managers are not equipped to evaluate architecture's importance.
A software developer is a stakeholder in the system and must actively struggle with other stakeholders to safeguard the architecture.
If architecture is addressed last, the system becomes ever more costly to develop and eventually change becomes practically impossible for part or all of it.
condition: architecture is deferred behind features

statement: There are three programming paradigms (structured, object-oriented, functional), and they are likely the only three because each removes a capability and little remains to remove.
Structured programming imposes discipline on direct transfer of control by removing unrestricted goto.
Object-oriented programming imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control via polymorphism.
Functional programming imposes discipline upon assignment through immutability.
Each programming paradigm removes a capability from the programmer rather than adding one; the paradigms tell us what not to do.

The three paradigms align with the three core concerns of architecture: structured programming with function, object-oriented programming with separation of components, and functional programming with data management.
All programs can be constructed from just three control structures — sequence, selection, and iteration (Boehm and Jacopini).
Structured programming lets a program be recursively decomposed into small, individually provable (falsifiable) functions.
Software is like a science: correctness is established by failing to prove incorrectness, since tests can show the presence of bugs but never their absence.
Architects should define modules, components, and services that are easily falsifiable (testable), applying restrictive disciplines analogous to structured programming at a higher level.
To the software architect, object orientation is the ability, through polymorphism, to gain absolute control over every source-code dependency in the system.
Polymorphism allows any source-code dependency to be inverted by inserting an interface, so the source-code dependency can point opposite to the flow of control (dependency inversion).
Source-code dependencies should be arranged so that the user interface and the database depend on the business rules, making the UI and database plugins to the business rules.
When dependencies point inward to the business rules, the business rules can be compiled, deployed, and developed independently of the UI and the database.
When a component's source code changes, only that component needs to be redeployed (independent deployability).
condition: modules are partitioned so dependencies do not cross component boundaries outward

statement: Object orientation's architectural contribution is making polymorphism safe and convenient, not adding a capability that was previously impossible.
A plugin architecture should be used so that modules containing high-level policy are independent of modules containing low-level detail.
Variables in functional languages do not vary; symbols are initialized but never modified.
All race conditions, deadlocks, and concurrent-update problems arise from mutable variables, and none of them can occur if no variable is ever updated.

Architects should segregate an application into immutable and mutable components, pushing as much processing as possible into the immutable components and driving as much code as possible out of the mutable ones.
condition: the application has concurrency concerns

statement: Mutable state that cannot be eliminated should be protected with transactional memory (a transaction- or retry-based scheme) to guard against concurrent updates and race conditions.
condition: mutation cannot be eliminated

statement: Immutability is practicable in real systems only when compromises (mutability segregation, transactional memory, event sourcing) are made, since unconditional immutability would require infinite storage and processing.
condition: bounded storage and processing are available

statement: Event sourcing stores the transactions rather than the resulting state and recomputes state by replaying transactions, eliminating mutable variables and therefore concurrent-update issues.
condition: enough storage and processing exist for the application's reasonable lifetime

statement: The rules of software architecture are independent of language, paradigm, and hardware and have not changed since 1946, because software is still composed of sequence, selection, iteration, and indirection.
The SOLID principles aim to create mid-level software structures that tolerate change, are easy to understand, and serve as reusable building blocks across many systems.
A 'class' in the SOLID sense is any cohesive grouping of functions and data, so the SOLID principles apply to every software system whether or not its language has classes.
The Single Responsibility Principle states that a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor (have one, and only one, reason to change).
An 'actor' is the group of one or more people who require a particular change to the system.
To satisfy the SRP, separate the code that different actors depend on into different modules.
Cohesion is the force that binds together the code responsible to a single actor.
Violating the SRP produces accidental duplication: when a shared subfunction serves two actors, a change demanded by one actor can silently corrupt behavior the other depends on.
Violating the SRP causes risky merges, because many methods responsible to different actors in one source file collide when changed concurrently.
The SRP recurs at higher levels: at the component level it becomes the Common Closure Principle, and at the architectural level it defines the axis of change that creates architectural boundaries.
The Open-Closed Principle states that a software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification, so behavior can be extended by adding code rather than changing existing code.
If simple extensions to the requirements force massive changes to the software, the architects have failed.

At the architectural level the OCP is realized by partitioning the system into components arranged in a dependency hierarchy that protects higher-level components from changes in lower-level components.
To protect component A from changes in component B, make component B depend on component A; dependency arrows should point toward the components you want to protect.
The component holding the highest-level policies (the business rules) should occupy the most protected position and depend only on abstractions, while peripheral concerns depend on it.
Insert interfaces to practice information hiding, preventing higher-level components from acquiring transitive dependencies on the internals of the components they use.
The Liskov Substitution Principle requires that subtypes be substitutable for their base types without changing the correctness of any program written in terms of the base type.
The LSP extends beyond class inheritance to any interface-and-implementation relationship, including Java-style interfaces, duck-typed classes, and services sharing a REST interface.
A single violation of substitutability can pollute a system's architecture with significant extra special-case mechanisms (added if-statements or configuration).
Do not hard-code a specific identifier to special-case a non-substitutable variant; drive the variation from a configuration database instead.
The Interface Segregation Principle advises designers to avoid depending on things they do not use.
Depending on a module that carries more than you need can force unnecessary recompilation and redeployment and can propagate that module's failures into yours.

In statically typed languages, import/include declarations create the source-code dependencies that force recompilation and redeployment, which is why dynamically typed languages tend to produce more flexible, less tightly coupled systems.
condition: the language is statically rather than dynamically typed

statement: The Dependency Inversion Principle states that the most flexible systems are those whose source-code dependencies refer only to abstractions, not to concretions.
It is the volatile concrete elements that you must avoid depending on; stable, nonvolatile platform facilities such as the String class are tolerable concrete dependencies.
exception: the concretion is a stable, nonvolatile platform/OS facility unlikely to change

statement: Interfaces are less volatile than their implementations, and good designers work to add functionality to implementations without changing the interfaces.

The DIP reduces to concrete coding practices: refer to abstract interfaces rather than volatile concrete classes, do not derive from or override volatile concretions, and create volatile concrete objects through Abstract Factories.
DIP violations cannot be entirely eliminated, but they can and should be gathered into a small number of concrete components (such as main) kept separate from the rest of the system.
The main component is the ultimate low-level/concrete detail: it instantiates the concrete implementations and injects them into the application behind abstractions.
Components are the units of deployment — the smallest entities that can be deployed as part of a system (jar files, gem files, DLLs).
Well-designed components always retain the ability to be independently deployable and therefore independently developable.

The Reuse/Release Equivalence Principle states that the granule of reuse is the granule of release: reusable components must be tracked through a release process with release numbers and documentation.
The classes and modules grouped into a component must share an overarching theme or purpose and be releasable together, not a random hodgepodge.

The Common Closure Principle says to gather into one component the classes that change for the same reasons at the same times and to separate those that change for different reasons or at different times; it is the SRP restated for components.
For most applications, maintainability is more important than reusability.
condition: the typical application, where change is ongoing

statement: Closure must be strategic: because 100% closure is unattainable, design classes to be closed against the most common kinds of change you expect or have experienced.

The Common Reuse Principle says not to force users of a component to depend on things they do not need: keep tightly coupled classes that are reused together in one component, and keep loosely related classes in separate components.
The Common Reuse Principle is the component-level generalization of the Interface Segregation Principle.

The three component-cohesion principles conflict (REP and CCP are inclusive and enlarge components, while CRP is exclusive and shrinks them), and good architects resolve the tension for the team's current concerns.
Early in a project develop-ability (CCP) matters more than reuse (REP), and the balance shifts as the project matures, so a component's composition is dynamic and evolves over time.
condition: as the project moves from early development toward being reused by other projects

statement: The Acyclic Dependencies Principle requires that the component dependency graph contain no cycles (be a directed acyclic graph).
Cycles in the component dependency graph make components hard to isolate, hard to unit-test, hard to order for building, and hard to release.
Break a dependency cycle either by applying the DIP (insert an interface to invert one edge) or by extracting the shared classes into a new component that both former participants depend on.
The component dependency structure cannot be designed top-down; it evolves with the system and maps the buildability and maintainability of the application rather than its function.
A primary goal of the component dependency structure is isolation of volatility: protect stable, high-value components from components that change frequently and capriciously.
The Stable Dependencies Principle says to depend in the direction of stability: a component intended to be volatile must not be depended on by a component that is hard to change.
Stability is the amount of work required to change a component; a component with many incoming dependencies is stable because changes must be reconciled with all its dependents.
Instability is measured as I = Fan-out / (Fan-in + Fan-out) in [0,1] (I=0 maximally stable, I=1 maximally unstable), and the SDP requires I to decrease in the direction of dependency.
Not all components should be stable; if every component were maximally stable the system would be unchangeable.

The Stable Abstractions Principle says a component should be as abstract as it is stable, so stable components should consist of interfaces and abstract classes whose stability does not block extension.
High-level policy should be placed in stable components (I near 0), while volatile code that must change easily belongs in unstable components (I near 1).
The SDP and SAP combined are the DIP for components: since dependencies run toward stability and stability implies abstraction, dependencies run in the direction of abstraction.
Abstractness is measured as A = Na/Nc in [0,1], and the Main Sequence is the line A+I=1 on which well-balanced components should sit or lie close.
Keep components out of the Zone of Pain (stable and concrete, e.g., a volatile database schema, hence rigid) and the Zone of Uselessness (abstract with no dependents).
Distance from the Main Sequence is D = |A + I - 1|; components whose D is far from zero, or whose D drifts over successive releases, should be re-examined and restructured.
Dependency-management metrics are imperfect measurements against an arbitrary standard, not absolute truth.
A software architect is and remains a programmer — among the best programmers — who keeps taking programming tasks so as to experience the problems being created for the rest of the team.
A system's architecture is the shape given to it by its builders: the division of the system into components, the arrangement of those components, and the ways they communicate.
The purpose of architecture is to facilitate the development, deployment, operation, and maintenance of the system, not primarily to make the system work.
The strategy of software architecture is to leave as many options open as possible, for as long as possible.
Architecture has little bearing on whether a system works: poorly architected systems can work fine, but they suffer in deployment, maintenance, and ongoing development.
The ultimate goal of good architecture is to minimize the lifetime cost of the system and to maximize programmer productivity.
A system that is hard to develop is unlikely to have a long, healthy life, so the architecture should make the system easy to develop for the team(s) building it.

Different team structures imply different architectural decisions, and a system driven solely by development schedule will gravitate toward a component-per-team structure even when that is not best for deployment, operation, or maintenance.
condition: the architecture is driven solely by development/team-schedule concerns

statement: A goal of architecture is that the system can be deployed easily with a single action and be immediately deployable after build, not relying on dozens of configuration scripts or manual setup steps.

Deployment strategy is seldom considered during initial development, which yields architectures that are easy to develop but very difficult to deploy (such as an unmanageable explosion of micro-services).

Architecture's impact on operation is less dramatic than its impact on development, deployment, and maintenance, because most operational difficulties can be resolved by adding hardware, and hardware is cheap while people are expensive.
A good architecture communicates and reveals the operational needs of the system, elevating use cases, features, and required behaviors to first-class, visible landmarks for developers.
Maintenance is the most costly aspect of a software system, and its primary costs are spelunking (digging through code to find where to change) and the risk of introducing inadvertent defects.

A carefully designed architecture mitigates maintenance cost by separating the system into components isolated behind stable interfaces, illuminating pathways for new features and reducing the risk of inadvertent breakage.
Keep software soft by leaving as many options open as possible for as long as possible; the options worth leaving open are the details that do not matter.

Every software system decomposes into policy (the business rules and procedures where the system's true value lives) and details (IO devices, databases, web systems, servers, frameworks, protocols) that merely enable communication with the policy.
The architect's goal is to shape the system so that policy is the most essential element and the details are irrelevant to it, allowing decisions about those details to be delayed and deferred.

It is unnecessary to choose a database, web server, REST/SOA/micro-service framework, or dependency-injection framework early in development, because the high-level policy should not care about any of them.
The longer a detail decision is deferred, the more information is available to make it properly and the more experiments can be run before the decision must be made.

Even when a detail decision has already been made by someone else, a good architect pretends it has not been made and shapes the system so the decision can still be deferred or changed for as long as possible.
A good architect maximizes the number of decisions not made.

Abstracting IO devices behind operating-system services (device independence) is an early instance of separating policy from detail, and it gave birth to the Open-Closed Principle before it was named.
A good architecture must simultaneously support the system's use cases and operation, its maintenance, its development, and its deployment.

The first priority of architecture is to support the system's use cases (its intent), and the most important thing architecture does for behavior is to make that intent clearly visible at the architectural level.

To support operation, the architecture must meet the required throughput and response, and leaving the execution mode (monolith, threads, processes, or services) open lets the system transition across that spectrum as operational needs change.
Conway's law: any organization that designs a system produces a design whose structure copies the organization's communication structure.
A system developed by many teams must have an architecture that partitions it into well-isolated, independently developable components that can be allocated to teams working independently.
Decouple the things that change for different reasons into horizontal layers such as the UI, application-specific business rules, application-independent business rules, and the database.

Separate application-specific business rules (such as input-field validation) from application-independent/domain business rules (such as interest calculation), because they change at different rates and for different reasons.
Decouple use cases from one another as thin vertical slices cutting through the horizontal layers, so new use cases can be added without interfering with existing ones.

The decoupling done for the sake of use cases also benefits operations, because components that must run at different throughputs end up separated and can run on different servers when decoupled in the right mode.

Beware accidental (false) duplication: two similar-looking sections that change at different rates and for different reasons are not true duplicates, and unifying them prematurely couples things that will later diverge.

Create a separate view model rather than passing a database record straight up to the UI even when they look alike, because that similarity is almost certainly accidental duplication and the separation keeps the layers decoupled.

Layers and use cases can be decoupled at three modes: source level (same address space, function calls), deployment/binary level (independently deployable jars/DLLs), and service level (separate execution units communicating over the network).
It is hard to know which decoupling mode is best early in a project, and the optimal mode may change as the project matures.

Defaulting to service-level decoupling is expensive in development time and system resources and encourages coarse-grained decoupling; it is preferable to push decoupling to the point where a service could be formed but keep components in the same address space as long as possible.

A good architecture lets a system be born as a monolith, grow into independently deployable units and then services, and slide back to a monolith as needs change, protecting the majority of the source code from those transitions.

Software architecture is the art of drawing boundaries that separate elements and keep each side ignorant of the other; boundaries drawn early defer decisions and keep them from polluting the core business logic.

What saps the human resources required to build and maintain a system is coupling, and especially coupling to premature decisions about frameworks, databases, web servers, utility libraries, and dependency injection.

Premature decisions are those that have nothing to do with the business requirements/use cases; a good architecture renders such decisions ancillary, deferrable, and not depended upon, and allows them to be made at the latest possible moment.
Making a premature architectural decision (such as a distributed three-tier design or a full service-oriented suite) before it is actually needed can multiply development effort enormously.
A three-tier structure is a topology, not an architecture, and is exactly the kind of decision a good architecture strives to defer.

Drawing a boundary between the business rules and the database, by placing all data access behind an interface, lets the database choice be deferred for a long time and changed later without disturbing the business rules.
Deferring the database behind an interface also keeps tests fast and avoids schema, query, connection, and server issues during early development.
Draw boundary lines between things that matter and things that do not: the GUI and the database do not matter to the business rules, so a boundary belongs between them.

The IO is irrelevant to the core model: the business-rule model does not need the interface and could execute its duties without ever being displayed, just as a game's model can run without being rendered.
Across a boundary, the less-relevant component should depend on the more-relevant one, so the dependency arrow points toward the core business rules.
Treat the user interface and the database as plugins to the core business rules so each can be replaced with a different technology without affecting the business rules.

A plugin architecture creates firewalls across which changes cannot propagate, producing deliberately asymmetric relationships (for example, ReSharper depends on Visual Studio, so Visual Studio is immune to ReSharper).

Boundaries are drawn where there is an axis of change — where components on each side change at different rates and for different reasons — which is the Single Responsibility Principle telling you where to draw boundaries.

To draw boundaries, partition the system into components (core business rules versus plugins) and arrange the dependency arrows to point one way, toward the core business — an application of the Dependency Inversion and Stable Abstractions Principles.
At runtime a boundary crossing is just a function on one side calling a function on the other and passing data; the real work is managing the source-code (compile-time) dependency direction.

Even a monolith (a single executable using source-level decoupling) has meaningful, valuable boundaries, because the ability to independently develop and assemble its components remains valuable even when they are statically linked.
Monolithic and component architectures almost always rely on dynamic polymorphism to manage internal dependencies, because the alternative of prolific pointers-to-functions is too dangerous.

When a high-level client must invoke a lower-level service, use dynamic polymorphism to invert the dependency against the flow of control, so the runtime dependency opposes the compile-time dependency.

Communications across source-level and deployment-level boundaries are cheap function calls and can be chatty, whereas local-process and service boundaries are progressively more expensive, so chattiness across them must be carefully limited.

A service is the strongest boundary (it assumes all communication is over the network, with latency from tens of milliseconds to seconds), and the source code of higher-level services must not contain any physical knowledge such as a URI of lower-level services.
Most systems other than pure monoliths mix boundary strategies, so a system's boundaries are typically a mixture of cheap chatty boundaries and latency-sensitive ones.
A software system is fundamentally a statement of policy: a detailed description of how inputs are transformed into outputs.

Separate policies and regroup them by how they change: policies that change for the same reasons and at the same times are at the same level and belong in one component, while those that change for different reasons or times belong in different components.
'Level' is the distance of a policy from the system's inputs and outputs; the farther from IO, the higher the level, and the policies that manage input and output are the lowest level.
Source-code dependencies should be decoupled from the data flow and coupled to level instead, so that low-level components depend on high-level components.

Higher-level policies tend to change less frequently and for more important reasons, while lower-level policies change frequently and urgently but for less important reasons, so pointing dependencies toward the higher level reduces the impact of change.
Critical Business Rules are rules or procedures that make or save the business money and would do so even if executed manually without any computer system.
Critical Business Rules and the Critical Business Data they operate on are inextricably bound and are therefore a good candidate to be combined into an Entity object.

An Entity binds Critical Business Data and Critical Business Rules into a single, separate module that is pure business, unsullied by database, UI, or framework concerns, and it does not require an object-oriented language.

A use case encapsulates application-specific business rules: it describes how an automated system is used (the input, the output, and the processing steps) and controls when and how the Entities' Critical Business Rules are invoked.
Use cases must not describe the user interface or delivery mechanism; how data gets into and out of the system is irrelevant to the use case.

Entities are higher level (general and reusable across applications, far from IO) while use cases are lower level (application-specific, closer to IO), so use cases depend on Entities and Entities have no knowledge of use cases (the Dependency Inversion Principle).

Use case objects should accept simple request data structures and return simple response data structures that depend on nothing (not framework types like HttpRequest/HttpResponse), so the use cases are not indirectly bound to UI or framework dependencies.

Request and response models should not reference Entity objects, even though they share data, because the two change for different reasons; coupling them violates the Common Closure and Single Responsibility Principles and produces tramp data and conditionals.
Business rules are the reason a software system exists — its core, most independent and reusable code — and should remain pristine, with lesser concerns such as the UI and database plugged into them.
A system's architecture should scream its use cases and domain (for example, 'Health Care System'), not the frameworks it uses (such as Rails, Spring, or ASP).

Architectures should be about use cases, not frameworks; frameworks are tools to be used, not architectures to be conformed to, and an architecture based on a framework cannot be based on the use cases.

The web is a delivery mechanism (an IO detail), not an architecture, so the decision to deliver over the web should be deferred and the system architecture kept as ignorant as possible of how it is delivered.
View every framework skeptically: decide how to use it and how to protect yourself from it, and develop a strategy that prevents the framework from taking over the architecture.

If the architecture is centered on use cases and frameworks are kept at arm's length, all the use cases can be unit-tested without the web server running, the database connected, or any framework in place.

Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters), DCI, and BCE architectures share the same objective of separation of concerns achieved by dividing software into layers, with at least one layer for business rules and another for interfaces.

A clean architecture produces systems that are independent of frameworks, testable (business rules testable without UI, database, or web server), independent of the UI, independent of the database, and independent of any external agency.

The Dependency Rule: source-code dependencies must point only inward toward higher-level policies, and nothing in an inner circle may know anything — names, classes, variables, or data formats — about an outer circle.

The clean-architecture layers from outer to inner are Frameworks and Drivers (details such as the web and database), Interface Adapters (MVC, data-format conversion), Use Cases (application-specific rules), and Entities (enterprise-wide Critical Business Rules), with abstraction and level increasing inward.
The four concentric circles are schematic; a system may need more or fewer layers, but the Dependency Rule always applies and source-code dependencies always point inward.
condition: however many layers a given system uses

statement: No code inward of the interface-adapters layer should know anything about the database, and if a SQL database is used, all SQL must be restricted to that adapters layer.

Cross a boundary against the flow of control using the Dependency Inversion Principle: the inner component defines an output-port interface that the outer component implements, so source-code dependencies always point inward regardless of control direction.

Only simple, isolated data structures (DTOs, structs, or function arguments) should cross a boundary; never pass Entity objects or database row structures across, because that would force an inner circle to know about an outer circle and violate the Dependency Rule.
Data passed across a boundary should always be in the form most convenient for the inner, higher-level circle.

Separating software into layers and conforming to the Dependency Rule yields an intrinsically testable system and lets obsolete external parts such as the database or web framework be replaced with minimum fuss.
The Humble Object pattern splits behavior into a humble module that holds the hard-to-test behaviors stripped to their barest essence and a separate module that holds the easy-to-test behaviors.
Make the View the humble object (it only moves data into the GUI and does not process it) and put all the testable formatting logic in the Presenter, which loads a View Model the View can display.
Everything the application controls on the screen should be represented in the View Model as a string, boolean, or enum, leaving the View nothing to do but load that data onto the screen.
Testability is an attribute of good architecture, and the separation of behavior into testable and non-testable parts often defines an architectural boundary.

Place polymorphic database gateway interfaces (one method per CRUD operation the application needs) between the use-case interactors and the database, implemented by humble objects in the database layer, so interactors stay testable via stubs and SQL stays out of the use-case layer.

There is no true object-relational mapper, because objects (a set of operations over hidden data) are not data structures (public data with no behavior); ORMs are really data mappers and belong in the database layer.
At each architectural boundary the Humble Object pattern tends to appear, dividing hard-to-test from easy-to-test behavior and thereby increasing the testability of the whole system.

Full-fledged architectural boundaries are expensive (reciprocal polymorphic interfaces, input/output data structures, dependency management, and multi-component administration), so an architect may build a partial boundary to hold the place for a full one later.
Anticipatory partial boundaries trade off against YAGNI ('You Aren't Going to Need It'); an architect may judge 'I might' and reserve the boundary, accepting the over-engineering risk.
condition: the architect judges a future boundary is plausible enough to reserve

statement: One partial-boundary technique is to do all the work for separable components but compile and deploy them as a single component, gaining the design readiness without the version-tracking and release-management burden of multiple components.

Partial boundaries built with the Strategy or Facade pattern can degrade if the full boundary never materializes, because without reciprocal interfaces only developer discipline prevents backchannel dependencies from crossing in the wrong direction.
It is a function of the architect to decide where an architectural boundary might one day exist and whether to fully implement, partially implement, or ignore it.
The API across a boundary is defined and owned by the upstream (using, higher-level) component, not by the implementer that satisfies it.

Architectural boundaries exist everywhere, and although full boundaries are expensive to build, they are even more expensive to add later once missing — even with comprehensive test suites and refactoring discipline.

Boundary decisions are not one-time: watch the system as it evolves, note where a boundary may be required, and implement it right at the inflection point where the cost of implementing it becomes less than the cost of ignoring it.

Every system has at least one Main component that creates, coordinates, and oversees the others; it is the ultimate detail and lowest-level policy, the entry point that nothing other than the operating system depends on.

Main should create all the factories, strategies, and global facilities and then hand control to the high-level abstractions; dependency-injection wiring belongs in Main, which then distributes those dependencies without further use of the framework.

Treat Main as a plugin to the application so you can have a different Main per configuration (dev, test, production, or per country, jurisdiction, or customer), which makes configuration much easier to manage.

Using services is not by itself an architecture; a system's architecture is defined by the boundaries that separate high-level policy from low-level detail and follow the Dependency Rule, not by the physical mechanism by which elements communicate.
Services are just function calls across process or platform boundaries; some are architecturally significant and some merely separate behaviors and are not.

The decoupling fallacy: services decoupled at the level of individual variables are still strongly coupled through the data they share, so adding a field to a shared record forces every service that uses it to change and to agree on its interpretation.

The fallacy of independent development and deployment: to the extent services are coupled by data or behavior, their development, deployment, and operation must be coordinated, and monoliths and component-based systems can build scalable systems too.

Cross-cutting concerns defeat functional-decomposition service layouts: a new feature that cuts across the services can force every one of them to change, so the services are not independently deployable.

Architectural boundaries run through services, dividing them into components, rather than between services; services should be given internal component architectures that follow the Dependency Rule so new features can be added as Open-Closed-conformant components.

Tests are part of the system and participate in the architecture; architecturally all tests are equivalent and form the outermost circle, depending inward on the system while nothing in the system depends on them.
Tests must be designed as part of the system; tests not well integrated into the design become fragile and make the system rigid and hard to change (the Fragile Tests Problem).

The first rule of designing for testability, as for any design, is do not depend on volatile things; because GUIs are volatile, design the system and tests so business rules can be tested without going through the GUI.

Create a testing API (a superset of the interactors and interface adapters) that lets tests bypass security, avoid expensive resources such as databases, and force the system into testable states, so the structure of the tests is decoupled from the structure of the application.

Avoid structural coupling between tests and production (a test class per production class and a test method per production method); hiding the application's structure behind a testing API lets production code grow abstract and general while tests grow concrete and specific, independently.
If a testing API's superpowers would be dangerous in production, keep the API and the dangerous parts of its implementation in a separate, independently deployable component.

Although software does not wear out, it can be destroyed from within by unmanaged dependencies on firmware and hardware; code is firmware not because of where it is stored but because of what it depends on and how hard it is to change as hardware evolves.
Non-embedded developers also write firmware whenever they bury SQL in their code or spread platform dependencies throughout it, such as not separating business logic from a mobile-platform API.

Merely getting an application to work (the App-titude test) is insufficient; the code must also be structured for a long useful life, following the make-it-work, then make-it-right, then make-it-fast sequence.

When embedded code is not structured with clean-architecture principles you can often test only on the target hardware, and that target-hardware bottleneck slows development; a clean embedded architecture is testable off the target.

Introduce a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) as the boundary between software and firmware, with an API tailored to the software's needs that hides hardware details (such as the storage medium or GPIO assignments) and provides seams for off-target testing.

Confine processor-specific C extensions and device-access registers to very few firmware files (a processor abstraction layer) and prefer standardized headers such as stdint.h over vendor-specific headers, to keep code portable and testable off-target.

Treat the operating system as a detail by isolating software behind an operating-system abstraction layer (OSAL), so the code is testable off the OS and switching RTOS/OS means writing a new OSAL rather than modifying scattered code.
A layered architecture is built on programming to interfaces: when one module interacts with another through an interface, one service provider can be substituted for another.

Use header files as interface definitions but limit their contents to the function declarations, constants, and struct names the caller needs; exposing implementation-only details creates clutter that leads to unwanted dependencies.

Excessive conditional-compilation directives keyed on target or OS (for example, thousands of repetitions of one #ifdef) violate the Don't Repeat Yourself principle; hide the hardware type under a HAL and use the linker or runtime binding instead.

From an architectural viewpoint the database is a detail — a utility and mechanism for moving data between disk and RAM — not an architectural element, and a good architect does not let such low-level mechanisms pollute the system architecture.
The data model (the structure given to data within the application) is architecturally significant, but the database that stores it is not: the data is significant and the database is a detail.

Relational tables may be convenient for some data access but are not architecturally significant, so knowledge of the tabular structure should be restricted to the lowest-level utility functions in the outer circles of the architecture.

Passing database rows or tables around the system as objects is an architectural error because it couples the use cases, the business rules, and sometimes even the UI to the relational structure of the data.

Database systems are prevalent mainly because disks are slow, which forces indexes, caches, query schemes, and a regular data representation; once data is loaded into RAM, programmers already reorganize it into lists, trees, and hash tables accessed by pointers.
Data-storage performance is a real but low-level concern that can be entirely encapsulated and separated from the business rules, with nothing to do with the overall architecture of the system.

A detail decision such as adopting an RDBMS is sometimes driven by irrational external market expectations rather than engineering need, and the right architectural response is to bolt the database onto the side behind a narrow, safe data-access channel while keeping the core independent of it.

The web changed nothing architecturally; it is one of many historical oscillations between centralizing computing power in servers and distributing it to terminals, and such oscillations are short-term issues to push away from the core business rules.

The web and the GUI are details, so decouple the business rules from the UI to ensure that marketing-driven interface changes cannot disturb the core (companies that failed to isolate business rules from the GUI serve as cautionary tales).
The GUI is a detail and the web is a GUI, so the web is a detail (an IO device) that should be placed behind a boundary keeping it separate from the core business logic.

Although the chatty UI-to-application dance is too GUI-specific to fully abstract away, the business logic can be modeled as use cases whose complete input and resultant output are carried in plain data structures, letting each use case operate the UI as a device in a device-independent manner.
Frameworks are not architectures; a framework author solves their own problems rather than yours and makes no commitment to you, while asking for a large, one-directional commitment from you.
Do not marry a framework: you may use it but should not couple to it; keep it as a detail in an outer circle, behind an architectural boundary, for as long as possible.

When a framework wants you to derive your business objects from its base classes, refuse and instead derive proxies kept in plugin components, integrating the framework so that only low-level components such as Main depend on it (for example, confine Spring annotations to Main, not business objects).

Coupling tightly to a framework carries real risks: the framework tends to violate the Dependency Rule by reaching into your Entities, you may outgrow it, it may evolve in unhelpful directions, and a better alternative you cannot switch to may appear.
Some frameworks, such as a language's standard library, must be adopted, but that should still be a conscious decision understood as a lifelong commitment for that application's life cycle.
exception: the framework is an unavoidable platform/standard library

statement: Begin architecting by identifying the actors and use cases, because the actors (per the Single Responsibility Principle) are the primary sources of change, and partition the system so that a change serving one actor does not affect any other actor.

Structure the build environment into fine-grained components (separated by actor and by role: views, presenters, interactors, controllers) so they could be deployed independently, while reserving the right to combine them into fewer deliverables as conditions change.

Using relationships should point with the flow of control while inheritance relationships point against it (the Open-Closed Principle), so dependencies point toward higher-level policy and changes to low-level details do not ripple upward.

A good component architecture separates along two dimensions at once: by actor (Single Responsibility Principle — different reasons to change) and by level (Dependency Rule — different rates of change).

Even the best design intentions can be destroyed at the implementation stage, so you must deliberately decide how to map the design onto code structures, how to organize that code, and which decoupling modes to apply at compile-time and runtime.

Package by layer (horizontal: web, business logic, persistence) is a quick start but does not scream the business domain and does not scale, while package by feature (vertical) screams the domain but is also suboptimal.

Package by component bundles all the responsibilities of a coarse-grained component (its business logic and persistence) behind one clean interface in a single package, giving a single place to go for that concept; such well-defined components in a monolith are a stepping stone to a micro-services architecture.

Overusing the public access modifier reduces packages to a mere organization mechanism rather than encapsulation, which makes the different architectural styles syntactically identical and impossible to enforce.

Use the language's access modifiers (package-protected, .NET internal, or module 'published' versus public) to hide implementation classes so the compiler enforces the architecture, and prefer compiler enforcement over self-discipline or post-compilation tooling.

Even a strict layered architecture can be subverted into a relaxed layered architecture — for example a controller bypassing the service layer to call the repository directly — while still producing an acyclic dependency graph.
Enforcing architectural rules through code review or post-compilation static analysis is fallible and has a long feedback loop, so leaning on the compiler gives faster and more reliable enforcement.
Everything on the domain 'inside' should be named in the ubiquitous domain language (for example 'Orders' rather than 'OrdersRepository').
Watch for coupling in other areas such as the data models, because the devil is in the implementation details.

A boundary can be dependency-normal (the source dependency points with the flow of control, hiding the device from the application) or dependency-inverted (control passes from the higher-level component to a plugin through a fixed polymorphic entry point, with no compile-time dependency on the plugin).

Splitting a program into independently compilable units dispatched through a fixed table of indirect vectors makes those units independently deployable — effectively polymorphic dispatch and a plugin architecture — even when built decades before object orientation named these ideas.
Software architectures can be wildly different yet equally effective (for example, a dataflow pipes-and-filters design and a one-task-per-terminal design both worked well for the same problem).
A from-scratch redesign team finds it very difficult to catch up with a large staff that is actively maintaining and extending the old system.

Smearing a third-party vendor's API or SQL calls throughout the code couples the system so tightly to that vendor that switching becomes impractical, which is why databases and third-party systems are details that must be isolated behind a boundary.

Externalizing an application's state machine into a configuration text file lets you change the application's flow and add new services without changing code (the Open-Closed Principle), enabling hot-swapping while the system runs.

Great architectures can lead to great failures: the architecture must be flexible enough to be right-sized to the problem, and architecting for the enterprise when all you need is a small tool is a recipe for failure, because excess layers add communication overhead that reduces productivity.

Pointing a system's dependencies in the traditional flow-of-control direction (GUI to rules to database) rather than toward high-level policy contributed to a product's demise, demonstrating in practice why dependencies should be directed toward policy.
You cannot make a reusable framework until you first make a usable one; reusable frameworks must be developed in concert with several reusing applications rather than designed for reuse up front.

A third-party database or framework adopted for its promised 'magic' can turn into a big, slow, intrusive, and expensive dependency that impedes progress at every level, reinforcing that such systems are details to be isolated behind a boundary.
Entire classes of software-architecture problems have no general good solution, only one messy set of trade-offs weighed against another.
An architect's core job is to objectively determine and assess the trade-offs on either side of a consequential decision and resolve it as well as possible.
Architects should not chase silver-bullet solutions, because no single technology or management technique by itself yields an order-of-magnitude improvement (Brooks).
Architects should aim for the least-worst combination of trade-offs rather than a single 'best' design, since 'best' falsely implies all competing factors can be maximized at once.
Online answers rarely transfer to architecture problems, because each conflates the specific environment and circumstances of the organization (every problem is a 'snowflake').
The book deliberately focuses on how architects make decisions and weigh trade-offs rather than on technology or implementation details, so the guidance survives ecosystem churn.
The software development ecosystem continuously and unpredictably replaces itself one piece at a time, so technology-specific writing becomes dated almost immediately.
Data tends to outlive the systems and architecture that manage it, so it demands diligent thought and design (Berners-Lee).
Adhering to a bounded context moves data (and transactionality) from an implementation detail into a first-class architectural concern, which is the source of many modern hard parts.
condition: when building microservices around bounded contexts

statement: Operational data (OLTP: sales, transactional, inventory) is what the business runs on, and interrupting it stops the organization from functioning for long.
Analytical data is used by data scientists and analysts for prediction and business intelligence, is typically non-transactional and often non-relational, and is not critical to day-to-day operation.
Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) — short one-to-two-page text files each describing one architecture decision — are one of the most effective ways to document architecture decisions.
An ADR should contain a Context section (problem plus alternatives), a Decision section (the decision plus justification), and a Consequences section (results and trade-offs considered).
Documenting an architecture decision and governing its proper use are two separate concerns.
An architectural fitness function is any mechanism that performs an objective integrity assessment of some architecture characteristic or combination of characteristics.
An architecture characteristic must be defined objectively and measurably before a fitness function can test it; vague goals like 'high performance' need a concrete measurable value.
condition: the characteristic must be objectively measurable

statement: Composite architecture characteristics such as 'agility' are not directly measurable and must be decomposed into measurable contributors (deployability, testability, cycle time).
Atomic fitness functions check a single architecture characteristic in isolation, whereas holistic fitness functions validate a combination of interlocking characteristics.
Improving one architecture characteristic often degrades another (e.g., security can affect performance; scalability and elasticity can be at odds), so combined effects need holistic checks.
A fitness function validates architecture characteristics while a unit test validates domain criteria; the dividing question is whether domain knowledge is required to run the test.
Fitness functions let architects automate architecture governance, replacing error-prone manual reviews and review boards that let important details slip through.
Code reviews catch modularity violations too late in the development cycle to govern rampant cross-component imports effectively.
A cycle-detection fitness function wired into the continuous build (e.g., JDepend) prevents the accidental introduction of component cycles, which damage modularity.
condition: when wired into the continuous integration build

statement: Layer-dependency fitness functions (e.g., ArchUnit, NetArchTest) let architects verify on an ongoing basis that developers respect defined architectural layers.
Fitness functions should run continually as part of continuous integration, because a validation that never runs cannot validate anything.
Some fitness functions must be manual (e.g., legal review of sensitive changes) and can be accommodated as manual stages in a deployment pipeline.
exception: when the validation cannot be automated

statement: Fitness functions must return objective values, but objective does not mean static — dynamic fitness functions return a value based on context (e.g., performance per user as load rises).
A standardized security 'slot' in every project's deployment pipeline would let an enterprise answer a zero-day exploit by inserting a version-check test everywhere instead of manual scans.
condition: if every project runs a standardized deployment pipeline

statement: Manual governance processes are error-prone and let critical details escape, as in the Equifax breach where an available patch was not fully applied for months.
Architects should not overuse fitness functions; they are a way to build an executable checklist of important-but-not-urgent principles, not to frustrate developers.
exception: avoid building an overly complex interlocking set that merely frustrates teams

statement: Codifying important-but-not-urgent principles as continually-run fitness functions counters the technical debt that accrues when teams defer fixes under urgency ('we'll fix it later').
In architecture, understanding why one choice has better trade-offs is more important than how it is implemented (the second law of software architecture).
Architecture concerns are structural and foundational and should change much less, whereas design concerns are more easily changed.
Two artifacts (including services) are coupled if a change in one might require a change in the other to maintain proper functionality.
A service is a cohesive collection of functionality deployed as an independent executable.
A component is an architectural building block performing a business or infrastructure function, usually manifested as a package, namespace, or directory grouping of source files.
Communication is synchronous if the caller must wait for the response before proceeding, and asynchronous if the caller does not wait for the response.
A workflow is orchestrated when a dedicated service's primary responsibility is to coordinate it, and choreographed when no orchestrator exists and participating services share coordination.
A workflow is atomic if all of its parts maintain a consistent state at all times; the opposite is the spectrum of eventual consistency.
A contract is the interface between two software parts (method calls, remote calls, dependencies); wherever two pieces of software join, a contract is involved.

Coupling in architecture splits into static coupling — how parts are wired together (dependencies, degree, connection points) — and dynamic coupling — how parts call one another at runtime (Page-Jones).
Static coupling can often be measured at compile time because it represents the static dependencies within the architecture.
Coupling is not inherently bad; architects must apply it appropriately, because a fully decoupled system cannot communicate (the dosage makes the poison).
Generic advice to 'decouple as much as possible' gives no guidance on how to decouple while still building useful systems.
Modern trade-off analysis proceeds in three steps: find the entangled parts, analyze how they are coupled, and assess trade-offs by the impact of change on interdependent systems.
Choosing microservice size is a pervasive problem: too-small services create transactional and orchestration issues, while too-large services create scale and distribution issues.
Microservices raised distributed-system complexity because the bounded-context philosophy moved the database inside the service boundary, making transactionality a first-class concern.
condition: in microservices built around bounded contexts

statement: Because every part of the enterprise is data-driven, all software architecture is ultimately in the service of data — ensuring the right data is available and usable across the enterprise.
An architecture quantum is an independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion, high static coupling, and synchronous dynamic coupling.
A well-formed microservice within a workflow is a common example of an architecture quantum.
An architecture quantum measures aspects of both topology and behavior — how parts connect and how they communicate with one another.
Static coupling is how static dependencies — operating system, frameworks, libraries via transitive dependency management, and other operational requirements — resolve via contracts.
Dynamic coupling is how quanta communicate at runtime, either synchronously or asynchronously.
Fitness functions for dynamic-coupling characteristics must be continuous, typically using monitors.
condition: for dynamic-coupling characteristics

statement: Static coupling describes how services are wired together, whereas dynamic coupling describes how services call one another at runtime.
Static coupling analyzes operational dependencies (a service is not operational without its database), while dynamic coupling analyzes communication dependencies (runtime calls).
Two services need not require each other to function, except during a shared runtime workflow.
exception: except during a runtime workflow

statement: Independently deployable means each architecture quantum is a separate deployable unit within the architecture.
A monolithic architecture, deployed as a single unit, is by definition a single architecture quantum.
In a microservices architecture a service represents an architecture quantum from an independently-deployable standpoint, contingent on its coupling.
condition: contingent on the service's coupling characteristics

statement: Making each architecture quantum a deployable asset gives architects, developers, and operations a shared scope and language: coupling, behavior, and deployability respectively.
The architecture quantum (static coupling) is one of the forces architects must weigh when striving for proper service granularity in a distributed architecture.
Service-granularity trade-offs around deployability include the required release cadence, which other services are affected, and the engineering practices involved.
Architecture has two common elements across definitions: the highest-level breakdown of a system into its parts, and the decisions that are hard to change.
Architecture is subjective — a shared understanding of a system's design held by its expert developers; once something proves easier to change than assumed, it ceases to be architectural.

Most nontrivial enterprise applications use a layered architecture of some form; layering is the most widely useful architectural pattern for them, though approaches like pipes-and-filters suit some situations.
exception: where another style such as pipes and filters is valuable

statement: Enterprise application data is persistent: it outlives individual program runs, the creating hardware, and the operating system, so on system replacement the data must be migrated rather than discarded.
Enterprise applications usually hold large data volumes — a moderate system has over 1 GB across tens of millions of records — so managing the data is a major part of the system.
Many users access enterprise-application data concurrently, creating the risk that two users access the same data at the same time in a way that causes errors, even when user counts are modest.

Enterprise applications rarely stand alone; they must integrate with other systems built at different times on different technologies, and integration is complicated by conceptual dissonance where the same field means subtly different things across divisions.
Business logic is a haphazard array of arbitrary special cases that is certain to change over time, so it must be organized as effectively as possible because change is the only certainty.

Not all enterprise applications are large; small systems often carry disproportionate value, and one of the best things a designer can do is turn a large project into a small one by simplifying its architecture and process.

Different enterprise applications have different difficulties, so no single architecture is right for all of them; choosing an architecture requires understanding the particular problems of your system and designing for them.
Treat 'always do this' design prescriptions with suspicion; much of the value in design lies in knowing the alternatives and judging the trade-offs of one over another.
Even when a pattern is chosen, it must be modified to meet the system's demands; a book can only supply information on which to base decisions, not a single solution.

No advice about performance should be treated as fact until it is measured on your own configuration, because designs are often adopted or rejected on performance assumptions that prove bogus once measured.
condition: until measured on the real setup used for the application

statement: Prefer to get a system running, instrument it, and then optimize through a disciplined process based on measurement, rather than optimizing speculatively up front.
exception: for architectural decisions whose performance impact is hard to fix by later optimization

statement: Whenever you perform a performance optimization, measure both before and after; otherwise you may merely be making the code harder to read for no gain.

A significant change in configuration — new VM, hardware, or database — can invalidate prior performance facts, so optimizations must be redone and re-verified after such a change, and a past optimization may even hurt in the new environment.
condition: after upgrading the virtual machine, hardware, database, or similar

statement: Minimizing remote calls has been sound performance advice for a long time because latency is usually the dominant cost in remote systems, but the tip should still be verified by measurement.

Responsiveness (how quickly a system acknowledges a request) is distinct from response time (how long it takes to process it); acknowledging a request before completing it can improve perceived performance even when response time is unchanged.

Latency is the minimum time to obtain any response even for no work, is usually the big issue in remote systems, and is the underlying reason to minimize remote calls; an application developer usually cannot reduce it.
Scalability measures how adding resources affects performance: vertical scalability (scaling up) adds power to a single server, while horizontal scalability (scaling out) adds more servers.
State performance as the precise term — throughput or response time — rather than the word 'performance', because a technique can improve one while degrading the other.

For enterprise systems it often makes sense to build for hardware scalability rather than for capacity or efficiency, because adding servers (or buying newer hardware) is frequently cheaper than adding programmers or hand-optimizing for a fixed platform.
A pattern is a common, effective solution to a recurring problem that you can apply a great many times without ever implementing it the same way twice.
Patterns are 'half-baked': you can never apply the solution blindly and must always finish it off in the context of your own project, which is why automated pattern tools have failed.
The primary value of patterns to an experienced designer is a shared vocabulary that improves communication of design, which is why pattern naming matters.
A pattern example is not the pattern: examples are deliberately simplified for understanding and must be reworked, not copied as canned solutions, when applied.

Layering breaks a complex system into a stack where each higher layer uses services of the layer below and the lower layer is unaware of the higher, and each layer usually hides the layers beneath it.

Layering yields important benefits: a layer can be understood in isolation, alternative implementations can be substituted, inter-layer dependencies are minimized, layers are good standardization points, and a built layer is reusable by many higher-level services.

Layering has downsides: layers do not encapsulate everything, so a change such as adding a UI field cascades through every layer, and extra layers can harm performance through repeated representation transforms.
The hardest part of a layered architecture is deciding which layers to have and what each layer's responsibility should be.

An enterprise application can be organized into three principal layers — presentation, domain, and data source — where presentation handles user interaction, domain holds the logic that is the real point of the system, and data source communicates with databases and other systems.
Letting the presentation access the data source directly, rather than having the domain layer completely hide it, is less pure but tends to work better in practice.

Enforce a steady dependency rule: the domain and data source layers must never depend on (call into) the presentation, which makes presentations substitutable and changeable without deep ramifications.

To detect domain logic that has leaked into the presentation, imagine adding a radically different layer (e.g., a command-line interface to a web app, or an XML file in place of the database); any functionality you would have to duplicate marks leaked domain logic.
Always perform some kind of layer separation — at least at the subroutine level — and choose the separation form (subroutine, class, or package) appropriate to the application's complexity.
Running all layers on the server is the simplest option and easiest to upgrade and fix; the main reasons to move logic to the client are responsiveness or disconnected operation.
Favor a Web presentation when you can and a rich client only when you must, because keeping clients up to date and avoiding compatibility errors is a cost even for simple rich-client systems.
exception: when tasks are too complicated for a web GUI to make the application usable

statement: Keep all code in a single process, on one node or replicated across a cluster, and do not separate layers into discrete processes unless you absolutely must, because separation both degrades performance and adds complexity (Remote Facade, Data Transfer Object).
exception: unless you absolutely have to distribute

statement: Distribution, explicit multithreading, object/relational paradigm chasms, multiplatform development, and extreme performance requirements (e.g., over 100 transactions per second) are 'complexity boosters' that each carry a high cost in development and ongoing maintenance.
Domain logic can be organized with one of three primary patterns: Transaction Script, Domain Model, or Table Module.

A Transaction Script organizes domain logic as a single procedure per user action or business transaction, taking input, validating and calculating, touching the database, and replying to the presentation.
Transaction Script offers a simple procedural model most developers understand, works well with Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway, and has obvious transaction boundaries.
As domain-logic complexity rises, Transaction Script tends to produce duplicated code that is hard to spot and remove and a tangled web of routines without clear structure.
condition: as the complexity of the domain logic increases

statement: A Domain Model organizes logic around the domain's nouns, with each object taking the part of the logic relevant to it, which lets increasingly complex logic be handled in a well-organized, extensible way.

The costs of a Domain Model come from the effort of learning it and from data-source mapping complexity: the richer the Domain Model, the more complex its mapping to a relational database (usually via Data Mapper).
A sophisticated data source layer behaves like a fixed cost: it takes substantial money or time to obtain a good one, but once you have it you can do a great deal with it.

A Table Module keeps a single instance per table (not one per row), works against a Record Set, and is a middle ground between Transaction Script and Domain Model that adds structure but forgoes fine-grained OO techniques like inheritance and strategies.
Table Module is most attractive in environments with strong Record Set tooling (such as .NET or COM); without such tooling it is not worth using.
condition: when the environment provides strong support for a common Record Set structure
exception: where there is no special Record Set tooling

statement: The choice among Transaction Script, Domain Model, and Table Module depends mainly on domain-logic complexity: Domain Model is unattractive for simple logic because its cost is not repaid, but the simpler patterns hit an exponential wall as complexity grows.
A team already familiar with Domain Model lowers its initial cost, so the better and more experienced the team, the more a Domain Model is favored.
The three domain-logic patterns are not mutually exclusive; it is common to use Transaction Script for some domain logic and Table Module or Domain Model for the rest.
If a design started with Transaction Script, do not hesitate to refactor toward Domain Model as logic grows; the reverse move from Domain Model to Transaction Script is usually less worthwhile.
exception: unless you can simplify the data source layer

statement: A Service Layer placed over a Domain Model or Table Module gives the application a clear use-case-oriented API and is a convenient place to put transaction control and security.
Fowler's preference is the thinnest Service Layer you can manage, added only when the application appears to need one, while acknowledging that many good designers always use a richer Service Layer.

If you decide to use a Domain Model, prefer to make it dominant rather than draining behavior into use-case controllers, because controller-entity style (like any Transaction Script) tends to encourage duplicate code.
exception: except when starting from Transaction Script with Row Data Gateway, where moving duplicated behavior to the gateways yields a simple Domain Model via Active Record

statement: A major reason for relational databases' success is SQL, a mostly standard database language whose core syntax is common and well understood despite vendor-specific extensions.

The choice of architectural pattern for how domain logic talks to the database is far-reaching and difficult to refactor, so it deserves careful attention and is strongly affected by how the domain logic is designed.

Separate SQL access from domain logic by placing it in classes based on the database's table structure (one class per table) forming a Gateway, so the rest of the application needs no SQL knowledge and all database access is easy to find and tune.
A Row Data Gateway has one instance per row returned by a query, while a Table Data Gateway has one instance per table and returns a generic Record Set.

Table Data Gateway is the obvious data-source choice when using Table Module because it fits a Record Set, and it can also organize stored procedures by wrapping their calls in an in-memory gateway that encapsulates the call mechanics.
condition: when using Table Module or routing all database access through stored procedures

statement: With a Domain Model, use Active Record when domain logic is simple and classes correspond closely to tables, and use Data Mapper when the situation is more complicated; do not use a plain Gateway as the primary persistence mechanism for a Domain Model.
Active Record can be reached by starting from a Row Data Gateway and adding domain logic to the class, especially when repetitive code appears across multiple Transaction Scripts.

Active Record breaks down as the Domain Model grows richer because the one-to-one match of domain classes to tables fails, relational databases cannot represent inheritance, and rich domain logic should be testable without always talking to the database.
condition: as the domain logic gets more complicated

statement: Data Mapper completely isolates the Domain Model from the database by making the mapping layer entirely responsible for translation, letting the two vary independently; it is the most complex mapping architecture but yields complete isolation.

Pick a single primary persistence pattern for an in-memory model rather than mixing them, because mixing primary persistence mechanisms gets very messy; a data Gateway may still wrap tables or services treated as external interfaces even under Data Mapper.
exception: wrapping external-interface tables or services with a Gateway

statement: Mapping objects to a relational database is estimated anecdotally at around a third of programming effort and continues as a cost during maintenance; object-oriented databases remove this mapping and thereby improve productivity.

Most projects avoid object-oriented databases primarily because of risk: relational databases are well-understood, proven, vendor-backed technology, and SQL provides a relatively standard interface for tools.

If you have a Domain Model, seriously consider buying an object-relational mapping tool, because commercial O/R tools are far more sophisticated than what can reasonably be hand-built, and weigh their price against the cost of writing and maintaining the mapping layer yourself.
condition: when you have a Domain Model

statement: Do not assume an object-relational mapping tool removes all the mapping effort; using and tuning the tool still takes a small but significant chunk of work, and knowing the mapping patterns helps you choose among its options.

A Unit of Work tracks every object read and every object modified and orchestrates all database writes when told to commit, concentrating complex commit processing in one place instead of scattered explicit save calls.

Use an Identity Map to record every row read so the same database row is never loaded into two in-memory objects; its primary purpose is to maintain correct identity (not to boost performance), though it doubles as a database cache.

Lazy Load replaces an object reference with a placeholder so the real object is pulled from the database only when the link is actually followed, preventing a single read from dragging an enormous object graph out of the database.
With row-based interaction classes, prefer separate finder objects to static find methods, because making find operations static stops you from substituting the database for testing via Service Stub.
condition: when database interaction classes are row-based

statement: Finder methods work on database state, not in-memory object state, so objects you have added in memory will not appear in query results; it is therefore usually wise to run queries at the beginning of the work.
When reading data, pull back multiple rows at once and never issue repeated queries on the same table for individual rows; it is almost always better to fetch too much data than too little.
exception: beware of locking too many rows under pessimistic concurrency control

statement: Use joins to load several tables in a single query, but bear in mind databases are optimized for roughly three or four joins per query and performance suffers beyond that, though cached views can recover some of it.
Always profile the application against your specific database and data, because general rules of thumb guide thinking but every one has surprising exceptions given each environment's caching schemes.

Objects and relations represent links differently — references and multivalued collections versus single-valued foreign keys — causing structural reversals; resolve this by keeping each object's relational identity as an Identity Field and wiring references with Foreign Key Mapping.
Use an Association Table Mapping — a separate relational table dedicated to the association — to map a many-to-many relationship, which relational databases cannot represent directly.
Avoid relying on collection ordering when persisting to a relational database; prefer unordered sets, because an arbitrarily ordered collection is very difficult to maintain in the database.

Defer referential-integrity checking to the end of the transaction whenever the database supports it; otherwise order updates carefully (for example by topological sort) to satisfy integrity and reduce deadlock-induced rollbacks.
condition: when the database can defer referential-integrity checking to transaction end

statement: Do not give small Value Objects such as date ranges and money their own table; embed their fields into the owning object as an Embedded Value, and since they have value semantics they need no Identity Map.

Serialized LOB stores a whole cluster of objects in a single column (for example as an XML document), saving many database roundtrips for hierarchic structures, but SQL cannot query inside it, so it is best used when you do not need to query the stored structure's parts.
condition: for a relatively isolated group of objects you do not query into

statement: Overusing Serialized LOB degrades the database into little more than a transactional file system.

Inheritance has no standard SQL mapping, leaving three options: Single Table Inheritance (one table for the whole hierarchy), Class Table Inheritance (one table per class), and Concrete Table Inheritance (one table per concrete class).
