The inheritance-mapping patterns trade data-structure duplication against access speed: Class Table Inheritance needs multiple joins (slower), Concrete Table Inheritance avoids joins but is brittle to superclass changes, and Single Table Inheritance wastes column space but is simplest and join-free.

A reasonable default for inheritance mapping is Single Table Inheritance because it is easy to do and resilient to many refactorings, falling back to the other two patterns as needed to handle irrelevant and wasted columns.

When using a Domain Model, build the model without regard to the database so the domain logic is simplest and treat the database as a way of persisting object data; beware a Domain Model that looks like a database design.
condition: when using a Domain Model

statement: Build up the database incrementally within short iterations (no more than six weeks, preferably fewer), integrating each piece of the Domain Model into the database as you go, rather than building a database-free model for months and persisting it afterward, which risks crippling performance problems.

Repetitive mapping code is a sign of something wrong with the design; Metadata Mapping boils the mapping down to a metadata file so repetitive code can be replaced by code generation or reflective programming.

Metadata Mapping provides the foundation for a Query Object (build queries in terms of in-memory objects without knowing SQL or the schema) and a Repository (which hides the database so callers cannot tell whether objects came from memory or the database).

Creating a database connection is often expensive, making a connection pool worthwhile; most platforms provide pooling, and if you must build it yourself, first verify that pooling actually improves performance in your environment.
Connections are expensive resources that must be closed as soon as you are done with them, and within a transaction every command must run on the same connection.
Make a connection available where needed via a thread-scoped Registry rather than threading it through many method calls, because multiple threads must not share the same connection.

Do not rely on garbage collection to close database connections, because closing then happens only when memory is reclaimed (possibly much later); explicit or transaction-tied closing is better, with garbage collection only as a backup.

Tie a connection's lifetime to its transaction — open it when the transaction begins and close it on commit or rollback — and let a Unit of Work manage both, since the transaction's visible completion makes it easier to remember to close.

Avoid `select *` combined with positional column indices, because adding or reordering a column then breaks code; prefer column-name indices, which are clearer though possibly slightly slower — measure to be sure.
Keep a simple create/read/update/delete test case for each database mapping structure to catch cases where the SQL drifts out of sync with the code.
Prefer static, precompilable SQL over dynamic SQL compiled each time, and avoid assembling SQL queries by string concatenation.

A web-server program can be structured as a script (which best interprets the request) or as a server page (which best formats the response), so a natural design uses a script for request interpretation and a server page for response formatting.

The first and most important reason to apply Model View Controller is to separate the models completely from the web presentation, which makes the presentation easier to modify, eases adding further presentations, and makes the domain logic easier to test.

An Application Controller is an intermediate layer that handles application flow — deciding which screens appear in which order — and can be made presentation-independent and reused when presentations share the same basic flow and navigation.

Use an Application Controller when the system has significant logic about screen order and navigation; a good test is that if the machine controls the screen flow you need one, and if the user controls it you do not.
exception: when a user can see any screen in any order

statement: If you use server-page (Template View) technology, be disciplined about keeping programming logic out of the page structure, often by delegating to a helper object, because embedding a full programming language in the page leads to messy, hard-to-maintain code.
condition: when using server page technology as the view

statement: A Two Step View splits rendering into producing a logical screen and then rendering it to HTML, concentrating HTML choices in one place so global look changes are easy; it works best where screens share a common logical layout and is well-suited to serving multiple front ends or output devices.
condition: where different screens use the same basic logical layout
exception: highly design-intensive sites that cannot share a logical screen structure

statement: Page Controller uses one input controller per page or action, while Front Controller routes all requests through a single handler that interprets the URL and dispatches, centralizing HTTP handling and avoiding web-server reconfiguration when the site's action structure changes.

Enterprise developers can hold a naive view of concurrency because transaction managers handle the hardest parts: as long as all data manipulation happens within a transaction, little goes seriously wrong.
condition: as long as all data manipulation is done within a transaction

statement: Offline concurrency — concurrency control for data manipulated across multiple database transactions — cannot be avoided, because many interactions with a system cannot be placed within a single database transaction.

A lost update occurs when one write overwrites another change made after the first read, while an inconsistent read occurs when two individually-correct values are read that were never correct at the same moment.

Concurrent programming must address not only correctness (safety) but also liveness — how much concurrent activity can proceed — and people often deliberately sacrifice some correctness to gain liveness, depending on the severity and likelihood of failures.

Isolation partitions data so any piece can be accessed by only one active agent at a time; good concurrency design creates such isolated zones and does as much programming as possible inside them, because isolation reduces the chance of concurrency errors.
Concurrency conflicts only occur on mutable shared data, so identifying data as immutable (or read-only and served from copies) lets you relax concurrency controls for it and share it widely.
An optimistic lock is fundamentally about conflict detection, while a pessimistic lock is about conflict prevention.

Pessimistic locking reduces concurrency because others must wait while a lock is held, whereas optimistic locking permits more progress (the lock is held only during commit) but forces conflict resolution, which is usually too hard to auto-merge for business data.

Choose between optimistic and pessimistic locking by the frequency and severity of conflicts: prefer optimistic locks when conflicts are rare or low-consequence because they give better concurrency and are easier to implement, but use a pessimistic technique when the results of a conflict are painful for users.
exception: use pessimistic when conflict consequences are painful for users

statement: Optimistic concurrency control typically detects conflicts using a version marker (a timestamp or sequential counter): compare the version you read against the shared data's version, and any difference indicates a conflict.

Prefer simple, conservative deadlock schemes for enterprise applications — such as acquiring all locks up front, enforcing a lock acquisition order, or using timeouts — accepting some unnecessary victims, because a missed deadlock scenario is worse than over-conservative victimization.

Software transactions should satisfy the ACID properties: Atomicity (all steps complete or all roll back), Consistency (resources in a consistent state at start and end), Isolation (results invisible to other open transactions until commit), and Durability (committed results survive any crash).

Keep transactions as short as possible and, as a general rule, never let a transaction span multiple requests (a long transaction); a simple effective model opens the transaction at the start of a request and completes it at the end.

Beware lock escalation: when a transaction locks too many rows, the database may escalate to a whole-table lock and shut everyone else out, which is why you should not keep a single shared 'object' table for data at the Layer Supertype level.

The four SQL isolation levels — serializable, repeatable read, read committed, read uncommitted — progressively admit more inconsistent-read errors (phantoms, then unrepeatable reads, then dirty reads) in exchange for greater liveness.

Serializable isolation guarantees correctness but badly hurts liveness, so throughput often forces reduced isolation; set the isolation level per transaction, balancing liveness against correctness for each, rather than using one level everywhere.

A system transaction (supported by RDBMS or transaction monitors) has no meaning to a business user, whereas a business transaction is the user's whole logical unit of work (such as login, select account, set up payments, click OK), and users reasonably expect it to display ACID properties.

Implementing an entire business transaction inside a single system transaction produces a long system transaction, which most transaction systems handle inefficiently and which turns the database into a major bottleneck, destroying scalability.

Long transactions are acceptable only when the database has modest concurrency needs; where you can get away with one it avoids many awkward problems and is worth doing, but the application will not be scalable.
condition: when concurrency needs are modest

statement: When long transactions are too risky, break the business transaction into a series of short system transactions and have the application supply the glue to preserve ACID across them — the problem of offline concurrency.

Atomicity and durability are the easiest ACID properties to support for a business transaction (by committing its change set inside a system transaction), while isolation is the hardest to enforce and isolation failures cause consistency failures.
Assume each business transaction executes within a single client session; designing a business transaction that spans multiple sessions is a reliable way to get badly confused.

As much as possible, let the transaction system handle concurrency, and only resort to offline-concurrency techniques when you cannot fit the business transaction into one system transaction or get away with a long transaction.

Make Optimistic Offline Lock the first choice for offline concurrency because it is easier to program and yields the best liveness; its limitation is that failure is only discovered at commit, so switch to Pessimistic Offline Lock when that late discovery is too painful for users.
exception: when late discovery of conflict is too costly

statement: Reduce offline-concurrency complexity with a Coarse-Grained Lock that manages a group of objects together and an Implicit Lock that spares developers from managing locks directly, which also avoids the hard-to-find bugs caused when someone forgets a lock.

Concurrency is not a purely technical decision to defer until requirements are complete: the choice of optimistic versus pessimistic control affects the whole user experience and requires domain input from the system's users.

Concurrency is one of the most difficult programming tasks because concurrent code is very hard to test with confidence and concurrency bugs are hard to reproduce and track down, so it is worth getting experienced help when you must tackle it.

Avoid explicit multithreaded programming with locks and synchronization as much as possible, so application developers almost never deal with these mechanisms directly, because such defects are easy to introduce and almost impossible to reproduce.

Process-per-session gives complete state isolation so application programmers avoid multithreading worries, but uses a lot of resources; pooled process-per-request uses far fewer processes with nearly as good isolation, provided every per-request resource is released at the end of the request.

Thread-per-request handles more load with less hardware because threads use far fewer server resources than processes, but provides no isolation between threads (any thread can touch any data it can reach).

Process-per-request is worth favoring over thread-per-request: it is less efficient but equally scalable and more robust (a haywire thread brings down only its own process), and the reduction in threading bugs is worth the extra hardware cost, especially for a less experienced team.

When using thread-per-request, create an isolated zone by having the thread make new objects as it begins handling the request and never publishing them where other threads can see them (for example in a static variable).
condition: when using thread-per-request

statement: Object creation is actually fast in modern virtual machines, so creating fresh objects per session rather than pooling them avoids many concurrency bugs and can improve scalability, since pooling forces synchronized access to the pooled objects.

In a multithreaded server avoid static, class-based, or global variables and singletons because every use of them must be synchronized; when you need global memory, use a Registry implemented with thread-specific storage.

The fundamental session-state question is to recognize that some sessions are inherently stateful and then decide what to do with that state, rather than getting lost in the technical debate over stateless versus stateful servers.

A stateless server object does not retain state between requests, which lets you pool objects so fewer objects serve more users; statelessness becomes more valuable the more idle users you have and fits well with HTTP being a stateless protocol.

Many client interactions, such as a shopping cart, are inherently stateful, forcing the session to be stateful; you can implement a stateful session on top of a stateless server, but you may not want to.

Session state is data relevant only to a single session within a business transaction, separated from other sessions, that must be committed to become record data; it often fails validation rules while being edited and need only be valid when the business transaction commits.
Distinguish session state, which must be stored between requests for correct behavior, from cached data, which can be lost without losing correctness.

Session state can be stored in three basic ways: Client Session State (on the client via URL, cookie, hidden field, or rich-client objects), Server Session State (in memory or as a serialized object on the server), and Database Session State (decomposed into database tables and fields).

Use Client Session State only when the session state is small, because all of it must travel across the wire with every request and, unless encrypted, can be tampered with by a malicious user (a security and integrity risk).
condition: only when the amount of session state is small

statement: Database Session State performs well for public retail systems with little per-session data but many idle users, whereas Server Session State performs better where Database Session State would mean moving masses of data in and out of the database each request.

Client Session State handles user and system cancellation and crashes most gracefully (you can simply forget the user, and it survives server or network failure), Server Session State survives a crash only if backed to a nonvolatile store, and Database Session State copes well with client, server, and network failure.

The three session-state storage approaches are not mutually exclusive and can be mixed, though mixing adds complexity, and you must always keep at least a session identifier in Client Session State even when the rest lives elsewhere.
Distributing objects has far more pitfalls than commonly realized, and although transparency middleware can hide many things, performance is usually not one of them.

A procedure call within a process is very fast, a call between processes is orders of magnitude slower, and a call to another machine is slower still, so the interface of an object used remotely must differ from that of an object used locally.

A local interface should be fine-grained (many small methods for OO flexibility), while a remote interface must be coarse-grained (obtaining or updating many fields per call) to minimize the number of calls, at the cost of being more awkward to program.

The First Law of Distributed Object Design is: don't distribute your objects — basing a distribution strategy on classes yields too many remote calls and an awkward, hard-to-modify system even when every remotable class has a coarse-grained interface.

To exploit multiple processors, prefer clustering: place all classes in a single process and run multiple copies of that process across nodes, so each process uses fast local calls and fine-grained interfaces for better maintainability.

Be parsimonious with object distribution: minimize distribution boundaries, but accept the unavoidable ones — client/server, application-server/database, web-server/application-server, software-package, and genuine application-server splits.

Design with fine-grained objects internally and place coarse-grained Remote Facade objects only at distribution boundaries to provide the remote interface, which keeps the distribution policy explicit so developers see where they pay the remote-call cost.

Pair a Remote Facade with a Data Transfer Object that bundles the needed data into one block for transfer; because the DTO appears on both sides of the wire, it must reference only other Data Transfer Objects and fundamental objects such as strings.

Between two systems built on the same platform, prefer that platform's native remote-call mechanism, and use XML Web services only when a more direct approach is not possible, such as when different platforms must communicate.
condition: when different platforms must talk to each other

statement: An asynchronous, message-based approach is often preferable to synchronous RPC for distributed systems and is the best use of Web services.

The strongest force selecting among Transaction Script, Table Module, and Domain Model is the complexity of the domain logic (currently impossible to quantify precisely), with the difficulty of the database connection as a secondary factor.

Available tools affect architecture: in theory you choose tools to fit the architecture, but in practice you often must match the architecture to your tools, and Table Module in particular becomes much stronger when the platform's tooling is built around a Record Set.

Adopt continuous integration, test-driven development, and refactoring (even if you reject the rest of extreme programming) because these practices make it much easier to change your mind when you discover that an architectural decision must change.

With Transaction Script, separate the database access into a Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway even in simple cases, and let rich Record Set tooling tilt the choice decisively toward Table Data Gateway.

When one request pulls data back for editing and a later request saves the changes, Optimistic Offline Lock is almost always the best choice, because it is easier to implement, fits users' expectations, and avoids a hung session leaving things locked.
condition: when an edit spans two requests (read then save)

statement: Connect a Domain Model to data with Active Record when it is simple and close to the database, and with Data Mapper as it grows complex (Data Mapper gives the most independence but is the most complex — get a mapping tool unless the team is strong or simplifications exist), recommending Unit of Work as the concurrency-control focal point.

The presentation layer is relatively independent of the lower layers; prefer an HTML browser interface over a rich client when you can get away with it, because rich clients need more client control and deployment and usually take more effort to program.

Use Model View Controller as the underpinning of an HTML application, choosing Page Controller for document-oriented sites with a mix of static and dynamic pages and Front Controller for more complex navigation and UI.

Do not put domain logic in stored procedures as an architectural principle, because it makes the application harder to maintain and locks you to a database vendor; move a method into a stored procedure only as a targeted optimization for a clear performance problem.
exception: as an optimization step where there is a strong, clear performance gain

statement: Web services are about application integration, not application construction, so do not break a single application into Web services that talk to each other unless you really need to; instead build the application and expose parts of it as Remote Facades.

Do not give EJB entity beans a remote interface: entity beans act as Domain Models or Row Data Gateways and need a fine-grained interface to do so, but a remote interface must always be coarse-grained, so keep entity beans local only.
condition: when using entity beans

statement: Treat mediating layers — such as an Application Controller between presentation and domain, or a Data Mapper between domain and data source — as optional patterns added when a base layer gets too complex, since they are useful some of the time but not all of the time.

A Transaction Script organizes business logic as one procedure per request from the presentation, calling the database directly or through a thin wrapper, with common subtasks factored into shared subprocedures.

Separate Transaction Scripts as much as possible — at least into distinct subroutines, better into classes separate from presentation and data source — and make no calls from a Transaction Script into presentation logic, to make the code easier to modify and test.

The strength of Transaction Script is its simplicity with very little performance or comprehension overhead for small amounts of logic, while its failing is that complex business logic becomes hard to keep well-designed, being especially prone to code duplication between transactions.
However committed to objects you become, do not rule out Transaction Script, because many problems are genuinely simple and a simple solution gets you up and running much faster.

A Domain Model is an object model of the domain that incorporates both data and behavior, clustering processes close to the data they work with, and using multivalued attributes, a complex web of associations, and inheritance.

There are two styles of Domain Model: a simple Domain Model (roughly one object per table, usable with Active Record) and a rich Domain Model (inheritance, strategies, and webs of small objects, better for complex logic but requiring Data Mapper).
Keep the minimum possible coupling between the Domain Model and the other layers, because business behavior changes a lot and the domain layer must remain easy to modify, build, and test.

Do not pre-emptively separate usage-specific behavior out of domain objects to prevent bloat; put behavior in the object that naturally fits and fix bloating only if it actually becomes a problem, because premature separation causes duplication that is harder to find, while bloating occurs less often than feared and is easy to fix.

Use entity beans as a Domain Model only for modest domain logic (roughly one entity bean per table, acting as Active Record); for richer logic with inheritance and strategies, prefer a POJO Domain Model with Data Mapper so the domain logic stays independent of the EJB container.
condition: when domain logic is modest versus rich

statement: Choose a Domain Model when the system has complicated, ever-changing business rules involving validation, calculations, and derivations, and choose a Transaction Script when you have only simple not-null checks and a few sums.

When using a Domain Model, make Data Mapper the first choice for database interaction, because it keeps the Domain Model independent of the database and best handles cases where the model and the database schema diverge.
condition: when using a Domain Model

statement: Domain Models work very well when similar conditionals recur, because the conditionals can be factored into the object structure (for example a strategy hierarchy), moving complexity out of algorithms and into the relationships between objects.

A Table Module handles the business logic for all rows of a table or view through a single instance that has no notion of per-object identity, so an identity reference (often the primary key) must be passed on each operation.

Table Module packages data with behavior while playing to a relational database's strengths, typically working on a Record Set produced by a SQL call, which keeps the behavior close to the data it acts on.
A benefit of Table Module is testability: you can create a Record Set in memory and test the module's logic without going to the database.

Use Table Module when you access tabular data through a Record Set and want that data structure central and straightforward to access, trading away Domain Model's power over complex logic for easier integration with table-oriented data structures.
condition: when accessing tabular data via a Record Set

statement: Table Module does not give the full power of objects — no direct instance-to-instance relationships and poor polymorphism — so prefer a Domain Model for complicated domain logic.
condition: for complicated domain logic

statement: Table Module works better than a combination of Domain Model and Active Record when other parts of the application are built around a common table-oriented data structure such as the .NET or COM Record Set.
condition: when the application is based on a shared table-oriented Record Set structure

statement: A Service Layer defines an application's boundary and its set of available operations, encapsulating business logic, controlling transactions, and coordinating each operation's response, so the interaction logic is not duplicated across the application's several client interfaces.

Distinguish domain logic (purely the problem domain) from application or workflow logic (application responsibilities such as notifying others), and factor each kind into a separate layer so the pure domain object classes stay reusable across applications.

Do not put application-specific logic into pure domain object classes, because doing so makes those classes less reusable across applications and harder to reimplement later, for example in a workflow tool.

A Service Layer has two basic implementation variations: the domain facade approach (thin facades over a Domain Model that holds all business logic) and the operation script approach (thicker classes that implement application logic and delegate domain logic to domain objects).

Start with a locally invocable Service Layer whose method signatures deal in domain objects, and add remotability only when needed (via Remote Facade or remote interfaces), because remote invocation forces costly Data Transfer Object signatures and incurs the First Law of Distributed Object Design.

An application with a web UI or web-services gateway need not run its business logic in a separate process from its server pages and web services; a colocated approach saves development effort and runtime response time without sacrificing scalability.

Identify Service Layer operations from the use-case model and user-interface design, driven by client needs, with an almost one-to-one correspondence between CRUD use cases and Service Layer operations.

Use a Service Layer when the business logic has more than one kind of client or its use-case responses must be transacted atomically across multiple transactional resources; you probably do not need one when there is a single client and single-resource responses.
condition: more than one client kind, or responses spanning multiple transactional resources
exception: a single client with single-resource use-case responses

statement: As soon as you envision a second kind of client or a second transactional resource in use-case responses, it pays to design in a Service Layer from the beginning rather than retrofit it.

A Table Data Gateway holds all the SQL for accessing a single table or view (selects, inserts, updates, deletes) and is usually stateless, so all other code interacts with the database only through its methods.

Avoid passing query results around as maps, because a map defeats compile-time checking and gives an inexplicit interface prone to misspelling bugs; prefer a Data Transfer Object, or in record-set environments the Record Set itself.
If all updates pass through a Table Data Gateway, base its returned data on database views rather than the actual tables, which reduces coupling between your code and the database structure.
condition: when all updates are done through the Table Data Gateway

statement: Table Data Gateway is the simplest database-interface pattern and pairs naturally with Table Module and Transaction Script, but it is used least with a Domain Model because Data Mapper gives better isolation between the model and the database.

A single Table Data Gateway interface can serve both raw SQL and stored procedures — stored procedures are often organized as Table Data Gateways — and its find procedures can return views that hide the underlying table structure.

A Row Data Gateway mimics a single record with one field per column and holds only database-access logic and no domain logic; the moment domain logic appears in it, it has become an Active Record instead.

Embedding database-access code directly in in-memory business objects increases their complexity and slows tests because the objects are tied to a database; a Row Data Gateway hides data-source access behind a record-like interface and works particularly well with Transaction Script.

Prefer Row Data Gateways that mirror the database structure, because using a gateway to shield domain objects from a changing database on a large scale leaves three data representations — business logic, gateway, and database — which is one too many.
Row Data Gateways are tedious to write but are excellent candidates for code generation from a Metadata Mapping, so they can be auto-generated during the build while Data Mappers are written by hand.

When business logic is repeated across multiple Transaction Scripts using a Row Data Gateway, moving that logic into the gateway gradually turns it into an Active Record, which is often good because it reduces duplication in the business logic.

An Active Record wraps a database row, encapsulates database access, and adds domain logic to that data, with the class data structure matching the database record closely (one field per column, typed as the SQL interface gives them).
Active Record is a good choice when domain logic is not too complex — create/read/update/delete plus derivations and validations based on a single record.
condition: when domain logic is not too complex

statement: Active Record's primary advantage is simplicity, but it works well only with an isomorphic schema where objects correspond directly to tables, so complex business logic needing relationships, collections, and inheritance should move to Data Mapper instead.
Active Record couples the object design to the database design, which makes it harder to refactor either design as a project goes forward.

Active Record is a good migration target when a Transaction Script with a Gateway begins to suffer code duplication: wrap the tables as a Gateway first, then gradually move behavior in so the tables evolve into Active Records.

A Data Mapper is a layer that moves data between in-memory objects and the database while keeping them independent, so the domain objects need no SQL, no schema knowledge, and need not even know a database is present.
The entire Data Mapper layer can be substituted — for testing or to let a single domain layer work with different databases.

A Data Mapper find typically loads a whole graph of objects rather than a single row, and joining related tables in one query is usually faster, so finders must know how clients use the objects in order to minimize database queries.

In-memory domain objects cannot be entirely ignorant of the mapping layer, because they may need to know about its finders and mechanisms such as Lazy Load to bound how much data a request pulls back.
Use Separated Interface to let domain code invoke find methods without depending on the Data Mapper: place the find methods the domain needs in an interface kept in the domain package.

Prefer creating domain objects with a rich constructor so they are well-formed with their mandatory data from the start (which also lets you enforce immutable fields), but for cyclic references create an empty object via a no-arg constructor and insert it immediately into the Identity Map to stop recursive loading.
exception: when objects have cyclic references

statement: Use one Data Mapper per domain class or hierarchy root when hardcoding mappers, or a single metadata-driven mapper, splitting only the find methods by domain class for large applications so developers can locate the finder they need.

Use Data Mapper when you want the database schema and the object model to evolve independently — most commonly with a Domain Model — accepting the cost of the extra layer; the test for needing it is the complexity of the business logic.
condition: when the schema and object model should evolve independently

statement: Do not choose Data Mapper without a Domain Model; a simple Domain Model over a database the developers control may access the database directly with Active Record, refactoring database behavior into a separate mapping layer only as things grow complex.
For most cases, buy a database-mapping layer rather than build one, because a full-featured object-relational mapping layer is a complicated beast to build and capable products already exist.

A Unit of Work maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out the changes and resolving concurrency, which avoids many tiny slow database calls and removes the need to hold a transaction open for the whole interaction.

With a Unit of Work, application programmers never call database-update methods explicitly; they tell the Unit of Work to commit, and it opens the transaction, does concurrency checking, and writes changes — freeing them from tracking what changed and from worrying about referential-integrity ordering.

Prefer object registration (registration calls placed inside the object's load and setting methods) over caller registration for a Unit of Work, because relying on the caller to register each changed object causes more confusion than it is worth.
Have every transaction write to its tables in the same fixed sequence — held in the Unit of Work — to greatly reduce the risk of database deadlocks.
Make a Unit of Work reachable by the objects that need it via a thread-scoped Registry (or by passing it in), and never let more than one thread access a single Unit of Work.
Unit of Work works with any transactional resource, not just databases, so it can also coordinate message queues and transaction monitors.

Use a Unit of Work to keep track of every manipulated object in one place so in-memory data can be synchronized with the database; the alternatives (explicit save per change, tracking variables, or per-object dirty flags) become unmanageable in a Domain Model's general object network.

An Identity Map ensures each object is loaded only once by keeping every loaded object in a map and looking it up there, which both preserves correctness (no two in-memory objects for one database row) and improves performance (no repeated loads).

Prefer an explicit Identity Map (a distinct lookup method per object type) over a generic one, for compile-time checking in a typed language and the clarity of an explicit interface, accepting the small cost of adding a method per map.
Prefer a single Identity Map per inheritance tree (with keys unique across the tree) rather than one per concrete class, because separate maps make polymorphic lookups awkward.
condition: when there is an inheritance hierarchy

statement: Put Identity Maps on a session-specific object so each session gets its own isolated instance — ideally inside the Unit of Work, otherwise a session-tied Registry — and keep a single map per session to avoid having to add transactional protection to the map.

Hold read-only Identity Maps in a process context shared by the whole process while keeping updatable maps in a session context, because immutable data needs no per-session isolation and process-wide sharing benefits performance.
condition: for objects that are read-only in all cases

statement: You do not need an Identity Map for immutable objects such as Value Objects, nor for a Dependent Mapping whose persistence is controlled by a parent, although a caching or correct-equality benefit may still justify one.
An Identity Map resolves update conflicts only within a single session and does nothing for conflicts that cross sessions, which require Optimistic or Pessimistic Offline Lock.

A Lazy Load is an object that does not hold all the data you need but knows how to get it, interrupting eager loading with a marker so related data is fetched only when actually used, which prevents one read from dragging in a huge object graph.

Lazy Load has four main implementations — lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder, and ghost — where lazy initialization is simplest but couples the object to the database (suiting Active Record and the gateways) while Data Mapper needs the extra indirection of a virtual proxy.

A virtual proxy looks exactly like the real object but loads it on first method call; beware that multiple proxies for one object have different identities, so override the equality method and use it consistently to avoid hard-to-track bugs.

Use a ghost — the real object in a partial, ID-only state that loads its full state when a field is accessed — and place it immediately in the Identity Map, which maintains identity and avoids problems from cyclic references when reading data.

Beware ripple loading: a collection of Lazy Loads accessed one at a time causes one database call per object; avoid it by making the collection itself a single Lazy Load that loads all its contents at once.
exception: when the collection is very large, where a Value List Handler is needed

statement: Handle differing per-use-case laziness by using separate database-interaction objects (for example an eager and a lazy mapper) or one loader deferring to a strategy; in practice only two degrees of laziness are needed — a full load and enough for identification in a list.

Do not use Lazy Load on a field stored in the same row as the rest of the object, because fetching extra data in one call usually costs nothing more; it is only worth considering when accessing the field requires an extra database call and the data is not used when the main object is.
condition: only when the field needs an extra database call and is not used with the main object

statement: Do not add Lazy Load unless you actively expect to need it, because it adds complexity to the program.

Identity Field stores a database table's primary key in the in-memory object's fields to tie the object to its database row, which is what lets you write the object's data back, since in-memory objects otherwise need no such key.
Prefer meaningless (surrogate) keys over meaningful keys such as a Social Security number, because meaningful keys are often neither unique nor immutable in practice once human error enters them.
exception: for small and/or very stable systems where a meaningful key may suffice

statement: Prefer simple (single-field) keys over compound keys for the uniformity of using the same key-handling code everywhere, since compound keys require special handling in concrete classes and carry meaning that threatens uniqueness and immutability.

Choose a key type with a fast equality operation and easy next-key generation — a long integer is often the best bet — and avoid dates or times in keys because they are meaningful and their fractional-second precision causes portability and identity problems.

Database auto-increment key generation usually cannot be used on a table whose rows you insert with connected objects, because you cannot easily obtain the generated key before the transaction commits to set it as the children's foreign key.
condition: when inserting connected objects within one transaction

statement: Prefer a separate key table (columns: name and next available value) for key generation, accessing it in a separate transaction so its row lock is held only briefly, and reserve many keys per call to cut database calls and contention.

Separate the code that generates new keys into its own class, which makes it easier to reuse across applications, to put key reservation in its own transaction, and to build a Service Stub for testing.

Use Identity Field when there is a mapping between in-memory objects and database rows (typically with a Domain Model or Row Data Gateway), and not when you use Transaction Script, Table Module, or Table Data Gateway.
condition: when mapping in-memory objects to database rows
exception: when using Transaction Script, Table Module, or Table Data Gateway

statement: A Foreign Key Mapping maps an object reference to a foreign key in the database by storing the linked object's Identity Field as a foreign key in the referencing record.

To map a one-to-many collection you must reverse the reference direction — put the owner's foreign key in each child record — because a collection cannot be stored in a single field without violating first normal form.

To update a foreign-key-mapped collection, choose among delete-and-insert, adding a back pointer, or diffing the collection; delete-and-insert is simple and works well but is only safe when the children are a Dependent Mapping owned by the parent.
exception: delete-and-insert requires the children to be a Dependent Mapping

statement: When diffing a collection to compute updates, prefer diffing against what you read the first time (kept in memory) over re-reading the database, to avoid an extra read, though Optimistic Offline Lock may require diffing against the database too.
exception: when Optimistic Offline Lock requires comparing against the database

statement: A mandatory back link simplifies collection updates by removing the need to detect removed items, and an immutable link simplifies them further so that adding always means insertion and removing always means deletion.

To avoid infinite cycles when loading linked objects, either create fully-formed objects and place Lazy Load at points that break the cycles, or create empty objects and insert them immediately into the Identity Map so a cycle finds the already-loaded object.
condition: when object links contain cycles

statement: Use Foreign Key Mapping for almost any inter-class association except a many-to-many one (which needs Association Table Mapping); use Embedded Value when the related object is a Value Object, and consider Dependent Mapping for a collection field with no back pointer.
exception: many-to-many associations, which require Association Table Mapping

statement: Issuing one query per table is conceptually clean but often inefficient because SQL calls are slow remote calls, so it is often worth gathering data from multiple tables in a single joined query.

Association Table Mapping stores a many-to-many association in a separate link table that holds only the two foreign keys, with one row per associated pair and a compound primary key, and has no corresponding in-memory object or ID of its own.
Naively loading through a link table costs one query per related object, which is horribly expensive, so join the target table to the link table to fetch all the data in a single query.

Treat a link table like a Dependent Mapping for updates — nothing else should refer to it — so you can freely create and destroy links, with the simplest update deleting all existing link rows and re-creating them.

Use Association Table Mapping for many-to-many associations, where there is no real alternative; it can map other associations but its extra join makes it usually inferior to Foreign Key Mapping, except when you cannot alter existing tables or the schema already has an association table.
condition: for many-to-many associations
exception: when you cannot add columns to existing tables, or an associative table already exists

statement: When an association table also carries information about the relationship itself (such as employment details on a person/company table), it really corresponds to a true domain object rather than a mere link.

Optimize multitable queries only when you need to, because the code is more complex and awkward; put more energy into speeding up your genuinely slow queries than into eliminating many less-important ones.

Dependent Mapping has one class (the owner) perform the database mapping for a child class (the dependent); each dependent has exactly one owner, no Identity Field, no Identity Map entry, and no finder, since all finds go through the owner.

With Dependent Mapping, every load of the owner usually loads its dependents (use Lazy Load if they are expensive and rarely needed), and updates are handled by deleting all the owner's dependent rows and reinserting, which avoids analyzing what was added or removed.
Making a dependent immutable simplifies tracking whether the owner changed, because any change becomes a remove-and-add, accepting a harder in-memory model in exchange for simpler database mapping.

Use Dependent Mapping when an object is referred to by exactly one owner (typically a collection with no back pointer whose members need no identity of their own), and avoid large graphs of dependents because nothing outside the graph can refer to a dependent.
condition: a dependent must have exactly one owner and no external references

statement: Do not use Dependent Mapping together with a Unit of Work, because the delete-and-reinsert strategy conflicts with the Unit of Work's change tracking and can leave orphan rows.
exception: when using a Unit of Work

statement: Embedded Value maps an object's values into several fields of its owner's table — a special case of Dependent Mapping with a single dependent value — and the embedded class has no persistence methods of its own.
Persist all simple Value Objects such as money and date range as Embedded Value, because they have no identity and you would never want a separate table for them.
condition: for simple Value Objects

statement: Use Embedded Value on a reference object mainly when the association is one-to-one and the dependent data has little relevance or query need outside the owner; for complex structures or larger subgraphs prefer Serialized LOB.
condition: single-valued (one-to-one) association with the dependent

statement: The key advantage of Embedded Value over Serialized LOB is that SQL queries can be run against the dependent's values, so choose Embedded Value when you need those values in a query, for example for separate reporting.

Serialized LOB saves a graph of objects by serializing them into one large object (BLOB or CLOB) stored in a single database field, avoiding the many slow, awkward joins a relational hierarchy would otherwise require.

A BLOB serialization is simplest and most compact but is opaque to casual viewing and has a serious versioning problem (a class change can make old serializations unreadable), whereas a CLOB — especially XML — is human-readable and tool-supported but more verbose.

When using Serialized LOB, store the LOB where it will not be duplicated — for example a shared customer LOB in its own customer table rather than copied into every order — and ensure the serialized data is reachable only from its single owner.
exception: when you deliberately want a historical snapshot, copying is acceptable

statement: Use Serialized LOB for a chunk of the object model that will not be queried via SQL from outside the application; it works poorly when objects outside the LOB need to reference objects buried inside it.
condition: when the serialized objects are not queried from outside the application
exception: when external objects must reference objects inside the LOB

statement: Single Table Inheritance maps all fields of all classes in an inheritance hierarchy into one table, using a type or code field to indicate which class to instantiate and leaving irrelevant columns empty.

Single Table Inheritance's strengths are a single table, no joins on retrieval, and that pushing fields up or down the hierarchy needs no database change; its weaknesses are confusing sometimes-irrelevant fields, wasted space from unused columns, a possibly oversized bottleneck table, and a single shared field namespace.

You need not use one inheritance-mapping form for an entire hierarchy: it is fine to map several similar classes with Single Table Inheritance while using Concrete Table Inheritance for any class that has a lot of specific data.

Class Table Inheritance uses one database table per class in the hierarchy, with each class's fields mapping to its own table and rows linked either by a shared primary key value or by foreign keys into the superclass table.

Class Table Inheritance's strengths are that every column is relevant per row (no wasted space, easy to understand) and the model-to-database relationship is very straightforward; its weaknesses are that loading touches multiple tables (joins or multiple queries), field refactoring up or down forces database changes, supertype tables become a bottleneck, and high normalization hinders ad hoc queries.
Concrete Table Inheritance uses one table per concrete class, each containing columns for that class and all its ancestors, so superclass fields are duplicated across the subclass tables.

Concrete Table Inheritance requires keys unique across all tables in the hierarchy rather than just per table, so you need a cross-table key allocation scheme and cannot rely on the database's per-table primary-key uniqueness.
condition: when using a table-wide Identity Field with Concrete Table Inheritance

statement: Concrete Table Inheritance's strengths are self-contained tables with no irrelevant fields (good for other applications), no joins when reading a concrete class, and access load spread across tables; its weaknesses are difficult primary keys, inability to enforce database relationships to abstract classes, table changes on field refactoring, superclass field changes touching every table, and a superclass find having to check all tables.

Inheritance Mappers organize database mappers as a hierarchy where each domain class has a mapper that loads and saves only its own class's data and chains to its superclass mapper, minimizing the mapping code while supporting both abstract and concrete loading and saving.

Separate the abstract-class mapper (which loads and saves that class's specific data and is used only by the concrete mappers) from a distinct top-level mapper that provides the abstract-type interface and delegates each find, insert, or update to the right concrete mapper, rather than tangling generalization and composition on one superclass mapper.

Declare find methods on the concrete mapper subclasses so they return the concrete type, because common OO languages cannot change a method's declared return type and returning an abstract type would force callers to downcast.

Metadata Mapping holds object-relational mapping details as metadata in a tabular form that generic code processes to read, insert, and update data, replacing the tedious, repetitive code of hand-written mapping.

Metadata Mapping can be realized two ways: code generation (mapper classes generated at build time, never hand-edited and not held in source control) or reflective programming (reading field and method names from metadata at runtime).

Reflective mapping lets you change the mapping file without recompiling (even at runtime) but is slower and harder to debug, whereas code generation is more explicit and debuggable though less dynamic; on balance code generation is usually preferable.

Build a minimal metadata scheme for current needs and evolve it, handling rare special cases by overriding the generic generated or reflective code in handwritten subclasses rather than adding complexity to the metadata to cover every special case.

Metadata Mapping can interfere with automated refactoring (renaming a private field can silently break the application because tools cannot find the name hidden in metadata), but it eases database refactoring since the metadata is a statement of the schema interface.

A Query Object is an Interpreter that builds a SQL query from a structure of objects referring to classes and fields rather than tables and columns, so queries are written independently of the database schema and schema changes are localized in one place.
Build a minimally functional Query Object for your current needs and evolve it, because enhancing it later when needs grow is no more work than building a fully capable one from the start.

A Query Object expressed in object and field terms needs a Metadata Mapping to translate to the schema, and it can additionally generate different SQL per database, cope with multiple schemas, and avoid redundant queries by selecting from the Identity Map.

Use a Query Object only with a Domain Model and Data Mapper (and a Metadata Mapping for serious use); most projects do not need one because specific finder methods already hide schema details, and you are almost always better off buying a tool, though a pared-down Query Object can suit a project that cannot justify a full one.
condition: when using Domain Model with Data Mapper

statement: A Repository mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers through a collection-like interface: clients declaratively build a query specification (a criteria object) and submit it for satisfaction, encapsulating query-construction code and presenting an object-oriented view of persistence.

Repository replaces specialized finder methods on Data Mapper with specification-based selection, so client code selects objects through satisfaction of a specification rather than executing a query and never sees that the objects are not stored directly in the Repository.

A Repository's object source need not be a relational database: swap the data-mapping component via strategy objects (such as a relational strategy versus an in-memory strategy) without changing client calls, which helps with multiple data sources and with fast in-memory unit testing.

Use a Repository in a large system with many domain object types and many possible queries to cut query-setup code so clients never think in SQL, and especially where multiple data sources or an in-memory test store are wanted.
condition: in a large system with many domain types and queries

statement: Model View Controller splits user-interface interaction into three roles: the model (a nonvisual object holding domain data and behavior), the view (the display of the model), and the controller (which takes user input, manipulates the model, and updates the view).

Model View Controller embodies two separations — presentation from model and controller from view — and separating presentation from model is one of the most fundamental heuristics of good software design.

Separating presentation from model matters because the two are different concerns needing different skills and libraries, because it lets multiple presentations (rich client, web, API, command line) reuse the same model, and because nonvisual model objects are far easier to test than visual ones.

Keep the model-presentation dependency one-way: the presentation depends on the model but the model must never depend on the presentation, which simplifies model development and lets presentations change or be added freely.

When several presentations of one model are on screen at once, keep them synchronized via the Observer pattern — each presentation observes the model and refreshes when the model emits a change event — so the model needs no dependency on its presentations.
condition: when multiple presentations of a model coexist on screen

statement: Apply the presentation-from-model separation as soon as there is any nonvisual logic, skipping it only in very simple systems whose model has no real behavior; the view-from-controller separation is less important and worth doing only when helpful (rarely for rich clients, commonly for web front ends).
exception: very simple systems whose model has no real behavior

statement: A Page Controller has one input controller per logical page or action of a website — the page itself in server-page environments or a separate object — responsible for decoding the URL and form data, invoking model objects, and choosing the view to display.
Pass all relevant data from the HTTP request to the model so the model objects need no connection to the HTML request, and keep any servlet-dependent code out of the model in a separate helper class.

Handle URLs with little or no controller logic with a server page and URLs with more complex logic with a script or helper; do not force everything into one mechanism, because uniformity buys either scriptlet-laden server pages or many trivial pass-through scripts.

Choose Page Controller over Front Controller when controller logic is mostly simple, because Front Controller adds overhead that only pays off with greater navigational complexity, and the two patterns can be mixed in one site without much trouble.

A Front Controller channels all of a website's requests through a single handler that performs common behavior (such as security, internationalization, and logging) and dispatches to command objects for request-specific behavior, removing the duplication of scattered input controllers.

A Front Controller is usually built in two parts: a Web handler that receives the requests, decides which command to run, and produces no response itself, and a hierarchy of command classes that need no knowledge of the web environment.

A Front Controller's Web handler can select commands statically (explicit conditional logic with compile-time checking) or dynamically (instantiate a command class by name), and dynamic selection lets you add new commands without changing the handler.

Use an Intercepting Filter — a decorator wrapping the Front Controller's handler — to build a filter chain for cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, logging, and locale identification, configurable at runtime.

Because a Front Controller creates a new command object per request, you need not make command classes thread-safe (avoiding multithreading headaches), but you must still avoid sharing other objects such as the model objects.

Choose Front Controller over Page Controller when a site has more navigational complexity, because only one controller need be configured in the web server (easing configuration and porting) and its single controller can be enhanced at runtime with decorators.
condition: when the website has significant navigational complexity

statement: A Template View renders information into HTML by embedding markers in an otherwise static HTML page, replacing the markers with computation results at request time, so the page can be laid out in the usual way, often by nonprogrammers using WYSIWYG editors.

Limit yourself to basic Template View behavior even when using scriptlet-capable server-page technology, because heavy scriptlets prevent nonprogrammers from editing the page, a page is a poor program module that loses structural design features, and scriptlets make it too easy to mingle and duplicate the layers of an enterprise application.
condition: when using server page technology

statement: Avoid scriptlets by giving each page a regular helper object that holds all the real programming logic, so the page only calls into the helper, keeping it a pure Template View that nonprogrammers can edit.

Treat a general-purpose conditional tag (a bare IF) as a bad smell, because it turns templates into their own programming language; prefer a focused tag (such as a highlight tag) driven by a single Boolean helper property, or move the condition into the helper.
Where a Template View must take on controller or model responsibilities beyond the view, keep that program logic in the helper rather than the page.

Choose Template View for its page-structure-oriented composition, which is easier for most people to learn and nicely supports a graphic designer and a programmer working in parallel, but watch its two weaknesses: it makes putting complex logic in the page too easy, and it is harder to test than Transform View (usually needing a running web server).

A Transform View processes domain data element by element, organized as separate transforms for each kind of input element (so the rules can be reordered without affecting output), in contrast to a Template View, which is organized around the page output.

The dominant Transform View technology is XSLT, a functional language that recognizes elements and invokes the appropriate rendering transforms; it is fed XML produced by the domain logic, a serializable Data Transfer Object, or a Transaction Script, and it is usually faster to hand it a DOM than a string.

Transform View avoids two of Template View's biggest problems: it is easier to keep the transform focused only on rendering HTML, and it is easy to run and capture its output for testing without a running web server.

Choose between Transform View and Template View mainly by the team's preferred environment and available tools — HTML editors favor Template View while XSLT tooling is less mature and harder to master — noting that XSLT is portable across web platforms and natural when the source is an XML document.

A Two Step View turns domain data into HTML in two stages — first into a logical, format-free presentation structure (a logical screen of fields, tables, headers), then rendering that structure into HTML — so all HTML formatting decisions live in a single second stage.

Two Step View's value is easy global appearance change: one second-stage change affects the whole site, and N screens with M appearances need only N first stages plus M second stages instead of N times M single-stage views.

Two Step View works only when a presentation-oriented logical screen can genuinely serve the desired appearance, so a design-heavy site where each page is meant to look different has too little commonality and finds the shared logical screen too constraining.
exception: design-heavy sites where each page must look distinct

statement: Two Step View requires programmers (not just designers) to write the renderer and controller objects and presents a harder programming model to learn, but it can reduce repetitive boilerplate and lets you provide different second stages for different devices.

An Application Controller is a centralized point for screen navigation and application flow (such as wizard-style ordered screens or conditionally shown screens) that removes the duplicated flow logic which otherwise scatters across several input controllers.

An Application Controller holds two collections of references — domain commands to run against the domain layer and views to display — selecting which to invoke based on application context, commonly using Command objects or reflective string references.

Prefer an Application Controller with no links to the UI machinery, so it can be tested independently of the UI and reused across multiple presentations, treating it as an intermediate layer between presentation and domain.

Because a user interface is often a state machine where events trigger different responses depending on object state, an Application Controller is particularly amenable to representing its control flow as metadata, set either by code or from a configuration file.

Use an Application Controller when there are definite rules about the order in which screens are visited and which view to show based on object state; a good signal is having to make similar flow changes in many places, while there is little value when any screen can be visited in any order.
condition: when the application has nontrivial screen-flow and navigation rules
exception: when any screen can be visited in any order

statement: A Remote Facade is a coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects that contains no domain logic and merely translates coarse-grained remote calls into the underlying fine-grained calls, buying network efficiency while preserving the clarity and control of fine-grained objects.

Prefer coarser-grained Remote Facades — few facades each with many small methods (perhaps one per family of screens), even a single facade for a moderate application — designed around a particular client's usage rather than one facade per use case.

Apply security (access control) and transactional control at Remote Facade methods, since each call makes a good transaction boundary — you do not want a transaction left open while control returns to the client, because transactions are not built for such long-running cases.

A Remote Facade must contain no domain logic — it is only a thin skin — so put any workflow or coordination logic in the fine-grained objects or in a separate nonremotable Transaction Script, ensuring the whole application can run locally without the facades and without duplicating code.

Use Remote Facade whenever you need remote access to a fine-grained object model (most commonly between a presentation and a Domain Model running in different processes), but not within a single process nor with an inherently coarse-grained Transaction Script.
condition: when a fine-grained object model must be accessed remotely
exception: within a single process, or with a Transaction Script

statement: A Data Transfer Object carries data between processes to reduce the number of expensive remote method calls, holding all the data for a call in a single serializable object.

A Data Transfer Object usually carries more data than the remote object requested and aggregates data from several server objects (an order plus its customer, line items, and products), because remote-call latency makes it better to send too much than to make multiple calls.

You usually cannot transfer Domain Model objects directly because they form a complex web that is hard to serialize and you do not want domain classes copied onto the other side, so transfer a simplified form via a Data Transfer Object of simple fields and a simple (typically hierarchic) graph present on both sides.

Design Data Transfer Objects around the needs of a particular client, which is why they often correspond to web pages or GUI screens, sharing a single DTO when different presentations require similar data.

Use a platform's built-in serialization for Data Transfer Objects whenever available, since DTOs are simple structures; otherwise generate the serialization (keeping the generator only as complex as needed) or use reflection, measuring its performance cost.

Prefer a change-tolerant serialization (XML, or a dictionary-based binary form) over a pure binary serialization for a Data Transfer Object, because pure binary breaks on any structural change — even adding an optional field — when client and server fall out of sync.

Use a separate assembler object (a Mapper) to build a Data Transfer Object from domain objects and to update the model from it, keeping the domain model independent of the DTO and the external interface formats, which change over time.

Use a Data Transfer Object whenever you need to transfer multiple items of data between two processes in a single method call, and especially when components communicate via XML, since a DTO encapsulates the painful XML DOM and is easy to generate.
condition: when transferring multiple data items between processes in one call

statement: The sound distribution approach is to design the application without distribution first and then layer distribution on top of it using Remote Facades and Data Transfer Objects, so core patterns keep their value across changing remoting technologies.

Optimistic Offline Lock prevents conflicts across a business transaction that spans several system transactions by validating, just before commit, that no other session has changed the records since this session loaded them — assuming conflict is unlikely so multiple users can work the same data at once.
An Optimistic Offline Lock must be acquired within the same system transaction that commits the changes, or the business transaction will not maintain record-data consistency.

The common Optimistic Offline Lock implementation associates a version number with each record: compare the session's version to the current version, add the version to the criteria of UPDATE and DELETE statements, and commit an incremented version, treating a returned row count of 0 as a conflict that must roll back.
Use a version count rather than a modification timestamp for optimistic concurrency checks, because system clocks are too unreliable, especially when coordinating across multiple servers.

Optimistic Offline Lock can also detect an inconsistent read by version-checking the records a transaction merely depends on (such as the customer address used for a tax calculation), but rereading the version to check works only at repeatable-read or stronger isolation, otherwise you must increment the version.
condition: depends on the system transaction isolation level

statement: Concurrency management in a business application is as much a domain (business) issue as a technical one, since whether a given overlap of two sessions truly constitutes a conflict is a business decision.

Make Optimistic Offline Lock the default approach to business-transaction conflict management because it is much easier to implement and less prone to defects than pessimistic locking, asking instead when the optimistic approach alone is not good enough.

Use optimistic concurrency when the chance of conflict between two business transactions is low, and use Pessimistic Offline Lock when conflict is likely or its cost is unacceptable, because announcing a conflict only at commit — after the user has finished work — is not user-friendly.
condition: when conflict probability is low
exception: when conflict is likely or its cost is unacceptable

statement: Pessimistic Offline Lock prevents conflicts by forcing a business transaction to acquire a lock on data before it starts using it, so that once a transaction begins you are fairly sure it will complete without being bounced — assuming the chance of conflict is high.

Pessimistic locking offers three lock types: an exclusive write lock (acquired only to edit, ignoring reads), an exclusive read lock (acquired even to load, severely limiting concurrency), and a read/write lock (read and write mutually exclusive but concurrent reads allowed, giving the best concurrency at the cost of complexity).

Choose the pessimistic lock type to maximize concurrency, meet business needs, and minimize code complexity, because the wrong locking strategy cannot be saved by a proper technical implementation — so the locking strategy belongs in the domain model and must be understood by domain modelers.

Implement Pessimistic Offline Lock with a single lock manager backed by exactly one lock table mapping locks to owners (a singleton in memory, or a database table once the application server is clustered), and have business transactions interact only with the manager, never with a lock object directly.

Acquire a pessimistic lock before loading the data (so you are guaranteed the latest version), lock the record's ID or primary key (so the lock can be obtained before loading), and release locks when the business transaction completes.

When a pessimistic lock cannot be acquired, have the lock manager throw immediately rather than wait, because across multi-system-transaction business transactions waiting for a lock invites deadlock and complicated timeout code; failing fast removes the burden of coping with deadlock.
Acquire contentious pessimistic locks as early as possible — ideally all of them before the user begins work — so that any failure to lock occurs early in the business transaction.

Manage lock timeouts for lost sessions, since a crashed client abandons its locks; ideally release a session's locks when the application server's HTTP session invalidates, or treat any lock older than a set age as invalid.
condition: particularly for web applications where sessions are regularly abandoned

statement: Use Pessimistic Offline Lock only where it is truly required (high conflict chance or unacceptable conflict cost), because locking every entity creates tremendous data contention; it is most effective as a complement to Optimistic Offline Lock rather than a replacement.
condition: when conflict chance is high or conflict cost is unacceptable

statement: Do not use offline locking techniques when a business transaction fits within a single system transaction; use the built-in mechanisms such as SELECT FOR UPDATE or entity-EJB locking instead, and remember that all offline locking techniques depend on the system having a real transaction monitor underneath.
exception: when the business transaction fits in a single system transaction

statement: A Coarse-Grained Lock covers a set of related objects with a single lock, which simplifies the locking action and frees you from having to load all members of the group in order to lock them, avoiding the performance and contention costs of per-object locks.

Implement a Coarse-Grained Lock by creating a single point of contention for the group (for example a shared version object under Optimistic Offline Lock, or a shared lockable token under Pessimistic Offline Lock) and providing the shortest possible path to find it.

For an aggregate — a cluster of objects with a single root access point and a boundary — use a root lock so that locking the root locks all members; implement navigation to the root (via direct links or a parent chain, using Lazy Load) so locking any member locks the root.
condition: when the related objects form an aggregate

statement: Use a Coarse-Grained Lock to satisfy business requirements (for example, locking a lease should lock all its assets) and because acquiring and releasing a single lock is cheaper, but beware of creating unnatural object relationships purely to facilitate one.

Implicit Lock has framework or Layer Supertype code acquire offline locks rather than relying on developers to do so explicitly, because a single forgotten lock can render an entire offline-locking scheme useless and such errors usually evade test suites.

Do not implicitly acquire write locks (exclusive write or the write part of read/write) because the framework cannot tell when to acquire them to fail fast and they most limit concurrency; instead ensure a write lock has been obtained before commit and throw a concurrency exception if not.

Implicit Lock lets developers ignore the mechanics of locking but not its consequences (such as deadlock with waiting schemes); its danger is that business transactions can fail in unexpected ways once developers stop thinking about locking.
Use Implicit Lock in all but the simplest applications that have no concept of a framework, because the risk of a single forgotten lock is too great.
exception: the simplest applications with no framework

statement: Client Session State stores session data on the client, sent with every request and returned with every response, which lets the server be completely stateless; even the most server-oriented design needs at least a client-held session identifier.

HTML Client Session State has three common forms: URL parameters (easiest for a small amount of data but limited by URL size and breaking bookmarks), hidden fields (serialize state into them but the data is visible in the page source), and cookies (sent automatically but size-limited and breakable if the user disables them).

Use Client Session State for stateless servers with maximal clustering and failover resilience, but recognize its cost grows with data volume (transfer time) and it is insecure — any client data can be viewed or altered, so encrypt anything sensitive and completely revalidate everything that comes back.
condition: best when the amount of session data is small

statement: Almost always use Client Session State for session identification (just a single number that burdens none of the storage schemes), and guard against session stealing by using a random or hashed session ID.

Server Session State keeps the session state on the server, in the simplest form a session object held in memory keyed by session ID, or serialized to a memento for persistent storage when memory or failover demands it.

To support clustering and failover, store passivated Server Session State somewhere generally accessible (a shared server, or a database session table holding a Serialized LOB) rather than on a single application server, accepting a longer activation time that caching can largely offset.

Do not blanket-prefer stateless session beans over stateful ones for performance; load-test first, because the performance difference appears only under heavy load and stateful beans are easier to program.

Server Session State's great appeal is simplicity — often no programming at all for the in-memory case — with the real programming effort appearing in session maintenance for clustering and failover, which can be more trouble than other options when session data is small or easily tabularized.

Database Session State stores session data as committed data in the database, with the server object pulling it per request via a client-held session ID, mixing data local to the current interaction with committed data relevant to all interactions.

Separate pending session data from record data so it does not appear in ordinary queries, using either a session-ID/isPending field on each row (invasive — every record query must filter it out) or a separate set of pending tables cloned from the real ones (less invasive but adds table-selection logic to the mapping code).

When using pending tables for Database Session State, clone them exactly from the real tables (same field names plus a session ID), which lets you forgo record-data integrity and validation rules until the session commits while keeping the mapping logic similar.
condition: when using separate pending tables

statement: You can avoid all the hassles of pending data by designing the system so that all data is treated as record data, which makes Database Session State much easier to work with when that design is feasible.
