Database Session State gains the pooling and clustering benefits of stateless servers but pays the per-request cost of reading and writing the data to the database (cacheable for reads, not writes); its clustering and failover are usually more straightforward than with Server Session State.

A Gateway encapsulates access to an external system or resource by wrapping its specialized API behind an interface that looks like a regular object, so the rest of the application need not understand the resource's API and swapping the resource only changes the Gateway.
Keep a Gateway as minimal as possible — focused only on adapting the external service and providing a good point for a Service Stub — and put any more complex logic in the Gateway's clients.

Consider a Gateway whenever you have an awkward interface to something external, even if you believe the resource will never change, because it contains the awkwardness, makes surrounding code easier to read, and gives a clear point at which to deploy Service Stubs for testing.
A Mapper is an insulating layer that controls communication between two subsystems without either subsystem being aware of it, invoked by a third subsystem or as an observer of one of them.

Prefer the simpler Gateway to a Mapper for most external-resource access, using a Mapper only when you must ensure neither subsystem has any dependency on the interaction — mainly complex, independent interactions such as database access (Data Mapper).
condition: when neither subsystem may depend on the interaction

statement: A Layer Supertype is a single superclass for all types in a layer that holds common features (such as Identity Field handling) you do not want duplicated across the system; use one, or several when a layer has more than one kind of object.

Separated Interface defines an interface in a separate package from its implementation, exploiting the fact that an implementation depends on its interface but not vice versa, so a client can depend on the interface package while remaining completely unaware of the implementation.

Place a Separated Interface in the client's own package when there is a single client (so the client developers own the interface definition), or in a third package when there are multiple clients or when the implementers own the definition.

Use Separated Interface only when you need to break a dependency or want multiple independent implementations, not for every class, because keeping separate interfaces and implementations (often with factory classes too) is extra work, and separating them later is a simple refactoring.

A Registry is a well-known, global-looking object used to find common objects and services when you have no appropriate object to navigate from; prefer a static-method interface but rarely static fields, since static mutable fields prevent substitution (for example for testing).

Implement a Registry to match its data's scope (process, thread, or session) behind a uniform interface the caller need not distinguish; do not use a singleton for mutable data in a multi-threaded environment (use thread-specific storage instead), reserving the singleton for immutable data.
exception: a singleton is fine for immutable process-scoped data

statement: Prefer an explicit Registry class over a bare map for global data, for explicit methods, type safety, and encapsulation that allows later refactoring; but treat any global data as guilty until proven innocent and use a Registry only as a last resort, preferring regular inter-object references.

A Value Object bases equality on its field values rather than identity, distinguishing it from a reference object whose equality is identity-based; Value Objects are small, easily created, and commonly passed around by value.

Make Value Objects immutable in languages without special value support, so that no field changes after creation, in order to avoid aliasing bugs where two owners share one value object and one owner's change unexpectedly alters the other's.
condition: in languages that lack first-class value-object support

statement: Do not persist Value Objects as their own complete records; persist them with Embedded Value (usually best because they are small and it allows SQL querying of their data) or Serialized LOB.

Represent monetary values with a Money Value Object holding an amount and a currency, because money is not a first-class type in mainstream languages, which leads to errors from mixing currencies and from rounding to the smallest currency unit.

Store a Money amount as an integral or fixed-decimal type and absolutely avoid any floating-point type, because floating point reintroduces exactly the rounding errors a Money class exists to prevent.

Make Money arithmetic currency-aware (treat adding different currencies as an error, or use a money bag), and distinguish proportional multiplication (such as a tax rate) from allocating a sum across several places, using an allocator function for the latter so that no pennies are lost or gained.

Encapsulate currency conversion in a convertor object rather than a simple exchange-rate multiplication, because some conversions (such as the fixed euro rates) require specific roundings that plain multiplication gets wrong.

Use a Money type for essentially all monetary numeric calculation, to encapsulate rounding behavior (reducing rounding errors) and to ease multi-currency work; the common performance objection rarely makes a noticeable difference and the encapsulation often makes tuning easier.

Instead of returning null — which defeats polymorphism and forces duplicated null-test code throughout the callers — or some other odd value, return a Special Case object that presents the same interface the caller expects.

Implement a Special Case as a subclass that overrides the type's methods with harmless behavior (for example a null customer), substituting an instance of it wherever a null would otherwise occur, and often share instances via a flyweight when the instances need not be distinguished.
exception: when distinct instances must accumulate state, such as charges against an occupant, keep them separate rather than sharing one flyweight

statement: A null can mean different things — no customer versus a customer who is not yet known — so consider providing separate Special Cases for the missing and the unknown cases, and a Special Case commonly overrides a method by returning another Special Case.

Use Special Case whenever multiple places in the system repeat the same behavior after a conditional check for a particular class instance or after a null check, replacing the duplicated checks with a polymorphic substitute.

A Plugin links classes during configuration rather than compilation, giving centralized runtime configuration so that establishing a new deployment configuration does not require editing conditional statements scattered across many factories, rebuilding, and redeploying.

Define each environment-varying behavior with a Separated Interface and have a Plugin factory state its linking rules at a single external point (such as a text or properties file), binding implementations dynamically at runtime so reconfiguration needs no rebuild.

Plugin works best in a language that supports reflection, where the factory maps interface names to implementation class names with no compile-time dependency and need not change when implementations are added; without reflection, still establish a central configuration point and use factory conditional logic.
Use Plugin whenever you have behaviors that require different implementations based on the runtime environment.
condition: when behavior must vary by runtime environment

statement: A Service Stub removes a dependence on a problematic (often remote, third-party) service during testing by replacing it with an implementation that runs locally, fast, and in memory, so an unreliable or undelivered service cannot slow down or break the development process.

Access the real service through a Gateway defined as a Separated Interface so a stub implementation can be substituted, load the desired implementation via a Plugin, and keep the Service Stub as simple as possible because complexity defeats its purpose.
Use a Service Stub whenever dependence on a particular service is hindering your development and testing.
condition: when a service dependency hinders development or testing

statement: A Record Set is an in-memory representation of tabular data that looks exactly like the result of a SQL query yet can be generated and manipulated by other parts of the system, which marries the ease of data-aware UI tooling with a real place to put business logic.

A Record Set is usually supplied by the platform (such as an ADO.NET data set or a JDBC 2.0 row set); disconnecting it from its data source lets it be passed around the network and serve as a Data Transfer Object, and platforms increasingly let it act as a Unit of Work that is returned to the data source and committed under Optimistic Offline Lock.

Prefer an explicit (typed) Record Set interface — such as ADO.NET strongly-typed data sets or your own code-generated record sets — over an implicit one, because implicit interfaces (and passing data around in dictionaries) lose type information and hide which columns or properties are available.

Use a Record Set when your environment relies on it as a common way of manipulating data (for example data-aware UI tools), and in that case organize domain logic with a Table Module: get a Record Set from the database, pass it to a Table Module for derived calculations, pass it to the UI for display and editing, pass it back to a Table Module for validation, then commit the updates.
condition: when the environment provides Record-Set-based data-aware tooling

statement: Developers commonly begin coding an application without a formal architecture in place.
Without a clear, well-defined architecture, most developers default to the traditional layered (n-tier) pattern, creating implicit layers by separating source-code modules into packages.
Separating modules into implicit packages without clear roles tends to produce unorganized modules lacking clear roles, responsibilities, and relationships — the 'big ball of mud' anti-pattern.
Applications lacking a formal architecture are generally tightly coupled, brittle, and difficult to change.
Without a defined architecture it is hard to determine an application's architectural characteristics (scalability, performance, responsiveness, deployment) without understanding every component.
Architecture patterns help define the basic characteristics and behavior of an application, with different patterns naturally favoring different qualities such as scalability or agility.
Knowing the characteristics, strengths, and weaknesses of each architecture pattern is necessary to choose one that meets specific business needs.
An architect must always justify architecture decisions, particularly the choice of an architecture pattern.
The layered (n-tier) architecture is the most common architecture pattern and the de facto standard for most Java EE applications.
The layered pattern closely matches traditional IT communication and organizational structures, making it a natural choice for most business-application development.
In the layered pattern, components are organized into horizontal layers, each performing a specific role such as presentation or business logic.
The layered pattern does not mandate a fixed number of layers, but most implementations use four standard layers: presentation, business, persistence, and database.
The business and persistence layers are sometimes merged into a single business layer.
condition: particularly when persistence logic such as SQL is embedded within the business-layer components

statement: Smaller applications may have only three layers while larger, more complex applications may have five or more.
condition: depending on application size and complexity

statement: Each layer forms an abstraction around the work needed to satisfy a business request, so one layer need not know how another performs its work.
Separation of concerns — each layer handling only its own logic — is a key strength of the layered pattern that makes applications easier to develop, test, govern, and maintain.
In a closed layer, a request must pass through the layer directly below it to reach lower layers.
The 'layers of isolation' concept means a change in one layer generally does not affect components in other layers.

Giving the presentation layer direct access to the persistence layer couples SQL changes to both the business and presentation layers, producing a tightly coupled application that is hard and expensive to change.
Layers of isolation also makes each layer independent with little knowledge of others' internals, so a presentation-framework change (e.g., JSP to JSF) leaves the business layer unaffected.
condition: as long as the contracts (e.g., model) between the presentation and business layers remain unchanged

statement: Although closed layers promote isolation, it sometimes makes sense to make a layer open so requests may bypass it.
Adding a shared-services layer below the business layer architecturally restricts access to shared service components to the business layer rather than the presentation layer.
condition: when common services should be reachable from the business layer but hidden from the presentation layer

statement: An open layer lets requests bypass it and go directly to the layer below, so a services layer marked open allows the business layer to reach the persistence layer directly.
Failing to document which layers are open or closed, and why, usually yields tightly coupled, brittle architectures that are hard to test, maintain, and deploy.
The architecture sinkhole anti-pattern occurs when requests pass through multiple layers as simple pass-through with little or no logic performed in each layer.
Use the 80-20 rule to assess the architecture sinkhole anti-pattern: roughly 20% pass-through and 80% business-logic requests is typical and healthy.
If most requests are simple pass-through, consider opening some layers, accepting that change control becomes harder due to reduced isolation.
condition: when the pass-through-to-business-logic ratio is reversed

statement: The layered pattern tends toward monolithic applications even when the presentation and business layers are split into separate deployable units.
The monolithic tendency of the layered pattern poses potential issues for deployment, robustness and reliability, performance, and scalability.
The layered pattern is a solid general-purpose pattern and a good starting point when the best-suited pattern is not yet known.
The layered pattern rates LOW on overall agility because its monolithic nature and tight coupling make changes cumbersome and time-consuming.
The layered pattern rates LOW on ease of deployment because a small change can force redeployment of the entire application and it does not fit a continuous-delivery pipeline.
The layered pattern rates HIGH on testability because layers can be mocked or stubbed to isolate tests.
The layered pattern rates LOW on performance because requests must traverse multiple layers to fulfill a business request.
exception: although some layered architectures can perform adequately

statement: The layered pattern rates LOW on scalability because tightly coupled, monolithic implementations have too broad a granularity, making scaling expensive.
The layered pattern rates HIGH on ease of development because it is well known, not overly complex, and organizations are commonly structured by layer.
Conway's law observes that a system's design tends to mirror the communication and organizational structure of the organization that builds it.
The event-driven architecture is a popular distributed, asynchronous pattern used to build highly scalable applications.
The event-driven pattern is highly adaptable, suiting both small applications and large, complex ones.
Event-driven architectures are built from highly decoupled, single-purpose event-processing components that asynchronously receive and process events.
The event-driven pattern has two main topologies: mediator and broker.
Use the mediator topology when an event requires orchestration of multiple steps through a central mediator.
condition: when an event has multiple steps needing orchestration

statement: Use the broker topology when events can be chained together without a central mediator.
condition: when the event flow is relatively simple and central orchestration is not wanted

statement: The mediator topology has four component types: event queues, an event mediator, event channels, and event processors.
The event mediator orchestrates the steps of an initial event but does not itself perform the business logic; it only knows the steps required.
An event-driven architecture commonly has from a dozen to several hundred event queues, which may be message queues, web-service endpoints, or a combination.
The pattern distinguishes an initial event, received by the mediator, from processing events that the mediator generates for the processors.
Event channels may be message queues or topics, but topics are most common in the mediator topology so multiple processors can each act on a processing event.
Each event processor should be self-contained and perform a single business task without relying on other event processors to complete its work.

The event mediator can be implemented with open-source integration hubs (e.g., Spring Integration, Apache Camel, Mule ESB) for simple flows, with BPEL and an engine for more sophisticated orchestration, or with a BPM such as jBPM for very large processes involving human interaction.
Match the event-mediator implementation to orchestration complexity; using a simple integration hub for complex orchestration, or a BPM for simple routing, is a recipe for failure.
In the broker topology there is no central mediator; the flow is distributed across event processors in a chain through a lightweight message broker such as ActiveMQ or HornetQ.
The broker topology has two component types: a broker, which may be centralized or federated, and event processors.
In the broker topology each event processor processes an event and then publishes a new event indicating the action it performed.
In the broker topology an event may be published but consumed by no processor.
condition: common when evolving an application or providing for future functionality

statement: The broker topology works like a relay race: once an event processor hands off its event, it is no longer involved in processing it.

The event-driven pattern is relatively complex to implement because of its asynchronous, distributed nature, requiring handling of remote availability, unresponsiveness, and broker or mediator reconnection.
The event-driven pattern lacks atomic transactions across a single business process because decoupled, distributed processors make a shared transactional unit of work hard to maintain.
Plan event-processor granularity around which events can run independently; if an undivided unit of work would be split across processors, the event-driven pattern is probably the wrong choice.
condition: when an operation that should be one transaction would be split across processors

statement: Settle on a standard data format such as XML or JSON and a contract-versioning policy from the start, because event-processor contract creation, maintenance, and governance is one of the hardest aspects of the pattern.
The event-driven pattern rates HIGH on agility because single-purpose, decoupled processors keep changes isolated and quick to make.
The event-driven pattern rates HIGH on ease of deployment, and the broker topology is easier to deploy than the mediator topology, whose mediator is somewhat coupled to its processors.
The event-driven pattern rates LOW on testability because generating events needs specialized test tooling and asynchronicity complicates testing.
The event-driven pattern rates HIGH on performance because decoupled, parallel asynchronous operations outweigh the cost of queuing and dequeuing messages.
exception: although a poorly designed messaging infrastructure can still perform badly

statement: The event-driven pattern rates HIGH on scalability because independent processors can each be scaled separately for fine-grained scalability.
The event-driven pattern rates LOW on ease of development because of asynchronicity, contract creation, and the advanced error handling needed for unresponsive processors and failed brokers.
The microkernel (plug-in) architecture is a natural fit for product-based applications.
A product-based application is one packaged and released in versions like a typical third-party product.
Internal business applications released like products, with versions, release notes, and pluggable features, also fit the microkernel pattern.
The microkernel pattern adds application features as plug-ins to a core, giving extensibility plus feature separation and isolation.
The microkernel pattern has two component types: a core system and plug-in modules.

The core system traditionally contains only the minimal functionality needed to make the system operational; in business applications it is the general business logic without custom special-case code.
Plug-in modules are stand-alone, independent components holding specialized processing and custom code that extend the core.
Keep inter-plug-in communication to a minimum to avoid dependency issues; plug-ins should generally be independent of one another.
exception: although a plug-in may be deliberately designed to require other plug-ins when necessary

statement: The core system locates plug-ins through a plug-in registry holding each plug-in's name, data contract, and remote-access protocol details.
Plug-ins can connect to the core via OSGi, messaging, web services, or point-to-point binding; the pattern requires only that plug-ins stay independent.
condition: the connection type chosen depends on the application type and specific needs

statement: When a third-party plug-in's contract cannot be controlled, place an adapter between the plug-in contract and your standard contract so the core needs no plug-in-specific code.
condition: when plug-ins are built by third parties using their own contracts

statement: When using standard plug-in contracts such as XML or a Java Map, create a versioning strategy from the start.
The Eclipse IDE exemplifies the microkernel pattern: a basic core editor that becomes a highly customizable product as plug-ins are added.
Internet browsers are another microkernel example, gaining capabilities through plug-ins beyond the core browser.

Insurance claims processing fits the microkernel pattern: a core holds the basic claim logic while each plug-in holds one state's specific rules, so state rules can be added, removed, or changed with little effect on the core or other plug-ins.
The microkernel pattern can be embedded within another architecture pattern to isolate a specific volatile area of an application.
The microkernel pattern supports evolutionary design and incremental development: build a solid core first, then add features without major core changes.

For product-based applications — especially products that release features over time and need control over which users get which features — the microkernel pattern should be the first-choice starting architecture.
condition: for product-based applications releasing features over time

statement: If the microkernel pattern stops satisfying requirements over time, the application can be refactored to another pattern better suited to those requirements.
The microkernel pattern rates HIGH on agility because changes are isolated in loosely coupled plug-ins and the core tends to stabilize quickly.
The microkernel pattern rates HIGH on ease of deployment because plug-ins can often be hot-deployed at runtime, minimizing downtime.
condition: depending on how the pattern is implemented

statement: The microkernel pattern rates HIGH on testability because plug-ins can be tested in isolation and mocked by the core.
The microkernel pattern rates HIGH on performance in practice because the application can be streamlined to only the features needed, even though the pattern is not inherently high-performance.
exception: although the pattern does not naturally lend itself to high performance

statement: The JBoss Application Server illustrates microkernel performance tuning: unused features such as remote access, messaging, and caching can be removed to free memory, CPU, and threads.
The microkernel pattern rates LOW on scalability because implementations are usually product-based, smaller, and deployed as single units.
exception: although plug-in-level scalability is sometimes possible

statement: The microkernel pattern rates LOW on ease of development because contract versioning, plug-in registries, granularity, and connectivity choices add complexity requiring thoughtful design and governance.
The microservices architecture is gaining ground as a viable alternative to monolithic applications and service-oriented architecture (SOA).
Because microservices is still evolving, there is confusion in the industry about what the pattern is and how to implement it.
A core microservices concept is the separately deployed unit: each component is deployed independently, enabling streamlined deployment, increased scalability, and high decoupling.
The key microservices unit is the service component, not the 'service', and it can range in granularity from a single module to a large portion of the application.
A service component contains one or more modules representing a single-purpose function or an independent portion of a large business application.
Choosing the right service-component granularity is one of the biggest challenges in a microservices architecture.

Microservices is a distributed architecture in which all components are fully decoupled and accessed through a remote-access protocol such as REST, AMQP, or JMS, which is how it achieves its scalability and deployment characteristics.
Microservices evolved from real problems with other patterns — monolithic layered applications and SOA — rather than being created as a solution waiting for a problem.

The path from monolithic applications to microservices was driven by continuous delivery; a monolithic application's tightly coupled single deployable unit makes it hard to change, test, and deploy, producing brittle 'monthly deployment' cycles.
Microservices addresses monolithic problems by splitting the application into multiple deployable service components that are developed, tested, and deployed independently.
SOA offers powerful abstraction, connectivity, and orchestration but is complex, expensive, hard to understand and implement, and usually overkill for most applications.
Microservices addresses SOA's complexity by simplifying the notion of a service, eliminating orchestration needs, and simplifying connectivity and access to service components.
Microservices has three common topologies: API REST-based, application REST-based, and centralized messaging.
The API REST-based topology exposes very fine-grained, self-contained services of one or two modules through a separately deployed web-based API layer.
condition: useful for websites exposing small self-contained services through an API

statement: The application REST-based topology receives requests through traditional web or fat-client business screens, with the UI deployed separately and accessing coarser-grained service components via REST.
condition: common for small-to-medium business applications of relatively low complexity

statement: The centralized messaging topology uses a lightweight central message broker instead of REST, providing advanced queuing, asynchronous messaging, monitoring, error handling, and better load balancing and scalability.
condition: typically used in larger business applications needing more control over the transport layer

statement: Do not confuse the centralized messaging topology with SOA or 'SOA-Lite'; its broker is only a lightweight transport and performs no orchestration, transformation, or complex routing.
The single-point-of-failure and bottleneck risks of a centralized broker are mitigated by broker clustering and broker federation.
If you must orchestrate service components from the user-interface or API layer, the service components are probably too fine-grained.
condition: if orchestration is needed from the UI or API layer

statement: If inter-service communication is needed to process a single request, the service components are probably too fine-grained or not partitioned correctly by business function.
condition: if inter-service calls are needed to process one request

statement: Handle a service component's need for another's data through a shared database rather than inter-service calls, to avoid undesired coupling.
For shared functionality it can be acceptable to copy small portions of logic across service components, violating DRY, to keep them independent and separately deployable.
exception: this trades redundancy for independence and is typically limited to small utility code

statement: If you cannot avoid service-component orchestration regardless of granularity, microservices is probably not the right pattern, since its distributed nature makes a single transactional unit of work across components very hard and would require a transaction-compensation framework.
condition: when service-component orchestration is unavoidable

statement: Microservices generally produces more robust, more scalable applications that better support continuous delivery than monolithic or SOA applications.
Microservices enables real-time production deployments, reducing the need for big-bang monthly or weekend deployments, because only changed service components need redeployment.

With a single service-component instance you can redirect users to a waiting page during a hot-deployment, while with multiple instances you can swap them in and out for continuous availability during deployment.
condition: depending on whether one or multiple instances of the service component run

statement: As a distributed architecture, microservices shares event-driven's challenges: contract creation, maintenance, and governance, remote-system availability, and remote authentication and authorization.
Microservices rates HIGH on agility because separately deployed, loosely coupled service components keep change isolated.
Microservices rates HIGH on ease of deployment because of the decoupled nature of its components.
Microservices rates HIGH on testability because isolated service components allow scoped, targeted testing and per-component regression testing instead of testing the whole monolith.
Microservices rates LOW on performance because its distributed nature does not naturally favor high-performance applications.
exception: although individual microservices applications can be built to perform well

statement: Microservices rates HIGH on scalability because each service component can be scaled individually for fine-tuned scaling.
Microservices rates HIGH on ease of development because isolated, smaller-scope components reduce the chance one change affects another and reduce cross-team coordination.
Most web-based business applications follow the flow browser to web server to application server to database server.
As user load increases, bottlenecks appear successively at the web-server, then application-server, then database-server tiers.
Scaling out web servers is relatively easy and inexpensive but under high load usually just moves the bottleneck to the application server.
Scaling application servers is more complex and expensive than scaling web servers and usually just moves the bottleneck to the database, the hardest and most expensive tier to scale.
In high-volume applications with extremely large concurrent user loads, the database is usually the final limiting factor on how many transactions can be processed concurrently.
Even with caching and database-scaling products, scaling out a conventional application for extreme loads remains very difficult.
The space-based architecture is specifically designed to solve scalability and concurrency problems and also suits applications with variable, unpredictable concurrent user volumes.
Solving extreme and variable scalability architecturally is often a better approach than scaling out a database or retrofitting caching into a non-scalable architecture.

The space-based (cloud) pattern removes the central-database constraint and uses replicated in-memory data grids to achieve high scalability; it is named after the tuple-space concept of distributed shared memory.
Application data is held in memory and replicated across all active processing units, so removing the central database removes the database bottleneck and yields near-infinite scalability.
Processing units can be started and shut down dynamically as load rises and falls, which addresses variable scalability.
The space-based pattern has two primary components: the processing unit and the virtualized middleware.
A processing unit contains the application modules, an in-memory data grid, an optional asynchronous persistent store for failover, and a replication engine.
The contents of a processing unit vary by application size: smaller applications use a single processing unit while larger applications split functionality across multiple processing units.
condition: depending on application size and functional areas

statement: The virtualized middleware controls data synchronization and request handling and contains four components: a messaging grid, a data grid, a processing grid, and a deployment manager, which may be custom-built or third-party.
The messaging grid manages input requests and session state, determining which active processing unit receives each request using an algorithm ranging from round-robin to next-available.
The data grid is the most important component of the space-based pattern; it works with each processing unit's replication engine to keep data synchronized on updates.
Every processing unit must hold exactly the same data in its in-memory data grid because the messaging grid may route a request to any unit.
Data replication between processing units happens in parallel and asynchronously, sometimes completing in microseconds.
The processing grid is an optional component that mediates and orchestrates requests spanning multiple processing-unit types.
The deployment manager dynamically starts and stops processing units based on monitored response times and load, and is critical to achieving variable scalability.
The space-based architecture is complex and expensive to implement.
The space-based pattern suits smaller web-based applications with variable load, such as social-media and bidding or auction sites.
condition: for smaller web-based applications with variable load
exception: not well suited to traditional large-scale relational-database applications with large amounts of operational data

statement: Although the space-based pattern needs no central datastore, one is commonly included to load the in-memory grid initially and to asynchronously persist updates.
It is common to partition volatile, widely used transactional data away from non-active data to reduce each processing unit's in-memory footprint.
Despite the 'cloud-based' alternative name, space-based processing units and middleware can run on local servers, not only on cloud or PaaS hosting.

Because space-based product implementations such as GemFire, GigaSpaces, and Oracle Coherence vary widely in cost and capability — especially replication speed — establish your goals and needs before selecting a product.
The space-based pattern rates HIGH on agility because processing units can be brought up and down quickly to respond to load changes and code changes.
The space-based pattern rates HIGH on ease of deployment because cloud-based tooling lets dynamic applications be pushed out to servers easily.
The space-based pattern rates LOW on testability because reproducing very high user loads in a test environment is expensive and time-consuming.
The space-based pattern rates HIGH on performance because of in-memory data access and built-in caching mechanisms.
The space-based pattern rates HIGH on scalability because little or no dependency on a centralized database removes the limiting bottleneck.

The space-based pattern rates LOW on ease of development because sophisticated caching and in-memory-grid products are unfamiliar and source code must be written carefully to protect performance and scalability.
When scalability is the primary architectural concern, the event-driven, microservices, and space-based patterns are good candidate choices.
Choosing the layered pattern means deployment, performance, and scalability may be risk areas to watch.
A pattern-analysis comparison guides selection, but you must also weigh infrastructure support, developer skill set, project budget, deadlines, and application size.
Choosing the right architecture pattern is critical because once an architecture is in place it is very hard and expensive to change.
Sharing a database among multiple services creates a coupling point that makes it hard to know which schema changes are safe and prohibits independent evolution of the coupled codebases.
condition: when a database schema is shared across multiple services

statement: Hiding information between modules is what lets the parts of a system be changed independently.
Exposing data and functionality only through service interfaces, with no direct datastore reads, shared memory, or backdoors, is the discipline that enables team autonomy.
Turning a set of largely independent applications into a web of highly connected synchronous services raises the chance that one flaky service degrades or halts the whole system.
Service-based architectures significantly increase the probability of being paged at 3 a.m. when one or more services go down.
Messaging systems decouple parts of a company so they can operate independently and make it easier to plug new systems into the real-time event stream.

Banks that had installed real-time trade eventing across product-aligned silos met the one-minute trade-reporting regulation easily, whereas a single batch-driven system on the critical path made it unattainable.
condition: under a regulation requiring trading activity to be reported within one minute

statement: Traditional messaging systems' absence of history limits their value, because business operations still need historical data even though recent events usually have more value.

A replayable log such as Kafka acts as an event store: a middle ground between a messaging system and a database that decouples services while providing a fault-tolerant, scalable shared source of truth.
Microservices do not share databases with one another (the IntegrationDatabase antipattern) because richly shared database APIs make it hard to reason about how one application affects others.
The business facts services choose to share ('data on the outside') are the most tightly coupled data of all, and that coupling worsens as an ecosystem gains more services.
The solution to tightly coupled shared data is to move it into your own application as pure data movement, giving a level of operability and control unachievable with a direct runtime dependency.
The replayable-log approach has two primary benefits: reacting to events happening now, and a central repository that can push whole datasets wherever they are needed.
Streaming is a fundamental shift in mindset that rethinks the business as an evolving stream of data and services as functions that transform those streams into something new.
As a ballpark, Kafka ingests at network speed but replication overhead typically divides that by three, so a three-node 10 GbE cluster ingests around 1 GB/s in practice.
Stream processing queries compute continuously: each time an input arrives the query is recomputed and a result is emitted only if its value changed.
Stateful streaming computations such as windowed counts require state to survive a crash/restart, and Kafka Streams and KSQL back that state to Kafka via a changelog topic.
A stream processing layer runs as a fault-tolerant cluster: if one node exits another picks up its work, and adding nodes automatically reroutes work and state.
Stream processors keep state in fast local stores and back writes up to Kafka, avoiding message-at-a-time network calls on high-throughput streams.
Kafka differs from REST/RPC by the presence of a broker that broadcasts messages and stores them, making it well suited to streaming and fire-and-forget messaging.

Kafka's home ground is event-based communication where events are business facts valuable to more than one service and worth retaining; pure request-response is often better served by a stateless protocol like HTTP.
condition: when there is no requirement for broadcast or for storage

statement: Kafka differs from an ESB by emphasising high-throughput events, distribution, high availability, storage, and linear scale-out, and by encouraging services to retain control rather than centralising orchestration.
Centralised ESB-style control, where a central team dictates schemas, flows, validation, and transformation, can constrain an organisation and make it hard for services to evolve at their own pace.
The core mantra of event-driven services is to centralise an immutable stream of facts while decentralising the freedom to act, adapt, and change.
Kafka is best understood as a database turned inside out: it is about real-time data movement and processing first, and long-term storage second.
Kafka's scalability comes largely from the simplicity of its partitioned-log abstraction, which encourages hardware-sympathetic sequential access patterns.
Kafka's architecture inherits more from storage systems like HDFS, HBase, and Cassandra than from JMS/AMQP messaging systems.
A log is O(1) for both reads and writes to a partition, so whether data is on disk or cached in memory matters far less than for index-based brokers that must keep hash tables or B-trees in memory.
Reading from Kafka uses zero copy: data is copied directly from the disk buffer to the network buffer without being imported into the JVM.
Because Kafka is log-structured, a consumer outage and large backlog does not significantly slow the infrastructure, unlike traditional brokers that slow as they fill.

In Kafka each log is a replica of a partition on a different machine, and the producer's partitioner spreads data round-robin or, when a key is supplied, by hash of the key so same-key messages share a partition and are strongly ordered.
Kafka provides ordering guarantees only within a partition, so messages that need relative ordering must be sent to the same partition by supplying the same key.
Global ordering requires a single-partition topic, which limits throughput to one machine but is typically sufficient for the use cases that need it.
condition: when global ordering across all messages is required

statement: Enable producer retries so transient failures are retried, but send batches one at a time per destination machine to avoid reordering when failures occur and batches are retried.
Kafka provides durability through replication, and with a replication factor of three two machines can be lost without losing data.
For sensitive service datasets, configure three replicas per partition, make the producer wait for replication to complete before proceeding, and enable producer retries.
Synchronous disk flush should be used sparingly because it significantly impacts throughput, especially in highly concurrent environments.
exception: highly sensitive use cases may require synchronous flush, in which case increase the producer batch size

statement: Event-driven services should run in a highly available configuration by default, since a second instance naturally load-balances and provides failover at essentially no extra cost.
exception: unless there is genuinely no requirement for high availability

statement: A single Kafka partition is only ever assigned to one consumer instance, an invariant that preserves ordering even as services fail and restart.
Kafka releases are always backward-compatible with the previous version, so a new version can be released without taking the system offline.

Compacted topics retain only the most recent event per key and support deletes, working like log-structured merge-trees; because compaction is asynchronous a compacted topic may temporarily contain superseded messages.
Compacted topics slow a dataset's growth in a data-specific way and make datasets smaller and easier to move, which speeds stateful stream-processing table loads.
Kafka can hold retention-based or compacted topics exceeding 100 TB, but it is a commit log with no broad query functionality, not a database.
The latest-versioned pattern combines a regular topic and a compacted topic linked by a Kafka Streams job, getting audit history plus a reduced footprint at the price of additional storage.
Kafka provides enterprise security: Kerberos or TLS client authentication, a Unix-like permissions system, network encryption, and authenticated Kafka-to-ZooKeeper communication.

Synchronous request-response composition feels natural, but as the number of independent services grows the web of synchronous interactions couples them and turns benign availability issues into widespread outages.

Synchronous fragility can be limited either by giving each service a significantly higher SLA than the overall system, or by breaking the synchronous ties using asynchronicity and a message broker as intermediary.
There are three distinct ways programs interact over a network -- commands, events, and queries -- and distinguishing them provides an important reference for interprocess communication.
A command is a request for an operation that changes system state, executes synchronously, and indicates completion with an optional result; consider restricting commands to inside a bounded context.
condition: prefer restricting commands to within a single bounded context

statement: An event is both a fact and a notification that something happened, carries no expectation of future action, and travels one way; use events when loose coupling matters, when the stream is useful to more than one service, or when data must be replicated.
A query is a side-effect-free request to look something up; use it for lightweight retrieval across service boundaries or heavyweight retrieval within a boundary.

Events wear two hats -- a notification hat that triggers services into action and a replication hat that copies data between services -- and from a service perspective they create less coupling than commands or queries.
A command is never an event: a command expects a future state change or side effect, whereas an event only states that something already happened.
Loose coupling, per Frank Leymann, reduces the number of assumptions two parties make about one another when they exchange information.
What people usually mean by loose coupling is closer to connascence: a measure of the impact that a change to one component will have on others.
Coupling matters only at the instant software is changed; if code were never changed, coupling would not matter at all, so coupling has a temporal element.
Loose coupling lets components change independently of one another, while tight coupling lets components extract more value from one another.
The path to loose coupling is not to share, because sharing always increases the coupling on whatever is shared.
Tight coupling can be beneficial when an interface is thin and changes infrequently, or when a component and its data change together, as with an application and its own database or DNS.
exception: when the shared component has a broad interface, many users, or changes frequently

statement: The coupling of a component is a function of its interface surface area, its number of users, and its operational stability and performance, with frequency of change as an addendum that gates whether coupling matters at all.
Messaging builds loosely coupled services by moving pure data from a highly coupled source into a loosely coupled subscriber, where any needed operations are then performed.
Request-driven approaches are more tightly coupled because functionality, data, and operational factors are concentrated in a single place.

Functional couplings are optional, but core data couplings are essential, because all significantly sized businesses have core datasets many programs cannot do without and there is no way to code around missing data.
With receiver-driven routing the receiver, not the sender, defines how messages are routed, so the receiver retains control of its participation and the system becomes pluggable.
Using events purely for notification means the sender has no knowledge of the receiver, the receiver decides whether to react, and coupling is reduced while pluggability is added.
Event-carried state transfer uses the event stream to replicate data from one service to another so it can be queried locally, advantageous in much the same way caching is.
Query by event-carried state transfer gives better isolation and autonomy, faster local data access, and offline availability.
condition: particularly when data from different services must be combined, spans geographies, or must be available offline

statement: The REST/RPC approach offers simplicity, a single authoritative copy of state, and centralised command-and-control workflows.
condition: particularly for use cases requiring synchronicity such as reading a just-updated value

statement: Blend the two event roles by use case: emphasise the notification hat for small, lightweight applications and the replication hat for larger architectures that need per-service data autonomy.
Jonas Boner argues that communication between microservices should be asynchronous message passing while logic inside each microservice runs synchronously.
exception: this strictly applies to independently deployable microservices; looser industry interpretations may not warrant so strong an assertion

statement: In the Event Collaboration pattern a set of services collaborate around one business workflow, each owning a subset of state transitions and raising events that trigger the next step, with no single service owning the whole process.

Choreographed event-collaboration systems are pluggable, because a service can change its internal event types freely so long as the externally consumed event remains, and they better suit larger, cross-team implementations.
Orchestration writes the whole workflow down in one place, which makes it easy to reason about, but couples the model tightly to the controlling service.
The notification and replication duality of events maps cleanly to stateless and stateful stream processing respectively.
Stateful stream processing via event-carried state transfer requires the joined dataset to be held in its entirety in Kafka and in in-process, disk-resident storage, which makes the service stateful.
condition: when joining to a table inside the stream processor

statement: Confining reuse within a bounded context comes from domain-driven design: broad reuse can be counterproductive, so model areas of the domain separately and have contexts interact through restricted interfaces such as events.
The imperative, command-driven programming model is a poor fit for estates where services are operated independently.

Dataflow and functional programming styles suit distributed, services-context design because state is not mutated in place but evolves from function to function, matching how stream processors operate.

Streaming inherits the benefits of functional and dataflow styles: inherent parallelisation, self-updating cached datasets, built-in resilience, easier reasoning via side-effect-free functions, a polyglot culture, and a higher level of abstraction.

The functional core, imperative shell pattern processes events asynchronously in a side-effect-free core wrapped by an imperative shell that marshals to and from outward-facing request-response interfaces.
Statelessness is valuable because stateless services start instantly and scale out linearly, but most applications are not truly stateless and merely push the state problem down into a database.
Local caching added to handle increasing traffic typically leads to cache-invalidation strategies and a spiral of coherence issues.
For many use cases the events that trigger a process contain all the data the program needs, so the processing can be stateless.

Stateful stream processing engines like Kafka's Streams API load all the data a computation needs ahead of time, which makes the application stateful and requires it to reacquire state after a restart.

A simple event-driven service that looks data up one message at a time suffers from constant remote lookups and from races when two related events are created at about the same time and arrive out of order.
A stateless streaming join buffers both streams until both events arrive, removing remote lookups and making the result independent of the order in which events arrive.
Even a stateless streaming join is slightly stateful, because Kafka Streams reloads each buffer's contents on restart to achieve deterministic join results.

A fully stateful streaming service preloads an entire reference stream into a local table, removing dependency on the source service's liveness, processing faster without network calls, and enabling more data-centric operations, at the cost of loading the dataset on startup.
Being stateful is made practical by standby replicas that keep a table replica up to date on another node, periodic disk checkpoints, and compacted topics that shrink the rebuild load.
Event Sourcing stores state changes immutably in the order they were created, yielding a comprehensive audit and the ability to rederive current state by replaying the log.

CQRS is a natural progression from Event Sourcing: write events to Kafka as the write model and asynchronously project them into a database as the read model, so the two can be optimised independently.
Command Sourcing stores the inputs coming into a service before anything happens, so the service can later be rewound and replayed to recover from a corruption.
The essence of Event Sourcing is representing a state change as an entirely new event appended to the log rather than overwriting the existing record as in a CRUD model.
A mutable, update-in-place database loses previous state, so recovering from a propagated data corruption is hard and largely manual.

With Event and Command Sourcing, recovering from a bug-induced corruption is comparatively simple: fix the bug, rewind the log, and replay so the database and downstream events are corrected automatically.
An ordered journal of state changes aids debugging and traceability, answering retrospective questions that mutable storage cannot.
Other database patterns such as staging tables, audit triggers, and bitemporal databases provide some auditability, but none lends itself to rewind-and-replay without significant extra effort.
With Event Sourcing the primary execution path serves both runtime execution and recovery, so there is little or no additional recovery code to write or test.
When Event Sourcing makes the event, not the database record, the source of truth, the state a service communicates and the state it stores internally are the same.
When a database update and a separate notification are not made atomically, a mid-point failure causes duplicate or missing notifications, and the two can also diverge as code churns.
CQRS separates the write path from the read path linked by an asynchronous channel, analogous to a database write-ahead log that journals durably before updating slower structures.
CQRS typically yields better overall read and write performance than an equivalent CRUD system, because inputs are journaled quickly and read-model index maintenance is batched.
The catch of CQRS is that the asynchronously updated read model runs slightly behind the write model, so a user may be unable to immediately read their own writes.
A materialised view precomputes and stores the result of a predefined query and is updated whenever an underlying table changes, trading storage for fast reads.
CQRS with Kafka can maintain many materialised views, each decoupled from the underlying events so they can be scaled independently and do not block the writing process.
Polyglot views let a single write model feed many read models in different databases, each tuned to a use case, such as a key/value store for website queries plus Elasticsearch for free-text search.
The most important rule for whole-fact-versus-delta modelling is to journal the whole fact exactly as it arrived, immutably, and perform any recombination on read.

Looking up and combining an out-of-band event with prior state from a database before journaling is usually a bad idea, because it fails to record exactly what was received and erodes the performance benefits of CQRS.
Change data capture is the most reliable and efficient way to write a database through into Kafka, because it repurposes the database's write-ahead log rather than issuing polling queries.
CDC is more accurate than query-polling because polling can miss operations when several occur on the same row within a polling period.
A database-fronted write-through into Kafka provides a consistency point so you can always read your own writes.
Writing through a Kafka Streams state store instead of an external database with CDC is faster because the store is local, can be made atomic via transactions, and needs less configuration.
Change data capture unlocks legacy systems: the database is a coherent seam from which events can be extracted to plug in new event-driven services and evolve away from legacy incrementally.
The MemoryImage pattern caches a whole dataset in memory for local querying instead of using an external database.
condition: when the dataset fits in memory and can be loaded in a reasonable amount of time

statement: An event-sourced view is a query resource created in one service from data owned by another, sourced directly from the log and regenerable at any time.
Aging in software is a function of how we choose to change it, not a function of time.

Modularising software over the network does not by itself improve sustainability, and breaking a monolith alone does little, because at company scale systems are more about people than about software.
Teams need autonomy to make progress without extensive interaction, but total independence also fails, so a balance must be struck across the linked factors of organisation, software, and data.
The Inverse Conway Maneuver changes the organisation to let the software structure follow, on the premise that software shape and organisation shape are intrinsically linked.
Reuse can be a bad thing: it lets software be developed quickly, but the more a component is reused the more dependencies it has and the harder it is to change.

Encapsulation is not always your friend, because real business services rarely keep a clean separation of concerns, so new requirements crosscut service boundaries and force several services to change at once.
Shared libraries and shared databases create the same coupling pain as a shared domain model, which is why microservices typically do not share a single domain model.
Two fundamental differences distinguish a service from a shared library: a service is run and operated by someone else, and a service has data of its own.
There is no workaround for not having data: if a service lacks data another owns, there is literally nothing it can do, unlike missing functionality which can be reimplemented.
The data dichotomy is that databases exist to expose and amplify the data they hold, while services exist to hide data so they can stay decoupled -- two fundamental opposing forces.
In the God Service problem, data services grow to expose an ever-increasing set of functions until they resemble a homegrown shared database and become tightly coupled and costly to evolve.

In the REST-to-ETL problem, clients extract data from a service to hold and manipulate it locally, to combine it, localise it, work offline, or escape the service's operational limits, which requires an imperfect polling mechanism.
The more mutable copies of a dataset exist, the more it diverges over time, and divergent datasets are very hard to fix in retrospect, with master data management being largely a Band-aid.
Shared data should be treated as a first-class citizen, because data on the outside is hard to change since many programs depend on it, which is exactly why it is the most important data of all.

Service interfaces, raw messaging, and shared databases each fail to handle the transition of data from outside to inside well, whereas a replayable log that is part messaging and part database handles it by adding a central reference.
Do not be afraid to evolve: start simple and change the approach when it becomes constraining, but not so late that change becomes too costly to schedule.
Sharing a replayable log balances decoupling and data access better than sharing a database, because it can hold datasets long-term and it facilitates event-driven reaction to the now.

Turning the database inside out, coined by Martin Kleppmann, splits a database's core components -- commit log, query engine, indexes, and caching -- into separate parts joined by the log, with Kafka as the commit log and a stream processor building indexes and views.
Pushing business logic into a database is widely felt to be a bad idea, whereas pushing data into your code opens opportunities to blend data and code together.

Jay Kreps's unbundling view casts a whole organisation's systems and data flows as a single distributed database, with query-oriented systems as indexes and stream processors as a view-materialisation mechanism.
Stream processing segregates responsibility for data storage in the log from the mechanism used to query it in the stream-processing API.
The log makes data available centrally with the simplest possible contract, keeping applications loosely coupled, while query functionality stays private to each service.

Lean data means selecting small, lean datasets -- just what is needed at a point in time -- pushed from a central event store into caches or controlled stores, supported by operations that make rederiving the views practical.
If the messaging layer remembers, downstream databases do not have to, because any data extracted from the log can be regenerated from it and so need not be stored reliably.
Long-lived databases accumulate errors because they are tweaked, copied between environments, and patched over a lifetime, so data-quality issues are unsurprising.
Streaming applies the infrastructure-as-code immutability mindset to data, keeping event-sourced views lean and rederiving them deterministically from the log.
Take only the data you need by stripping incoming messages to the minimal fields, which keeps views small, read-optimised, and loosely coupled and lets more rows fit in memory or disk.
The drawback of lean data is that needing more data means going back to the log, most cleanly done by dropping the view and rebuilding it from scratch.

Because worst-case regeneration time is the limiting factor for rebuilding views, pick a write-optimised database or cache such as an in-memory store, a journaling-disabled store, or a log-structured store.
Because rebuilding an event-sourced view can take minutes or hours, regenerate views in advance or in parallel and switch from the old view to the new one once it is fully caught up.
Operators lose trust in tools that are not regularly used, especially data scripts, so when moving between environments prefer recreating views directly from the log over copying database files.
As a yardstick, RocksDB bulk-loads about 10M 500 KB objects per minute, Badger about 4M 1 KB objects per minute per SSD, and Postgres about 1M rows per minute.

Data divergence arises because data passes through several models -- a wire model, an internal domain model, a database model, and outbound schemas -- and each translation introduces an opportunity for misinterpretation, like a game of telephone.
Semantic conflicts, such as whether a supplier is a customer during a merger, are the trickiest data-divergence issues and arise where teams, departments, or companies meet.

A streaming platform reduces the telephone effect by connecting applications to a single shared source of truth, and because data is retained immutably it is easier to locate when an error was introduced and to apply fixes.
The term consistency is overused: consistency in the CAP theorem differs from consistency in ACID transactions, and there is a spectrum of strong-to-eventual guarantees.
Intuitive, ACID-like consistency means a written record stays written, a read returns the most recently written value, and operations in a transaction become visible at once.

Groups of services generally lack strong consistency guarantees, because as data moves from service to service it becomes visible to users at different times unless all services coordinate around a single database and global consistency model.
A single global consistency model is not always desirable, because disconnected distributed or mobile components are inconsistent by definition until they resynchronise and converge.
condition: when applications are distributed across geographies or devices that can be disconnected

statement: Distributed transactions such as XA are difficult and expensive to scale, work poorly across geographies, and are relatively slow, which led most implementers to design around the need for them.
Event-driven systems sit in a middle ground between offline-tolerant and strongly consistent designs, often using some form of eventual consistency.
Eventual consistency leverages asynchronous broadcast, deliberately removing the need for global state and avoiding synchronous execution.
Eventual consistency has two consequences: timeliness, where concurrent consumers lag one another, and collisions, where concurrent changes to the same entity can be lost when later coalesced.
A lack of timeliness causes problems only when services are linked, such as a confirmation email whose link outruns the lagging orders view; otherwise decoupled concurrent processing is beneficial.
Serial execution can be reintroduced where necessary by blocking until the view is updated, or by having the owning service raise a View Updated event that triggers the dependent service.
Collisions occur only under concurrent execution, and conflict-free replicated data types merge concurrent changes with guaranteed integrity but offer a relatively limited set of operations.

A good compromise for large business systems is to keep timeliness, which allows many read-only replicas, but remove collisions by disallowing concurrent mutation, assigning a single writer per data type or per state transition.
The single writer principle, named by Martin Thompson, assigns responsibility for propagating events of a specific type to a single service, isolating consistency concerns into owning services.

The single writer principle lets versioning and consistency checks be applied in one place, isolates each business entity's evolution logic to one service, and dedicates dataset ownership to a single team that can specialise.
Isolating responsibility for a dataset's evolution to a single service and team is especially advantageous in domains with complex business rules, such as finance.
condition: in domains where data requires rich domain knowledge to model and evolve

statement: The Command Topic variant uses two topics -- a Command topic writable by any process for the initiating event, and an Entity topic writable only by the owning single writer -- enforceable through topic permissions.
The single-writer-per-transition variant has services own individual state transitions of a shared topic rather than all transitions in it.
Kafka transactions guarantee that messages sent to different topics within a transaction are all written or none, and that messages sent to a single topic are never duplicated even on failure.
Kafka transactions can join writes to state stores and writes to output topics together atomically.
Identity should correlate with the real world, such as an OrderId or PaymentId, and a logically mutable entity should also carry a version identifier.
Optimistic concurrency control uses a server-side version comparison to reject a write made against stale data, and can be implemented in synchronous or asynchronous systems equivalently.
The single writer principle and related patterns are useful patterns rather than general solutions, and there will always be exceptions.
exception: particularly where the implementation is constrained, for example by legacy systems

statement: Kafka's transactions aim to produce predictable, repeatable results even when things fail, and in a services context they remove duplicates, send groups of messages atomically across topics, and tie state-store writes to message sends.
Retries, needed because a called service may temporarily be down, can cause duplicate processing, which produces real errors such as taking a payment twice.

Many systems are naturally idempotent because a database deduplicates by primary key, an instance of the end-to-end principle, but this works only if every call carries an identity key and is deduplicated against a history of those keys.

Without transactions, event-driven systems must deduplicate on every received message and choose a careful unique ID on every sent message, which is at best a hassle and at worst a breeding ground for errors.
Kafka's transactions wrap each step of a service chain in exactly-once guarantees, but only over the Kafka portions of a system, not over external technologies.

With the producer and consumer APIs, exactly-once requires sending the validated output and committing the consumer offset inside a single transaction; with the Kafka Streams API it requires only enabling a configuration.
Exactly-once is both idempotence and atomic commit, addressing the two duplication opportunities: failure when sending to the broker, and failure when reading before offsets are committed.

Broker idempotence gives each producer an identifier and each message a sequence number so the broker discards a message already in the log, which is far more efficient than storing every key ever seen in a database.

Kafka's transactions adapt Chandy and Lamport's Snapshot Marker model: begin and commit marker messages flow through the streams and consumers buffer messages until the commit marker, so only committed data is ever read.

A transaction coordinator atomically marks each transaction committed and maintains a transaction log, implementing two-phase commit, and there are many coordinators so there is no single point of failure.
Transactional overhead is dispersed across batches, so committing every 100 ms with a 1 KB message size adds about a 3% overhead compared with in-order, at-least-once delivery.

Because Kafka Streams state stores are backed by Kafka topics, transactions can tie state-store writes and output messages together, mimicking atomic messaging-plus-database that traditionally required slow protocols like XA.
Transactions encapsulate deduplication entirely inside a service, keeping its contract clean, whereas idempotence relies on every downstream service correctly implementing deduplication.
Transactions are preferable to idempotence when a stream has no clear concept of identity, because then constructing a key is brittle and error-prone.
condition: when events lack a clear, natural concept of identity

statement: Kafka transactions work only when both the input and the output go through Kafka; calls to an external service, database, or stdout are not covered and can be duplicated.
A committed Kafka transaction cannot be rolled back, so multi-service transactions should be implemented with sagas.
A committed Kafka transaction gives no guarantee about when an arbitrary consumer will read the messages, identical to the contract offered by a transactional database.
Kafka transactions are not currently supported for consumer groups, so use the Kafka Streams API where consumer groups are fully supported.

Transactions matter most in complex Event Collaboration workflows because the end-to-end principle is hard to apply, intermediary topics are numerous, and one-to-many DSL operations like flatMap are hard to make idempotent manually.
Coarse-grained services still have their place, because transactions remove only one of the many problems that come with distributed systems.
Schemas are the APIs of event-driven services, creating a logical coupling between publisher and subscriber based on the schema they share.
Most projects in the Kafka space use Avro for schemas, with Protobuf and JSON Schema also popular, and the Confluent Schema Registry provides a central repository and verification.
Use a schema technology that validates backward compatibility, because that property is essential; do not use Java serialization or any non-evolvable format across services that change independently.

Adding a field is a backward-compatible schema change: programs on the old schema still read messages without seeing the new field (forward compatibility), and programs on the new schema read the whole message (backward compatibility).
You cannot move or remove a field from a schema compatibly, although a move can be synthesised with a clone, duplicating the data until a breaking change can be released.
The Confluent Schema Registry maps topics to their schemas and enforces compatibility rules before messages are added, so incompatible messages fail on publication.
Schema-on-read, a late-bound approach, lets many incompatible schemas coexist in the same topic and pushes format translation into the application layer.

Schema-on-read is pragmatic because recent data is often more valuable, so programs can move forward without migrating older data, and it is simple to implement when parsing code for the previous schemas already exists.
Non-backward-compatible schema changes are handled with the Dual Schema Upgrade Window, where two topics for the old and new schemas coexist to give services a window in which to upgrade.

Of the four dual-schema migration approaches, the up-convert and internal-migration options handle back-population of historic messages and so suit long-retention Event-Sourcing topics, whereas dual-publish and down-convert do not.
The single writer principle makes a non-backward-compatible schema upgrade simpler, because multiple writers of the same data would force a conjoined release.

The best way to collaborate on a schema change is to use GitHub, because schemas are code that should be version-controlled and pull requests let interested parties review, comment, and audit consensus without unduly impeding the implementer.
Email-based schema coordination lacks structure and accountability, and a central schema team stifles progress because changes must wait for that team and a sign-off.
Schemas cannot prevent a semantic error such as an invalid country code, a negative quantity, or corrupt bytes, which can stall processing until the issue is fixed.
Kafka has no native dead letter queue, but consumers can place an unreadable message onto a separate error topic so processing continues and the error topic can be reprocessed later.
By default Kafka retains data for two weeks, tunable to an arbitrarily large or small period, and an Admin API can delete messages older than a specified time or offset.

When using Kafka for Event Sourcing or as a source of truth you typically do not need delete; removal of a record is performed with a null value or delete marker so the fully versioned history stays intact.

Regulatory requirements like GDPR's right to be forgotten require data to be physically removed, for which compacted topics deleting by key with a null value are the common tool, with crypto-shredding as an alternative.
condition: when a regulatory requirement demands physical removal of data

statement: In a compacted topic a record is deleted by writing a new message with the same key and a null value; it is marked for removal and physically deleted when the compaction process runs, a mechanism closer to Cassandra and HBase than to a relational database.
When the topic's ordering key differs from the key you must delete by, use a composite key with a custom partitioner that partitions only on the ordering portion.
condition: when the partitioning/ordering key differs from the key you need to delete by

statement: With change data capture, deleting a record in the originating database propagates through Kafka to downstream Connect sinks automatically; without CDC a custom delete mechanism is needed.
Segregate private internal topics from shared business topics using the authorization interface to assign read/write permissions, enforced by convention or fully secured via TLS or SASL.
The Kafka Streams API is the most complete toolset for building event-driven services in a distributed, asynchronous world, supporting event-driven, streaming, and stateful-streaming service types.

Kafka Streams is a JVM DSL combining a declarative interface for joins, filters, grouping, and aggregation with functional per-message methods such as map, flatMap, transform, and peek, and the two can be blended.
KSQL is a SQL-like wrapper over the Kafka Streams API that can run standalone as a sidecar and be called remotely.
condition: used when the service is not running on the JVM

statement: A stream-stream join buffers incoming streams for a defined retention period and overflows the buffers to disk-backed state stores, so the join completes regardless of which event arrives later, behaving like a logical AND.
A Kafka Streams table is a local, usually compacted, manifestation of a complete topic held by key -- effectively a stream with infinite retention -- and is commonly used for enrichments.

Global KTables are broadcast, giving every instance a full copy that can be joined on any attribute at the cost of more disk, while regular KTables are partitioned, can be joined only by primary key, and may require rekeying.
A state store can save application-specific state like a database, backed up to Kafka via a changelog topic and restorable after a restart.
In the order-validation ecosystem, routing validation results through a separate Order Validations topic preserves the single-writer relationship between the orders service and the Orders topic.
Most streaming services follow a Join-Filter-Process pattern: join a set of streams and tables, filter and often aggregate, then run business logic one event at a time and emit to another stream.

Event-sourced views in Kafka Streams push data into state stores partitioned across instances, and GET requests are routed to the instance holding the requested key's partition via interactive queries.
