A blocking HTTP GET, essentially long polling, can collapse the asynchronicity of CQRS to appear synchronous, letting a client read its own writes by blocking until the event arrives or a timeout passes.
Scaling a stateful critical section such as reserving inventory reliably requires enabling Kafka transactions and partitioning the data by the relevant business key beforehand.
condition: when the critical section is scaled out across several threads or machines

statement: Stateful stream processing avoids remote transactions and cross-process coordination by partitioning the problem over threads or processes using a chosen business key.

Partitioning routes all the state for one computation to a single thread, similar to the Map phase of MapReduce, which is how streaming systems achieve high per-message throughput, but it works only if a logical key cleanly segregates all operations.
condition: only if a logical key cleanly segregates both the state needed and the state operated on

statement: A rekey redistributes data by a new key, for example via selectKey, pushing data through an intermediary topic so it is co-partitioned for a subsequent operation.
A Kafka Streams state store is programmed like a hash map but is persisted to Kafka and restored if the process restarts, and writes to it partake in Kafka's transactions.
To join on a foreign key, rekey the stream so records land on the same instance as the corresponding table partition (co-partitioning), after which the join needs no additional network access.
Real pipelines chain operations needing different data distributions, requiring repartitioning, such as rekeying from ProductId back to OrderId before writing to a destructive Orders view.
The keys used to partition event streams must be invariant if ordering is to be guaranteed, so an order's partitioning keys must remain fixed across all messages relating to that order.
Waiting for N events arriving on a single topic is implemented by grouping by the key, counting occurrences with a windowed aggregator, and filtering the output for the required count.
Any distributed system carries a baseline cost, so always weigh better nonfunctional properties against the simplicity of a single-process design.

A holistic streaming ecosystem mixes implementation patterns: multiple event-sourced views in different stores such as Cassandra, Solr, and in-memory, CQRS read/write splits, CDC for legacy services, and archiving all events to HDFS with point-in-time snapshots.
The streaming model brings a mindset shift toward asynchronous, functional, and data-centric design compared with the procedural nature of traditional service interfaces.

Standby replicas, checkpoints, and compacted topics mitigate the risks of pushing data to code, but there is always a worst-case scenario where service-resident datasets must be rebuilt, which must be considered in any system design.
Every integration solution must contend with four fundamental challenges: networks are unreliable, networks are slow, any two applications differ, and change is inevitable.

Distributed computing across a network must be prepared for a far larger set of failures (delays and interruptions across phone lines, LAN segments, routers, switches, and public networks) than a process running on a single computer.
Sending data across a network is multiple orders of magnitude slower than making a local method call.
A widely distributed solution should not be designed the same way as a single application, because doing so can have disastrous performance implications.
condition: designing a distributed or integration solution

statement: An integration solution must interface across systems that use different programming languages, operating platforms, and data formats.

An integration solution should minimize the dependencies between systems by using loose coupling, because otherwise a change in one system can cascade as an avalanche of changes across all connected systems.
Developers have addressed integration with four main approaches: File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation, and Messaging.
File Transfer integration requires the applications to agree on the filename and location, the file format, the timing of writing and reading, and who deletes the file.
Shared Database integration has multiple applications share one schema in a single physical database, so no data has to be transferred or duplicated between them.
Remote Procedure Invocation exposes part of an application's functionality for synchronous, real-time remote access by other applications.
Messaging has one application publish a message to a common channel that other applications read later, requiring agreement on the channel and message format, with asynchronous communication.
Because each integration style has distinct advantages and disadvantages, an application may integrate using several styles at once, choosing at each integration point the style that suits it best.
Messaging is high-speed, asynchronous, program-to-program communication with reliable delivery, in which programs exchange data packets called messages over channels.
A message has two parts: a header carrying meta-information used by the messaging system, and a body carrying the transmitted application data, which the messaging system ignores.

A messaging system (message-oriented middleware) manages messaging the way a database system manages persistence, and an administrator must configure it with the channels that define the communication paths between applications.
A messaging system is needed because computers and the networks connecting them are inherently unreliable, and a sender being ready to send does not mean the receiver is ready to receive.
A messaging system achieves reliable delivery by repeatedly retrying transmission until it succeeds.
Message transmission proceeds in five steps (Create, Send, Deliver, Receive, Process), of which only the Deliver step is carried out by the messaging system moving the message between computers.
Under send-and-forget, once the message is stored in the channel the sender can proceed with other work without waiting for the message to be delivered or processed.
Under store-and-forward, the messaging system stores the message at each computer along its path, repeatedly forwarding and re-storing it until it reaches the receiver.
Messaging is more immediate than File Transfer, better encapsulated than Shared Database, and more reliable than Remote Procedure Invocation.
If remote communication is not needed, messaging is not needed, and a simpler solution such as shared memory or concurrent collections is sufficient.
condition: the components do not need to communicate remotely (e.g., run in the same process)

statement: Asynchronous communication lets the sender batch requests at its own pace and the receiver consume them at its own different pace, so both applications can run at maximum throughput instead of waiting on each other.
Asynchronous communication lets the receiver control the rate at which it consumes requests, avoiding the overload that too many simultaneous remote procedure calls can inflict on a single receiver.

Messaging is more reliable than a remote procedure call because it uses store-and-forward, and reliability can be increased further by storing messages to disk rather than memory (Guaranteed Delivery).
Messaging is well suited to applications that run disconnected from the network and synchronize later, because data can be queued as it is created and held until the application reconnects.
condition: the application is designed to operate disconnected and sync when a connection is available

statement: Using callbacks instead of blocking keeps only a small, known number of listener threads blocked, leaving most threads free for real work and making the thread state easy to re-establish after a crash.
Which benefits of messaging matter most depends on the current requirements of the particular applications involved.
Asynchronous messaging is not a panacea: it resolves many integration challenges but also introduces new ones, so its consequences must be weighed when deciding to use it.
Asynchronous messaging requires an event-driven programming model split into many event handlers, which is more complex and harder to develop and debug than a single sequential method.

Message channels guarantee that a message is delivered but not when, so messages sent in sequence can arrive out of sequence, and messages that depend on each other need special handling to re-establish their order.
When a scenario requires an immediate result (for example a user awaiting a ticket price), a messaging system must bridge the synchronous and asynchronous worlds, typically via Request-Reply.
condition: the use case cannot operate in send-and-forget mode and needs a timely response

statement: For a bulk or initial data replication step, ETL (extract, transform, load) tools are more efficient than messaging; messaging is best suited to keeping the systems in sync after the initial replication.
condition: bulk/initial data replication versus ongoing incremental synchronization

statement: Many messaging implementations rely on proprietary protocols, and even common specifications like JMS do not control the physical implementation, so different messaging systems usually cannot connect directly to one another.
An n-tier distributed application is application distribution, not integration, because its tiers are tightly coupled, communicate synchronously, and serve human users who expect rapid response.
Integrated applications are independent programs that can each run by themselves and coordinate loosely and asynchronously, tolerating broader time constraints than interactive human users.

Patterns are documented as a pattern language, a web of interrelated patterns where each represents a design decision and leads to others, in order to convey expert knowledge that can be applied even to problems the authors did not foresee.
A pattern should be prescriptive, telling the reader what to do, and should document why the problem is hard, which tempting solutions do not work, and why the offered solution is best.
Besides Messaging, the pattern language has six root patterns: Message Channel, Message, Pipes and Filters, Message Router, Message Translator, and Message Endpoint.
A single business transaction from the customer's perspective can span five or six internal systems, which is why those applications must be integrated.
Application integration must provide efficient, reliable, and secure data exchange between multiple enterprise applications.
Enterprise integration is inherently hard because it must deal with multiple applications running on multiple platforms in different locations, making 'simple integration' close to an oxymoron.

Successful enterprise integration requires a shift in corporate politics, establishing communication between business units and IT departments, because once applications are integrated no group exclusively controls its application — each is part of an overall flow.

Once critical business functions run through an integration solution, that solution becomes vital to the business, and a failing or misbehaving integration solution can cost millions in lost orders, misrouted payments, and lost customers.

Integration developers typically have limited control over the participating applications, which are often legacy or packaged systems that cannot be changed merely to be connected, forcing developers to compensate for application deficiencies and differences.

A common presentation format such as XML does not imply common semantics; resolving the semantic differences between systems is a particularly difficult and time-consuming task that involves significant business and technical decisions.

Operating and maintaining an EAI solution can be even more daunting than building it, because its distributed, multi-technology nature makes deployment, monitoring, and troubleshooting require a combination of skill sets that often does not exist in one place.
Integration patterns are nuggets of advice that describe solutions to frequently recurring problems, not copy-paste code samples or shrink-wrap components.

Six types of integration project recur in practice: Information Portal, Data Replication, Shared Business Function, Service-Oriented Architecture, Distributed Business Process, and Business-to-Business integration, and many projects combine several of these types.
Functionality that several systems implement redundantly should be exposed once as a shared business function (service) available to the other systems.

The choice between replicating data and calling a shared business function is driven by how much control you have over the systems and by the data's rate of change, since calling a shared function is more intrusive and frequently-read but rarely-changed data favors replication.
condition: deciding how to share a piece of data or function across systems

statement: A service-oriented architecture is defined by two key elements: service discovery via a centralized service directory, and negotiation, in which each service describes its interface so consumers can form a communications contract.

A distributed business process adds a business-process-management component that coordinates the execution of a business function across multiple existing systems which already contain the needed functionality.

Business-to-business integration raises additional issues beyond internal integration — transport protocols, security, and the critical importance of standardized data formats among collaborating partners.
The core principle of loose coupling is to reduce the assumptions that two parties make about each other when they exchange information.
The more assumptions two parties make about each other and their shared protocol, the more efficient their communication can be but the less tolerant the solution is of interruptions or change.

A local method invocation is the canonical example of tight coupling: it assumes the same process, the same language or bytecode, an exact parameter list and types, synchronous and immediate execution, and no concern about eavesdropping.

Packaging remote data exchange in local method-call semantics (RPC/RMI) is appealing for familiarity and for deferring the local-versus-remote decision to deployment, but remote communication invalidates many local-call assumptions, so this abstraction is misleading.
Trying to portray remote communication as a variant of a local method invocation typically results in brittle, hard-to-maintain, and poorly scalable solutions.

Loose coupling provides important benefits such as flexibility and scalability, but it introduces a more complex programming model and makes designing, building, and debugging harder, so it is not a panacea.

A naive byte-stream TCP/IP integration is tightly coupled through four assumptions the parties make about each other: platform technology (number/object representation), location (hard-coded address), time (all components available simultaneously), and data format (parameter list and types).

Transferring numbers as raw bytes works only if all connected computers share the same internal representation, because integer width (32 versus 64 bit) and byte order (big-endian versus little-endian) differ across systems.
Communication should be made independent of a specific machine, because hard-coding a machine location breaks when the function moves, the machine fails, or the data must go to more than one machine.
A connection-oriented protocol such as TCP/IP creates a temporal dependency that requires both machines and the network to be available at the same time.

To loosen coupling, send to an addressable channel rather than a specific machine, queue requests in the channel to remove the temporal dependency, wrap data in self-contained messages, and allow data-format transformation inside the channel.
A channel is a logical address that the sender and receiver both agree on without being aware of each other's identity.

A complete loosely coupled middleware solution provides channels (to move data), messages (agreed-upon data), translation between data formats, routing to the correct systems, systems management for monitoring, and endpoints to connect applications not built for integration.

A Canonical Data Model defines message formats that are independent of any specific application, so that when one application's internal format changes only its Message Translator must change rather than every other application.
The common combination of a Splitter, a Router, and an Aggregator is itself a reusable pattern called a Composed Message Processor.

A Recipient List addresses each recipient specifically and so gives tight control over who receives a message, unlike a Publish-Subscribe Channel; combined with a Dynamic Router (whose routing changes from control messages) it forms a Dynamic Recipient List.

A Publish-Subscribe Channel has drawbacks: any subscriber can listen without the publisher's knowledge, and it works efficiently only on local networks, since across a wide-area network a separate copy must be sent to each recipient.

Interface granularity is a trade-off: fine-grained interfaces are flexible but cause sluggish, tightly coupled systems through excessive remote calls or messages, while coarse-grained interfaces are more efficient and less coupled but can limit flexibility.
Prefer well-defined, self-contained business actions (such as 'Change Address' or 'Place Order') as integration operations, because they give more flexibility in orchestrating business processes.

For data that changes infrequently (such as a catalog updated quarterly), prefer File Transfer over a real-time messaging infrastructure, especially across public networks, where FTP works well but most asynchronous messaging does not.
condition: infrequent or bulk data exchange, possibly across public networks

statement: Direct Shared-Database access is the simplest and most efficient way to serve a synchronous status query and always returns current data, at the cost of tightly coupling the querying application to the database schema.
Enterprise integration is the task of making separate applications work together to produce a unified set of functionality.

Choosing and designing an integration approach involves several criteria: application coupling, integration simplicity, integration technology, data format (and its evolution and extensibility), data timeliness, whether data or functionality is shared, and asynchronicity.
An integration interface should be specific enough to implement useful functionality yet general enough to allow that implementation to change as needed.
Data should be exchanged frequently in small chunks rather than waiting to exchange a large set of unrelated items, because latency lets shared data become stale and makes integration more complex.

Do not choose one integration style to use always; choose the best style for each particular integration opportunity, and different integration points (or different partner applications) may each use a different style.
Files are a universal storage mechanism built into every enterprise operating system and available from every enterprise language, requiring minimal specialized hardware or software.

In File Transfer integration, each application produces files of data others consume, integrators take responsibility for transforming between formats, and files are produced at regular intervals driven by the business cycle.

A key advantage of File Transfer is that integrators need no knowledge of an application's internals: the file's contents and format become the application's interface, so applications stay decoupled and can change internally as long as the file format is preserved.

File Transfer requires the applications to agree on file naming conventions and directories, keep filenames unique, agree on which application deletes old files, and use a locking mechanism or timing convention so a file is not read while it is still being written.

The main weakness of File Transfer is that updates tend to occur infrequently, so systems get out of synchronization and may act on stale data; production frequency must be chosen according to the consumers' freshness needs.
Shared Database integrates applications by having them store the data they wish to share in a single common database.

A Shared Database keeps integrated applications consistent and lets transaction-management systems handle simultaneous updates as gracefully as possible, and because the time between updates is small, errors are easier to find and fix.
Using a Shared Database forces semantic dissonance to be confronted and resolved early, before the software goes live and collects large amounts of incompatible data.

The biggest difficulty of Shared Database is designing a unified schema that meets multiple applications' needs — technically hard and often politically fraught — and external packages frequently will not work with any schema but their own.

Multiple applications frequently reading and modifying the same data in a Shared Database can cause performance bottlenecks and deadlocks, a problem made worse when the database must be distributed across computers.
Semantic dissonance — different systems attaching different meaning to the same concept — is much harder to deal with than inconsistent data formats.

Remote Procedure Invocation applies the principle of encapsulation to integration: an application asks another directly for data it owns or calls it to modify that data, so each application preserves the integrity of its own data and can change its internals without affecting the others.

RPC implementations include CORBA, COM, .NET Remoting, and Java RMI, which vary in platform support and ease of use and often add capabilities such as transactions, while Web Services (SOAP/XML over HTTP) are currently the most ubiquitous and pass through firewalls easily.

RPC fitting developers' familiar procedure-call habits is more a disadvantage than an advantage, because remote and local calls differ greatly in performance and reliability, and ignoring those differences leads to slow, unreliable systems.

Encapsulation reduces coupling compared with a large shared data structure, but RPC still leaves applications fairly tightly coupled, because the remote calls and their sequencing dependencies tie the systems into a growing knot that is hard to change independently.
People often design an integration the way they would design a single application, unaware that the rules change once communication becomes remote.
Use Messaging to transfer packets of data frequently, immediately, reliably, and asynchronously, using customizable formats.
Asynchronous messaging is fundamentally a pragmatic reaction to the problems of distributed systems, because sending a message does not require both systems to be up and ready at the same time.

Thinking about communication asynchronously forces developers to recognize that working with a remote application is slower, which encourages designing components with high cohesion (most work done locally) and low coupling (selective work done remotely).

Messaging lets messages be transformed in transit without either the sender or the receiver knowing about it, which decouples applications and lets integration be developed separately from the applications.
Asynchronous design has a learning curve and makes testing and debugging harder, and the freedom to transform messages often leaves integrators writing a lot of messy glue code.
Messaging is not as slow as many people assume: messaging systems in financial services routinely pass thousands of stock quotes or trades through the system every second.

Six basic concepts underpin the whole messaging pattern language: channels, messages, multi-step delivery (Pipes and Filters), routing (Message Router), transformation (Message Translator), and endpoints.
Connect two applications with a Message Channel, where one application writes information to the channel and the other reads it.

Use a different Message Channel for each type of information, so a sender adds data to the channel dedicated to that information and a receiver selects a channel by the type it wants, assuring that whichever application retrieves the data is interested in it.

Channels are logical addresses whose physical implementation — direct endpoint connections, a central hub, or several logical channels carried over one physical channel — is hidden from the applications.

A messaging system does not come preconfigured with the channels applications need; developers decide which channels are required and an administrator configures them, so the number and purpose of channels tend to be fixed at deployment time.

Calling JMS createQueue or .NET new MessageQueue does not allocate a new queue resource; it only provides access to a queue already created separately through the messaging system's administration tools.

Channels are cheap but not free — each consumes memory (and persistent channels consume disk), and every implementation has practical limits — so a system that may need thousands of channels requires a highly scalable implementation whose scalability is tested.
condition: the design may require very large numbers of channels

statement: A well-designed set of channels forms a Message Bus that acts like a messaging API for a whole group of applications, and because mixing data types on one channel causes confusion, separate Datatype Channels should be used.
A message channel transmits discrete units of data such as records, objects, and database rows, not a continuous stream.
Because two separate processes have separate memory spaces, transmitted data must be marshalled into a byte stream by the sender and unmarshalled by the receiver, which then holds its own local copy.

Package the information into a Message — a data record the messaging system can transmit through a channel — consisting of a header (information the messaging system uses, such as origin and destination) and a body (the data, transmitted as-is and ignored by the system).

Choose the message type by intent: a Command Message to invoke a procedure in another application, a Document Message to pass a set of data, an Event Message to notify another application of a change, and Request-Reply when a reply is expected.

If data is larger than one message can hold, break it into a Message Sequence; if it is useful only for a limited time, set a Message Expiration; and because all senders and receivers must agree on format, specify a Canonical Data Model.
Use the Pipes and Filters architectural style to divide a larger processing task into a sequence of smaller, independent processing steps (filters) connected by channels (pipes).

Each filter exposes the same simple interface — receive a message on the inbound pipe, process it, publish the result to the outbound pipe — so filters can be composed into different solutions and steps can be added, removed, or rearranged without changing the filters themselves.

Splitting processing into smaller, well-defined components increases reuse and lets different steps run on different machines, languages, or technologies, for example confining a decryption step to the one machine that holds the private key.

Design components to communicate through an abstract pipe interface so the implementation can be swapped between a Message Channel and a lighter in-memory queue when all components reside on the same machine (the Messaging Gateway).

A downside of Pipes and Filters is the larger number of channels and the per-hop overhead of converting message data into and out of the infrastructure's format, so a long chain of filters trades performance for flexibility.

Connecting filters with asynchronous channels creates a processing pipeline in which each stage runs in its own thread or process and starts the next message immediately, significantly increasing throughput over strictly sequential processing.

Overall pipeline throughput is limited by its slowest stage, so deploy multiple parallel instances of that stage behind a Point-to-Point Channel with Competing Consumers, which guarantees each message is consumed by exactly one of the N processors.
condition: one stage is the throughput bottleneck

statement: Running parallel instances of a stage can cause messages to be processed out of order, so when order is critical either run a single instance of each stage or use a Resequencer; parallelization works best when each filter is stateless.
exception: a stateful stage, such as a de-duplicator that keeps message history, cannot be freely parallelized

statement: Insert a Message Router, a special filter that consumes a message from one channel and republishes it to a different channel depending on a set of conditions.

A key property of a Message Router is that it does not modify the message content, concerning itself only with the message's destination, and the surrounding components are completely unaware of its presence.

The key benefit of a Message Router is that the routing decision criteria are kept in a single location, so adding message types or processing components or changing rules requires changing only the router, and because all messages pass through it they are processed one-by-one in order.

A Message Router can itself increase coupling because it must know all possible destinations, becoming a maintenance bottleneck when destinations change often; in that case prefer reactive filtering (a Publish-Subscribe Channel with Message Filters) over predictive routing.
condition: the set of possible destinations changes frequently

statement: A Message Router adds a processing step whose decode-and-re-encode overhead can make it a bottleneck; running routers in parallel or adding hardware preserves throughput, but message latency will still increase.

Heavy, deliberate use of routers can turn loose coupling into a liability by obscuring the overall flow of messages, complicating testing, debugging, and maintenance; use Message History or a compiled map of each component's channel subscriptions to reconstruct the flows.

Message Router variants include the fixed router (one input and one output, to decouple subsystems or relay messages), the Content-Based Router (decides by message content), the Context-Based Router (decides by environment, for load balancing, test, or failover), stateless versus stateful routers, and routers driven by a Control Bus or configured as a Dynamic Router.

The Message Router is central to the Message Broker implemented in virtually all commercial EAI tools, which accepts, validates, transforms, and routes messages so the applications need not be aware of each other; the Message Broker is the integration equivalent of the GoF Mediator.
Use a Message Translator between other filters or applications to translate one data format into another; it is the messaging equivalent of the GoF Adapter.

Avoiding translation by forcing all applications onto one common internal format is usually infeasible — legacy data-format changes are risky and costly, physical representations still differ, and it tightly couples the applications, violating loose coupling.

Do not hard-code data-format translation into the Message Endpoint, because that requires access to the endpoint code (usually unavailable for packaged applications) and reduces the opportunity for reuse.

Message transformation spans four layered levels, loosely borrowing from the OSI model: Transport, Data Representation (syntax), Data Types, and Data Structures (application); the layering lets you work at one level of abstraction without regard to the lower layers.
Create one Message Translator per transformation layer and chain them with Pipes and Filters, so each layer's translator is reusable and the layers are interchangeable.

Decoupling is layered: a Message Channel decouples applications from each other's location, a Message Router decouples them from agreeing on a destination, and a Message Translator removes the data-format dependency — decoupling being the essential tool for managing change.

Message Translator specializations include the Content Enricher (adds data), the Content Filter (removes data), the Claim Check (removes data but stores it for later retrieval), the Normalizer (converts many formats into one consistent format), the Canonical Data Model (decoupling via multiple translators), and the Messaging Bridge (transport-layer translation connecting messaging systems).
Connect an application to a messaging channel using a Message Endpoint, a client of the messaging system that the application uses to send or receive messages.

A messaging system is a server whose client API is domain-specific (messaging) rather than application-specific, so an application needs custom endpoint code that unites the application with that API.

A Message Endpoint encapsulates the messaging system from the rest of the application and customizes the general messaging API for a specific application and task, so switching messaging APIs or transports requires rewriting only the endpoint code.

A single Message Endpoint instance either sends or receives but not both, and is channel-specific, so an application uses multiple endpoints for multiple channels (or multiple endpoints on one channel for concurrent threads); an endpoint is a specialized Channel Adapter built into its application.

Design a Message Endpoint as a Messaging Gateway to hide the messaging code from the application, optionally using a Messaging Mapper to move data between domain objects and messages, a Service Activator to give asynchronous access to a synchronous service, and a Transactional Client for explicit transaction control.

Endpoint receiving styles include the Polling Consumer and the Event-Driven Consumer; multiple consumers can share a channel as Competing Consumers or via a Message Dispatcher; a Selective Consumer chooses which messages to take; a Durable Subscriber avoids missing messages published while it is disconnected; and an Idempotent Receiver detects and handles duplicates.
A non-transactional filter loses the message if it fails after consuming it but before sending it onward, which is unacceptable in production; a Transactional Client solves this.
condition: production environments where message loss is unacceptable

statement: The set of message channels available to an application tends to be static and agreed at design time, rather than created and discovered dynamically at runtime.
exception: the reply channel in Request-Reply, and subscriptions to hierarchical channels, which can be dynamic

statement: Message channels are for practical purposes unidirectional, so two applications that need a two-way conversation require two channels, one in each direction.

Designing the needed set of channels is iterative: the first applications determine the channels the messaging system must provide, and later applications reuse those channels or require new ones as their functionality grows.
Send a message on a Point-to-Point Channel to ensure that exactly one receiver consumes that particular message.

A Point-to-Point Channel may have multiple receivers for concurrent consumption (Competing Consumers), but it ensures only one of them consumes any given message, so the receivers need not coordinate and consumption can be load-balanced across multiple computers, making it highly scalable.
Send an event on a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which delivers a copy of the message to each subscriber.

A Publish-Subscribe Channel conceptually splits one input into one output channel per subscriber, so each subscriber receives the event exactly once and consumed copies disappear; it builds on the GoF Observer pattern and the POSA Publisher-Subscriber pattern.

A Publish-Subscribe Channel lets you eavesdrop on channel traffic for debugging without disturbing the existing flow, but that same eavesdropping is a security risk, so subscribing to a channel should be restricted by security policy.
Many messaging systems let subscribers (but not publishers) use wildcard characters to subscribe to multiple channels at once, while publishers must always publish to a specific channel.
Use a separate Datatype Channel for each data type, so that all messages on a given channel are of the same type and the receiver, knowing the channel, knows how to process them.

A receiver must know a message's type — its data structure and format — to process it; because a channel acts like a collection and a receiver like an iterator, homogeneous channels are far more useful, which is the main reason messaging systems need many channels.

When there are more data types than it is practical to give each its own channel, let multiple types share one channel using a Selective Consumer per type, or a Message Dispatcher that routes each message to a type-specific performer.
condition: more data types than separate channels are practical

statement: When a receiver gets a message it cannot process, it should move that message to an Invalid Message Channel, rather than put it back on the channel, silently discard it, or ignore it.

A message is neither inherently valid nor invalid — the receiver's context and expectations decide; a message valid for one receiver may be invalid for another, so such receivers should not share a channel, and it is the sender's responsibility to send only messages the channel's receivers will consider valid.

Distinguish a message-processing error (an invalid message) from an application error (a well-formed message whose content is semantically wrong, such as deleting a nonexistent record), and do not route the application error to the Invalid Message Channel; implementing the receiver as a Service Activator or Messaging Gateway makes this distinction clear.

Treat the Invalid Message Channel like an error log that must not be ignored — monitor it and alert administrators when it holds messages — because its contents indicate application integration problems.
When the messaging system determines it cannot or should not deliver a message, it may move the message to a Dead Letter Channel.

A dead message is one the messaging system cannot deliver, determined automatically from the message header, whereas an invalid message is delivered successfully but cannot be processed by the receiver, which the developer must handle based on the body or specific header fields.

A message can become undeliverable for many reasons — a misconfigured or deleted channel, expiration or timeout, a Selective Consumer everyone ignores, or a bad header — and each machine typically has its own local Dead Letter Channel that records where the message died and its original destination channel.
Use Guaranteed Delivery to make messages persistent so that they are not lost even if the messaging system crashes.

By default a messaging system stores messages in memory, so a crash loses them; Guaranteed Delivery persists each message to a local data store, completing a send only once the message is safely stored and not deleting it until it has been stored at the next hop.
Persistence increases reliability at the expense of performance, so when losing messages on a crash is acceptable, avoid Guaranteed Delivery so messages move through the system faster.
condition: losing messages on a crash is acceptable

statement: Guaranteed Delivery can consume large amounts of disk during high-traffic outages, so configure a retry timeout; and because reliability is measured in nines and is never truly 100% (a failed or full disk can still lose messages), Guaranteed Delivery is designed to resist expected outages, not to be bullet-proof.
It is useful to turn off Guaranteed Delivery during testing and debugging, because stale messages left queued on a channel are processed before new ones and create a common debugging pitfall.
condition: testing and debugging

statement: With a JMS Publish-Subscribe Channel, Guaranteed Delivery only assures delivery to active subscribers, so an inactive subscriber needs a Durable Subscriber to avoid missing messages.

Use a Channel Adapter to connect an application not built for messaging: it accesses the application's API or data to publish messages and receives messages to invoke the application's functionality, without modifying the application.

A Channel Adapter can connect at the user-interface layer (screen scraping, which needs no internal access but is brittle and slow), the business-logic layer (an API, usually the most stable and efficient and the best choice when a well-defined API exists), or the database layer (non-intrusive and able to use triggers, but it pokes application internals and risks brittleness against an unpublished schema).

A Channel Adapter usually needs a Message Translator because its message format closely mirrors the adapted component's internal structure rather than the Canonical Data Model, and it is typically implemented as a Transactional Client so each unit of work succeeds in both systems.

A Metadata Adapter (Design-Time Adapter) does not invoke application functions but extracts metadata describing the application's data formats, which can then configure Message Translators or detect format changes.
Use a Messaging Bridge — a set of Channel Adapters connecting corresponding channels — to replicate messages between two messaging systems.

A standardized API such as JMS does not make two messaging systems interoperate; it only makes them look the same to a client, while genuine interoperability requires the same message format and transfer mechanism, which products from different vendors rarely share.
Structure the middleware connecting applications as a Message Bus so they work together in a loosely coupled way and applications can be added or removed with minimal impact on the others.

A Message Bus combines a common data model (a Canonical Data Model), a common command structure, and a messaging infrastructure, and it forms a simple service-oriented architecture whose request channels act as a directory of the available services.

Choose a message's intent deliberately: a Command Message to invoke a specific function on the receiver, a Document Message to pass data without dictating what to do with it, and an Event Message to notify the receiver of a change.

For a Request-Reply exchange, send the request as a Command Message and the reply as a Document Message, have the requestor specify a Return Address, and include a Correlation Identifier in the reply so the requestor can match it to the originating request.

There are two common Request-Reply scenarios: Messaging RPC, where the requestor wants a function's return value, and Messaging Query, where the requestor wants the results of a remotely executed query.

Use a Command Message to reliably invoke a procedure in another application; it builds on the GoF Command pattern and is usually sent on a Point-to-Point Channel so each command is consumed and invoked once.
Unlike a synchronous RPC that simply fails if the call cannot be made right now, a Command Message can keep retrying asynchronously until the remote procedure is successfully invoked.

Use a Document Message to reliably transfer a data structure between applications, passing the data and letting the receiver decide what to do with it, unlike a Command Message which dictates behavior.

A Document Message differs from an Event Message mainly in timing and content: the document's content is what matters and its timing matters less, so Guaranteed Delivery may apply while Message Expiration usually does not, and it is usually sent on a Point-to-Point Channel to avoid duplication.
An RPC over messaging is implemented as Request-Reply using a pair of Point-to-Point Channels, with the call carried as a Command Message and the reply as a Document Message.
Use an Event Message for reliable, asynchronous event notification between applications.

Event notification via RPC forces the receiver to accept the event immediately and requires the announcer to know every listener, whereas an asynchronous Event Message lets the subject send the notification when it is ready and each observer receive it when the observer is ready, which is how the Observer pattern is implemented over messaging.

An Event Message differs from a Document Message in timing and content: an event's content is often minimal (sometimes empty) while its timing is critical, so Message Expiration is very helpful for events but Guaranteed Delivery usually is not.

Choose between a push and a pull event model: the push model combines the event with its new state and is efficient only if all observers want those details, while the pull model sends a small Update event and lets interested observers fetch details via a State Request and a State Reply.
condition: deciding how much state to include in an event notification

statement: Event Messages are usually broadcast on a Publish-Subscribe Channel, and because a busy receiver can often safely ignore them, the subscribers can usually be non-durable.
To make messaging two-way, send a pair of Request-Reply messages, each on its own channel: a requestor that sends the request and waits for the reply, and a replier that responds.

A Request-Reply request channel may be Point-to-Point or Publish-Subscribe, but the reply channel is almost always Point-to-Point, because broadcasting a reply to anyone but the requestor makes no sense.

A requestor can receive a reply by Synchronous Block (a single thread blocks as a Polling Consumer — simple but hard to recover after a crash and limited to one outstanding request) or by Asynchronous Callback (a separate thread invokes a callback — allowing many outstanding requests to share one reply channel and easy recovery, at the cost of callback complexity).

A Request-Reply pair has three common meanings — Messaging RPC (a Command request and a Document reply carrying a return value or exception), Messaging Query (a Command query and a results reply), and Notify/Acknowledge (an Event request and a Document acknowledgement) — and a reply is one of void, a result value, or an exception.
The request message should contain a Return Address that indicates the channel on which to send the reply.

A Return Address encapsulates the knowledge of which channels to use within the requestor, so the replier need not hard-code reply channels, can serve multiple requestors that each need a different reply channel, and can send the reply to a separate callback processor rather than to the requestor itself.
A Return Address belongs in the message header rather than the body because it is not part of the data being transmitted; it is analogous to the reply-to field of an email message.
Each reply message should contain a Correlation Identifier — a token whose value matches the originating request's unique ID — so the requestor can match the reply to the request that caused it.

Without a Correlation Identifier an asynchronous caller cannot reliably match replies to requests: sending one request at a time is far too slow, and assuming replies arrive in the same order as requests is faulty because messaging does not guarantee delivery order.

The Correlation Identifier (and the request ID) belongs in the message header, its value may be either the request's message ID or a business-object ID that lets the requestor go straight to the originating business task, and keeping message-ID and correlation-ID as separate fields allows request-reply pairs to be chained; it is a simpler form of the Asynchronous Completion Token.

When a data set is too large for a single message, send it as a Message Sequence, marking each message with a sequence identifier, a position identifier, and a size-or-end indicator so the receiver can reassemble the whole even if parts arrive out of order.

If a receiver expects a Message Sequence, send every message as a sequence (even a sequence of one) so that missing sequence fields do not make a lone message look invalid, and if a receiver gets only some messages of a sequence it should reroute them to the Invalid Message Channel.

A Message Sequence is incompatible with Competing Consumers or a Message Dispatcher, because if different consumers receive different parts none of them can reassemble the whole, so a sequence must be transmitted on a single-consumer channel.

Use a Transactional Client to send or receive an entire Message Sequence atomically, so none of the messages are delivered or consumed until all are present (and they are then often received in order); an alternative to sending a large document is a Claim Check, storing the document and transmitting only its receipt.
Set a Message Expiration to specify how long a message remains viable, after which consumers ignore it.

Messaging guarantees eventual delivery but not how long it takes, so in unreliable circumstances a message can take a very long time; an expired, unconsumed message is treated as if it were never sent, and most implementations reroute it to the Dead Letter Channel while others simply discard it.

Specify Message Expiration relatively (expiration time equals sent time plus time-to-live) rather than absolutely, letting the messaging system handle timezone and clock differences; and because a reply with an expiration can leave the requestor never knowing whether its request was received, design the requestor to handle missing replies.
condition: using expirations, especially on reply messages

statement: Design a data format with a Format Indicator so each message states which format it uses, allowing old-format and new-format messages to coexist on the same channels as the format evolves.

A Format Indicator can be implemented as a version number, a foreign key pointing to a schema document, or an embedded format document (schema); a version number or foreign key fits in a header field, while an embedded schema requires a two-part body of schema plus data.

Letting new-format messages share the existing channels and distinguishing them with a Format Indicator is better than creating a separate set of channels per format, which would explode the channel count and configuration complexity.
A send-and-forget request succeeds even when the replier is not yet running, because the messaging system holds the message until the replier becomes available.

When implementing the Observer pattern over messaging, prefer the push model by default, because the pull model is more complex: it needs more channels (including a temporary one per observer), three messages per update per interested observer instead of one, more code, and more threads.
condition: implementing distributed event notification and unsure which model to use

statement: Publish-Subscribe Channels make the Observer pattern far easier to use in distributed environments, because notify and update reduce to sending and receiving messages while the messaging system handles distribution, concurrency, and reliability — sometimes justifying the use of messaging for notification alone.

Avoid creating a separate channel for every aspect that can change, because a channel explosion taxes the messaging system through wasted resources, load that is hard to distribute, per-message overhead, subscriber confusion, and many threads polling mostly-empty channels.

Send similar notifications that go to the same set of observers on one channel, and keep notifications aimed at different observer audiences on separate channels, balancing the risk of channel explosion against delivering irrelevant traffic.

Because a Datatype Channel requires all messages on a channel to share a format (for example the same XML root element, differing only in optional nested elements), receivers that want only some of those messages use Selective Consumers.

Message Routing patterns fall into Simple Routers (variants of the Message Router that take one inbound channel to one or more outbound channels), Composed Routers (combinations of simple routers), and Architectural Patterns based on routers.
Use a Content-Based Router to inspect a message's content and route it to the proper destination, so the producer sends to a single channel and stays decoupled from the specific destination channels.

A Message Filter is a special Content-Based Router that passes a message to another channel only if its content matches certain criteria and otherwise discards it; it differs from a Selective Consumer in that the filter is part of the messaging system while a Selective Consumer is built into a Message Endpoint.

A Content-Based Router routes predictively to a single channel with total control but depends on knowing all destinations, whereas an array of Message Filters on a Publish-Subscribe Channel filters reactively, spreading routing logic across filters and avoiding a single component dependent on all destinations.

Use a Dynamic Router when routing rules must change at runtime, modifying its logic through control messages sent to a designated control port; the dynamic mechanism can be combined with most forms of Message Router.
A Recipient List is a Content-Based Router that routes a single message to more than one destination channel while keeping tight control over the set of recipients.
A Splitter breaks a message that contains a list of items into individual messages so that each item can be routed and processed individually.

An Aggregator receives a stream of messages, identifies related ones, and combines them into a single message; it is a stateful router that stores messages until its completion conditions are met, consuming many messages before publishing one.

A Resequencer puts out-of-sequence messages back into order; it is a stateful router that may buffer messages until the missing one arrives, and unlike an Aggregator it publishes the same number of messages it consumes.

A Composed Message Processor and a Scatter-Gather both route a single message to multiple participants concurrently and reassemble the replies into one message (parallel routing); the Composed Message Processor keeps control over the set of sources, while the Scatter-Gather uses a Publish-Subscribe Channel so any interested component can participate.

Sequential routing — passing a message through a series of steps — can use a Routing Slip, which specifies the entire path centrally like an office routing slip, or a Process Manager, which is more flexible but requires the message to return to a central component after each step.
Define a channel for each recipient and use a Recipient List to inspect an incoming message, compute the list of desired recipients, and forward a copy of the message to each recipient's channel.

A Recipient List has two logical parts — computing the recipient list (from the message content plus rules, or from a list attached by the originator) and sending a copy to each recipient — and like a Content-Based Router it usually does not modify the message contents.

For a robust Recipient List, consume the incoming message only after all outbound copies have been sent, making the whole operation atomic and restartable via a single transaction, a persisted record of who has been sent to, or idempotent receivers that tolerate resends.

An idempotent function does not change the system state when applied repeatedly, so making receivers idempotent (inherently, or by inserting a duplicate-eliminating Message Filter) lets a sender safely resend a message whenever delivery is in doubt, much as TCP/IP does.
Ensure that recipients cannot subscribe directly to a Recipient List's input channel, because doing so would bypass the control the Recipient List is meant to exercise over who receives messages.

Whether broadcasting to all recipients or sending individual messages is more efficient depends on the infrastructure: IP multicast can reach many recipients in a single transmission on a local Ethernet segment but not across the Internet, so the farther apart the recipients are, the more a Recipient List outperforms a Publish-Subscribe Channel.

If on average most potential recipients want a given message, broadcasting it and letting the few non-participants filter it out can be more efficient; if only a small fraction are interested, a Recipient List is almost always more efficient.

Predictive routing with a Recipient List gives central control but must know the participants and be updated as they change, whereas reactive filtering with a Publish-Subscribe Channel and an array of Message Filters needs no knowledge of participants and makes adding or removing them easy; the former suits business transactions like request-for-quote, the latter suits event notifications.
Use a Splitter to break a composite message into a series of individual messages, each containing the data related to one item.

Repeat the necessary common fields (such as the order number and customer ID) in each child message a Splitter produces, to make each child self-contained for stateless processing and to allow the items to be reconciled later by an Aggregator.

A Splitter has variants: an Iterating Splitter walks the child nodes of a message tree and is completely generic, while a Static Splitter breaks a large message into a known fixed set of sub-messages and is functionally equivalent to a broadcast channel followed by Content Filters.
Use a stateful filter, an Aggregator, to collect and store related messages until a complete set has been received, then publish a single message distilled from them.

Unlike stateless routers such as a Content-Based Router, an Aggregator is stateful because it must retain information across messages; designing one requires choosing a correlation rule, a completeness condition, and an aggregation algorithm.

An Aggregator may be self-starting (creating a new aggregate when an unmatched message arrives, needing no prior knowledge) or initialized (told up front, for example the expected count from a copy of the original request), and it must track and periodically purge already-closed aggregates so the list does not grow without bound.

Choose an Aggregator's completeness condition by what is known: 'Wait for All' gives the best basis for a decision but is the slowest and most brittle and needs the expected count; 'Time Out' decides on whatever arrived in time; 'First Best' is fastest but discards information; and 'Time Out with Override' and 'External Event' are further options.

Common Aggregator aggregation algorithms are selecting the single best answer, condensing data (such as averaging or summing numeric fields), and collecting the messages for later evaluation by another component or a human.

Use a stateful filter, a Resequencer, to buffer out-of-order messages and republish them in the correct order to an order-preserving output channel, publishing the same number of messages it consumes and without modifying their contents.

Messages get out of order because different messages take different processing paths or run at different speeds; keeping messages in order is easier than reordering them, but throttling to one message at a time defeats parallelism and requires control over the message source.

A Resequencer needs a dedicated, consecutive Sequence Number — distinct from a Message Identifier or Correlation Identifier, which need only be unique rather than numeric or consecutive — and because a single consecutive-number generator can become a bottleneck, the numbering is best built into the Splitter that produces the messages.

Prevent Resequencer buffer overrun by throttling the producer with active acknowledgement of a negotiated window size (as TCP/IP does) or, when approximate data is acceptable such as voice over IP, by computing stand-in messages for the missing ones.
condition: long or interrupted out-of-sequence streams that could overflow the buffer

statement: Use a Composed Message Processor to split a composite message, route its sub-messages to the appropriate destinations, and re-aggregate the responses into a single message, presenting itself to the rest of the system as a single filter with one input and one output channel.
Use a Scatter-Gather to broadcast a message to multiple recipients and re-aggregate their responses into a single message.

A Scatter-Gather has two distribution variants: via a Recipient List, which controls the recipients but must know each one's channel, or auction-style via a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which uses a single channel but relinquishes control over who participates.

Aggregating responses in a Scatter-Gather is harder than in a Composed Message Processor because the number of participating recipients may be unknown, and because synchronizing parallel activities lets a single slow activity hold up subsequent processing — a cascading Aggregator can mitigate this by letting later tasks start on a subset of the results.

An Aggregator can serve as a missing-message detector by routing a message through both an unreliable component path and a reliable Guaranteed-Delivery bypass and recombining them with a Time-Out-with-Override condition, raising an alert when only the bypass copy arrives.
Attach a Routing Slip to each message specifying its sequence of processing steps, and wrap each component with a router that reads the slip and forwards the message to the next listed component.

A Routing Slip combines the central control of computing the path up front with the efficiency of a hard-wired chain, because the message never returns to a central router and the per-component router is generic, so routing logic can change centrally without touching component code.

A Routing Slip's limitations are that the message grows by carrying process state (so losing the message also loses where it was going next) and the path is fixed once the message is underway, so it cannot depend on intermediate results and a central entity must determine all steps in advance.

Use a Routing Slip for a sequence of binary validations, stateless transformations, or data-gathering steps that make no decisions; when the flow must branch on intermediate results or run steps in parallel, use a Process Manager instead.
condition: the step sequence is dynamic but linear and free of mid-flow decisions

statement: A Routing Slip can act as a Chain of Responsibility in which each component either accepts a message or passes it on, avoiding the duplicate processing of a Publish-Subscribe-plus-filters approach, at the cost of more traffic — on average about half the number of systems versus a single message for a Content-Based Router.
Use a central Process Manager to maintain the state of a multi-step sequence and determine the next step based on intermediate results, enabling branching and parallel steps.

A Process Manager produces a hub-and-spoke flow in which all traffic passes through the central hub, which risks becoming a performance bottleneck; its versatility lets it solve almost any integration problem, but using it for every situation is overkill and adds overhead.

A Process Manager separates a process definition (the template) from a process instance (an active execution with a unique process identifier), runs many instances in parallel, and needs a Correlation Identifier to match each incoming message to the right instance.

A Process Manager makes state explicit — unlike a Pipes-and-Filters architecture where the channels themselves hold the state — which enables powerful process reporting and easier debugging by querying instance state, at the cost of a more complex component.

A process definition's semantics mirror a UML activity diagram: an activity, a fork (equivalent to a Publish-Subscribe Channel), a join (equivalent to an Aggregator), and a branch or decision (equivalent to a Content-Based Router).

To keep a central Process Manager from being a single point of failure or a bottleneck, persist process-instance state and run multiple Process Manager instances in parallel (instances are independent), accepting that a shared state database can itself become a bottleneck.

Use a central Message Broker that receives messages from many sources, determines each message's correct destination, and routes it, implementing the broker's internals with the routing design patterns.

Direct point-to-point channels between every pair of applications explode into unmanageable integration spaghetti and make the system brittle to maintain, which a central Message Broker avoids by decoupling senders from destinations.
The Message Broker is an architecture pattern (comparable to Pipes and Filters), not a single design pattern, and it is not monolithic — it is built internally from the routing patterns.

Because routing everything through one Message Broker can create a bottleneck, deploy multiple instances of a stateless broker (a Point-to-Point Channel ensures only one consumes each message), or use several specialized brokers or a Message Broker hierarchy to avoid an unmaintainable über-broker.
A Message Broker usually uses a Canonical Data Model internally to avoid the N-square problem, in which the number of translators needed grows with the square of the number of participants.

Message Channels and Message Routers remove location dependency, but message formats impose a further dependency, so if one application must format its messages in another's data format the decoupling is only an illusion that a Message Translator removes.

Any integration solution can be viewed as two parallel systems — one handling message data and one handling metadata (the data describing message formats) — and a Channel Adapter can extract metadata into a central repository to configure Message Translators.

Use an Envelope Wrapper to wrap application data in an envelope compliant with the messaging infrastructure (adding header fields, encryption, or security credentials) and to unwrap it at the destination so the recipient receives clear data.

Because routing and transformation components can read only header fields, promote any body field they need up into the header, and chain wrappers and unwrappers (tunneling) to carry a message across multiple messaging infrastructures.
Use a Content Enricher to access an external data source and augment a message with information the originating system could not supply.

A Content Enricher's added data comes from computation (needing no external source, like a basic Message Translator), from the environment (such as a timestamp), or — most commonly — from another system such as a database, file, LDAP directory, or a user.

Because a Content Enricher is inherently tightly coupled to its data source and the lookup is synchronous, a synchronous protocol such as HTTP or ODBC may perform better than asynchronous messaging for that lookup.

Use a Content Enricher to resolve references (keys or IDs) carried in a message, trading reduced message size against extra lookups; this pays off when a message passes through many intermediaries and is enriched just before the final recipient.

Prefer a Content Enricher over modifying or coupling the source and destination applications, and rather than having one system instruct another, publish an Event Message and let each consumer decide what to do.
Use a Content Filter to remove unimportant data items from a message, leaving only the important ones, and to flatten an over-nested message structure into a simpler form.

Use a Content Filter for security — stripping data a requestor is not authorized to see — and to tame large standardized B2B documents whose hundreds of nested fields make visual transformation tools unusable and debugging painful.

Store a message's data in a persistent store and pass a Claim Check key to subsequent components, which use a Content Enricher to retrieve the data later, reducing the data volume carried without losing information.

A Claim Check is worthwhile because transporting large data through every routing step — with marshalling and possible encryption at each hop — is inefficient and some systems cap message size; it is especially effective when the data never needs to leave the originating component.

For a Claim Check key, use a business key or a newly generated unique ID rather than the message ID, because the message ID changes per message and overloading it with retrieval semantics causes conflicts; manage the stored data by delete-on-read, by expiration plus garbage collection, or by retention.

A Claim Check can hide sensitive data from an external party (sending only what is needed and merging the stored data back on return), and special or expiring keys let the retrieving Content Enricher block invalid or replayed messages; a Process Manager can itself act as the Claim Check store.

The three sequencing architectures trade off as follows: distributed Pipes and Filters supports complex flow with no central point of failure but is hard to change and offers no central administration; a Routing Slip is easy to change and mostly distributed but supports only simple linear flow; and a central Process Manager supports complex flow with central administration and reporting but risks a hub-and-spoke bottleneck.
Use a Normalizer to route each incoming message type through a custom Message Translator so that all the results match a single common format.

A Normalizer's Message Router detects each message's type — via a type field, the XML root element name, XPath sub-node tests, the field count and data types, or the filename or folder as a surrogate Datatype Channel — which also lets one transformation be shared across partners that use the same format.

When integrating many partners, plan for a high rate of format change (partners use different formats, those formats evolve, and partners join and leave) and isolate those changes so they do not ripple through the rest of the system.
condition: B2B integration with many partners

statement: Design a Canonical Data Model that is independent of any specific application and require each application to produce and consume messages in this common format.

Translating directly between every pair of applications makes the number of Message Translators grow roughly with the square of the number of applications (six applications need about thirty translators), whereas a Canonical Data Model needs only translation to and from itself (twelve for six applications), so it pays off as the number of applications grows.

Make an application conform to the Canonical Data Model by changing its internal format (rarely feasible), by a Messaging Mapper inside a custom application, or by an external Message Translator for a packaged application whose source code is unavailable.

A Canonical Data Model adds double-translation overhead — two steps and added latency — compared with direct translation, so use the more maintainable Canonical Data Model unless performance requirements forbid it, mitigated by the fact that translations are often stateless and can be load-balanced.
A Canonical Data Model need only model the portion of data that participates in messaging, not the complete data model of every application, which significantly reduces the complexity of defining it.

A Canonical Data Model lets developers and business users discuss the integration solution in the company's business-domain terms rather than a specific package's representation, and defining one is often the first step to resolving semantic dissonance between applications.
Specify a Format Indicator on the Canonical Data Model, because the canonical format is likely to change over time.

A synchronous, sequential broker is simpler because it avoids concurrency and threads but is inefficient, whereas an asynchronous, parallel broker that issues all requests at once can be roughly n times faster for n recipients, at the cost of having to accept replies in any order.

Asynchronous invocation over a message queue also lets you run multiple instances of a service to relieve a bottleneck, because the reply is delivered to a channel rather than to a specific component instance.

Choose the addressing scheme for sending to multiple providers: Fixed (a hard-coded list), Distribution (a Recipient List with broker-side match criteria, giving control and efficiency but requiring broker logic), or Auction (a Publish-Subscribe Channel where any interested provider may bid, making the broker maintenance-free but pushing work to the providers).

When aggregating replies on a single response channel, include a sender-identifying field and pass the expected count to the Aggregator (an Initialized Aggregator); under an auction where the count is unknown, use a completeness condition independent of the total, such as a minimum number of responses with a timeout fallback.
condition: aggregating responses from a variable set of providers

statement: Handle concurrent client requests either with multiple instances (a process pool assigned via a Message Dispatcher, giving predictable resource use and process reuse) or with a single event-driven instance (efficient when mostly waiting on external replies but limited in scalability), and combine both techniques for high volume.

Equip each message with a Correlation Identifier when handling concurrent requests, because replies for different clients may arrive on a shared channel and must be matched back to the correct originating request.
Because HTTP is inherently unreliable and was designed for synchronous document retrieval, Web Services that use HTTP almost always use synchronous request/response messaging.

Synchronous Web Services let the client learn the outcome quickly, but they force the server to hold many concurrent open connections and to add trap, recover, and reroute logic for failed invocations, increasing server complexity.

SOAP Encoding (the 'encoded' style) has been rendered obsolete by literal ('doc/literal') encoding, in which the type mapping is supplied externally by an XML-schema (WSDL) document; and a Document binding with literal encoding is commonly used to represent RPC semantics as a Command Message.

A WSDL document effectively specifies a Canonical Data Model that both parties use, with the double-translation realized by a Messaging Mapper or Gateway in the service consumer and a Remote Facade in the service provider.

Use a Messaging Gateway (the Gateway pattern) to keep messaging-API-specific code out of the application, which both abstracts the communication details and improves testability by allowing a Service Stub to replace the real external service.
Keep a Messaging Gateway's interfaces minimal — for example, separate sender and receiver interfaces each with a single method — so they are easy to implement and to stub for testing.

Implementing a broker as a single Process Manager component that runs all its functions internally eliminates the overhead of passing messages across queues between those functions, at the cost of having to maintain multiple concurrent process instances.
Because message queues are unidirectional, establishing a request-response interaction with another component requires a pair of queues.
A Recipient List that distributes a request together with an Aggregator that recombines the replies form a distribution-style Scatter-Gather.

When a Recipient List sends a separate message — each with its own message ID — to several recipients, do not correlate the replies by message ID; instead generate one correlation identifier per aggregate and carry it on every outgoing message so all related replies map back to the same aggregate.

To let an Aggregator determine completeness by count, require every selected participant to send a reply even when declining (for example, a reply carrying an error code), while keeping the option to change the strategy, such as cutting off the bidding after a fixed time.
condition: aggregating a known set of participants where some may decline

statement: A Messaging Gateway should expose methods that make no reference to messaging at all, hiding correlation and asynchrony from the caller, and it can let the caller pass an arbitrary Asynchronous Completion Token that the gateway stores keyed by the request's Correlation Identifier and returns with the reply.

Create a separate Messaging Mapper that holds the mapping logic between domain objects and the messaging infrastructure, such that neither the domain objects nor the infrastructure are aware the Messaging Mapper exists.

Messages differ fundamentally from domain objects because most messaging infrastructures support only scalar data and not object references or inheritance, so object graphs cannot be passed by reference through messaging.

Serializing a whole object into an opaque string field is a poor way to put an object in a message, because a Message Router cannot route on its properties, it resists testing and validation, and language-runtime serialization is generally incompatible across languages.

Keep mapping code out of the domain object, because embedding it blends low-level messaging concerns with application logic, couples the domain object to the messaging API, and destroys the object's reusability in contexts that do not use messaging.

A Messaging Mapper differs from a messaging abstraction layer (a Gateway): with an abstraction layer the domain objects still know about it, whereas with a Messaging Mapper the domain objects have no idea messaging is involved; the Mapper is typically invoked through events or the Observer pattern.

Use a Messaging Mapper together with a Message Translator for an extra level of indirection — the Mapper resolves object references and data-type conversions in the application's language while the Translator handles structural mapping to the Canonical Data Model — accepting that a domain change may then require changes to both.

Reduce a Messaging Mapper's repetitive field-copying with reflection-based generic mapping or a configurable code generator rather than hand-coding each field, since the generic mapper need be written only once.

Use a Transactional Client — make the client's session with the messaging system transactional — so that the client can set transaction boundaries that span several messages or coordinate messaging with other resources.

A messaging system uses transactions internally, so a Message Endpoint's send and receive are transactional even unknowingly (consistent and isolated, and durable only with Guaranteed Delivery); a Transactional Client extends this so the application can control the transaction boundaries.

Use a Transactional Client for send-receive pairs, message groups, message-and-database coordination, and message-and-workflow coordination, so that all parts succeed or roll back together; coordinating two messaging systems, a database, or a workflow engine requires a distributed transaction.

A request sender cannot send a request and wait for its reply within a single transaction, because the request is never actually sent until the transaction commits, so the reply would never arrive; a single transaction only works for a replier that receives a request and sends the reply.

A Transactional Client works well with a single Polling Consumer but does not work well with an Event-Driven Consumer or a Message Dispatcher and can cause problems for Competing Consumers, because an event-driven consumer must commit the receive before the application can decide to reject the message.
