Use a Polling Consumer (a synchronous receiver) that explicitly calls to receive a message only when the application is ready, so it consumes messages at its own rate rather than the rate at which they arrive.

Control how many messages are processed concurrently by limiting the number of polling threads, which keeps the receiver from being overwhelmed (extra messages queue up); use a blocking receive for a single channel, and a timeout or non-blocking receive to poll multiple channels or do other work with one thread.
A consumer that polls too often or blocks threads for too long is inefficient, in which case an Event-Driven Consumer may be the better choice.

Use Competing Consumers — multiple consumers on one Point-to-Point Channel — to consume messages concurrently across threads, applications, and computers, giving virtually unlimited processing capacity bounded only by the messaging system's delivery rate.

Competing Transactional Clients can waste significant effort processing messages whose receive operations must be rolled back because a competitor already consumed the work, so their performance should be measured carefully on the specific messaging implementation.
Create a Message Dispatcher on a channel that consumes each message and distributes it to a performer, acting as the Mediator that coordinates the consumers of a single channel.

A Message Dispatcher consists of a dispatcher that consumes and delegates and performers that process (each optionally in its own thread); because the dispatcher does little work and does not block when performers run in their own threads, it can dispatch as fast as the system delivers and avoids becoming a bottleneck.
A Message Dispatcher with type-specific performers can support multiple data types on one channel and implement Selective Consumer behaviour, serving as an alternative to separate Datatype Channels.

Unlike Competing Consumers, a Message Dispatcher's performers typically all run in the same application as the dispatcher, because a performer in another application would require the remote-procedure-style communication that messaging aims to avoid.

Implement a Message Dispatcher as a Polling Consumer rather than an Event-Driven Consumer, because event-driven consumers do not work well with transactional clients and a transactional dispatcher needs a separate session per performer to commit or roll back each performer's message.
condition: the dispatcher must be a Transactional Client

statement: Make a consumer a Selective Consumer that filters the messages its channel delivers, receiving only those whose selection value matches its criteria.
Put a message's selection value in its header rather than its body, so that a Selective Consumer can evaluate it without having to parse the body.

When using Selective Consumers on a Point-to-Point Channel — where they become competing and selective — design the criteria so at least one consumer matches every valid selection value, or unmatched messages will clutter the channel until they expire.

A Selective Consumer is more dynamic than a Content-Based Router, because a new filtering option needs only a new consumer (which can be created while the system runs) rather than a new output channel, whereas changing a Content-Based Router is more static and can strand messages already routed onto the old channels.

A Selective Consumer keeps unwanted messages available for other receivers, whereas a Message Filter prevents unwanted messages from reaching any receiver; use a Selective Consumer when one receiver wants to ignore messages that others want, and a Message Filter to drop messages no receiver wants.

Do not use Selective Consumers emulating Datatype Channels to hide messages from certain applications for security, because the messaging system usually does not authorize selection criteria, so a malicious but authorized consumer can change its criteria to read unauthorized messages; separate Datatype Channels are needed to lock applications out.
Use a Durable Subscriber to make the messaging system save messages published on a Publish-Subscribe Channel while the subscriber is disconnected (inactive) and deliver them when it reconnects.

A Publish-Subscribe subscriber that is disconnected when a message is published normally misses it (unlike a Point-to-Point channel, which retains messages), so a durable subscription introduces a third 'inactive' state — disconnected but still subscribed — between subscribed and unsubscribed.

A durable subscription behaves identically to a non-durable one while the subscriber is active; the difference appears only on disconnect, and an inactive durable subscriber that never reconnects accumulates messages without bound, so use Message Expiration or a saved-message limit.

Choose subscription durability by need: a display GUI showing only the current value can be a non-durable subscriber, while a component that must not miss any update (such as a range-tracking database) should be a Durable Subscriber.
condition: deciding whether a Publish-Subscribe subscriber must survive disconnects

statement: Design a receiver to be an Idempotent Receiver — one that can safely receive the same message multiple times — because even a once-sent message can be received more than once, for example when a lost acknowledgement triggers a resend.

Idempotency is achieved either by explicit de-duplication (tracking already-received unique message identifiers in a buffer whose size depends on how many messages the sender may send before acknowledgement) or by defining message semantics so a repeat has no effect (for example, 'set the balance to $110' instead of 'add $10').

Do not overload a business field such as an order number as the de-duplication key, because tying infrastructure de-dup semantics to a business field breaks when the business later allows legitimate repeats (such as amending an order); use a separate unique message identifier instead.

Allowing duplicates and making the receiver idempotent can increase throughput compared with eliminating duplicates in the infrastructure, which is why some systems offer only 'at least once' delivery; a resend-on-failure combined with idempotent receivers also recovers cleanly from a failed distributed transaction.

Use an Event-Driven Consumer (an asynchronous receiver) that the messaging system automatically hands messages to as they arrive, so the consumer sits dormant with no active threads until invoked, avoiding the wasted polling of a Polling Consumer on an empty channel.

An Event-Driven Consumer bridges the messaging system's invocation and the application's callback through an application-specific implementation that conforms to the messaging system's API (such as JMS MessageListener.onMessage); typically only one thread runs through a consumer, so it processes one message at a time.

In JMS an Event-Driven Consumer that is also a Transactional Client does not work as expected, because MessageListener.onMessage cannot throw a checked exception to trigger a rollback and a runtime exception loses the message; use a message-driven EJB for transactional event-driven behaviour.
condition: combining event-driven consumption with transactions in JMS

statement: Design a Service Activator that connects messages on a channel to a service, so a single service can be invoked both via messaging and via non-messaging techniques without being reimplemented for each style; the service is written as though always invoked synchronously and need not know it is being invoked through messaging.

A Service Activator handles all messaging details (as a Polling or Event-Driven Consumer), extracts from the usually-Command message which service to invoke and with what parameters, invokes the service like any other client, and optionally returns a reply; if it cannot process the message it routes it to an Invalid Message Channel, whereas errors within the service are application errors.

Loose coupling and indirection are an 'architect's dream, developer's nightmare': they add flexibility but make testing and debugging harder, because a producer does not know its consumers, a reply may not even be designed for, and delivery time is not guaranteed.

Message monitoring works at two levels: System Management tracks message counts and processing times using only header fields, whereas Business Activity Monitoring inspects the payload (for example, the dollar value of orders placed in the last hour).
Use a Control Bus, which uses the same messaging mechanism as the application data but on separate channels, to manage and monitor a distributed integration system from a central console.

A Control Bus carries configuration, heartbeat, test, exception, and statistics messages, letting components read configuration from a central repository rather than per-machine property files and be reconfigured at runtime.

Architect each message-processing component around three interfaces: an inbound data interface, an outbound data interface, and a control interface that exchanges control messages with the Control Bus.

Construct a Detour as a context-based router controlled by the Control Bus that in one state routes messages through extra validation, logging, or debugging steps and in the other routes them straight to the destination — analogous to assert statements enabled only in a debug build.

Insert a Wire Tap — a fixed Recipient List with two output channels — to publish each incoming message unmodified to both the main channel and a secondary inspection channel, so a Point-to-Point channel can be observed without disturbing its flow or changing its semantics.

A Wire Tap cannot alter the messages flowing through it (use a Detour for that) and adds latency by consuming and republishing; because republished messages receive new message IDs, do not correlate the tapped copies by message ID.

Attach a Message History — a list, kept in the header, of every component the message has passed through — so the flow of messages in a loosely coupled system can be analyzed and debugged without introducing dependencies between components.

A Message History lets a subscriber detect and ignore a message that originated from itself, breaking the infinite-loop risk when an application both publishes to and subscribes to the same Publish-Subscribe event channel, such as in address-change propagation.

Use a Message Store to capture information about each message in a central, persistent location, enabling reporting against message data that the transient, per-message Message History cannot provide.

Feed a Message Store asynchronously by sending a duplicate of each message (often via a Wire Tap) on a fire-and-forget secondary channel so the main flow is not slowed, store only the key fields needed for analysis to limit traffic and storage, and add a purging mechanism because the store grows large.

Use a Smart Proxy to track a Request-Reply service whose replies go to caller-specified Return Addresses: store each original Return Address and replace it with the Smart Proxy's own reply channel, then route each incoming reply back to the stored original address.

A Smart Proxy can store the original Return Address and Correlation Identifier either inside the message (requiring the service to copy the field) or in its own storage; it should generate its own Correlation Identifier, because a shared reply queue carrying several requestors' messages makes the original unreliable, and it must restore the original Correlation Identifier and Return Address on the reply.

A Smart Proxy can also add Return-Address support to a service that only replies to a fixed channel, and it is well suited to measuring per-message processing time and the number of outstanding requests and reporting summary metrics to the Control Bus on a timer rather than per message, since inserting the proxy already doubles message volume.

Use a Test Message to actively verify that a component is not just alive but processing correctly, because a heartbeat operates only at the component level and cannot detect a component that garbles its outgoing messages due to an internal fault.

A Test Message setup has a Test Data Generator, a Test Message Injector that tags test messages (ideally via a dedicated header field rather than overloading a business field), a Test Message Separator (often a Content-Based Router, unneeded if the component supports a Return Address), and a Test Data Verifier that compares actual to expected results.

Active monitoring with Test Messages probes a component through the same processing path as real messages, achieving a deeper level of testing than passive heartbeats, but it adds processor load and possible pay-per-use cost and does not work with stateful components that cannot distinguish test data from real data.
exception: stateful components that would, for example, record test orders as real ones

statement: Use a Channel Purger to remove unwanted left-over messages from a channel, which otherwise disturb tests or block a restarted component that keeps failing immediately on a bad message.

Persistent, asynchronous messaging can leave a stale message on a channel that a naive receiver mistakes for its current reply; a Correlation Identifier lets the receiver detect and discard such a stale message, and a Channel Purger can optionally store removed messages for later inspection, editing, or re-injection.
When managing integration components, treat each as a black box monitored from the outside, because in most integration scenarios you do not have access to the application internals.

Knowing which pattern to use is not enough; the value comes from working out how best to implement and incorporate it into the system to solve the actual problem, taking the technology platform and other design criteria into account.

Let subscribers filter by selectively subscribing to fine-grained per-topic channels rather than filtering a single broad stream after receipt, when the platform makes channels cheap (such as TIBCO subject-based virtual channels), recognizing that using many channels to avoid filtering is a nonstandard use of channels.
condition: the messaging platform makes channels very cheap to create

statement: The choice between fewer channels (per-trader) and many channels (per-trader-per-bond) came down to the location of logic: the per-trader approach would force the generic Analytics Engine to become a Content-Based Router with application-specific routing, violating its reusability as a generic Message Bus server, so the per-bond approach was chosen.
Place a Content-Based Router near the client to collapse a large number of upstream channels into a manageable few, rather than making client desktops subscribe to thousands of channels.

Because a channel need not be used in both directions, pick the channel type per direction: Publish-Subscribe for server-to-client (so a trader logged in at several workstations receives every update, and for multicast) and Point-to-Point for client-to-server (direct delivery to a single server), gaining both benefits without either drawback.

To throttle an overwhelming update stream without losing data, prefer an Aggregator that merges successive partial field updates over a time-based Message Filter that drops messages, because the filter would discard fields that update independently and so harm data integrity.
condition: high-frequency updates where different fields update in separate messages

statement: An Aggregator reduces traffic substantially only when many messages concern the same correlated entity within the window; if updates are spread thinly across many entities, the gain is small.

When the consumer rather than the message flow is the bottleneck, turn the consumer into a Polling Consumer — for example a background thread that requests an update with a Command Message and processes the returned set as a Document Message — so the client controls its own intake and cannot be overloaded.
condition: the consumer is the bottleneck, not the channel

statement: Competing Consumers cannot speed up a Publish-Subscribe Channel, because every consumer would receive every message; use a Message Dispatcher instead to get parallel processing on a Publish-Subscribe Channel.

A flood of expired messages piling up in the Dead Letter Channel is a clear sign that the message flow exceeds the consumers' processing rate (slow consumers), and the queue can grow large enough to crash the server.

Patterns help design and maintain a system but do not compensate for poor up-front design: a parallelizing Message Dispatcher improved a client-bottleneck crash, but the real fix was refactoring the message-flow architecture.

Standardizing a pattern's implementation strategy does not make the pattern obsolete; it strengthens it by making separate implementations interoperable and extending the pattern's reach to broader scales, such as applying Correlation Identifier or Message Router at the business-process level rather than to raw messages.

A business process component unites a set of web services and the definition of how messages flow into and out of them behind a single endpoint, so that a client need not implement its own Process Manager to coordinate the services and their dependencies.

BPEL4WS essentially defines a Process Manager declared in XML that creates Routing Slip, Durable Subscriber, Datatype Channel (its 'containers'), and related constructs, so developers declare service linkages and message flow rather than hand-coding the messaging between services.
Scalability is a measure of how well a solution continues to fit a problem as the scope of that problem increases.
Scalability and performance are distinct properties and must not be conflated.
Horizontal scalability — adding capacity by adding more of the same hardware or software — is the only true form of scalability and the preferred default approach.
Scaling horizontally does not by itself guarantee a safe or correct architecture.
Vertical scaling (adding storage, processors, or RAM to a single machine) is an expensive strategy that should be reserved for problems that genuinely cannot be solved with horizontal scaling.
condition: only when the problem is academically difficult to solve horizontally

statement: A 'difficult' scaling problem here means one that is academically difficult — no legitimate solution exists on the market — not one that is merely inconvenient.
Large ACID-compliant databases are an example of a component that is hard to scale horizontally and requires tremendous compromise to do so.
Serving DNS, FTP, and static web content are well-understood problems that are horizontally scalable by nature.
Even an inherently horizontally-scalable system still requires great care to build correctly.
Build a system for current demand but architect it so that scaling up to far larger load requires no application or architectural redesign.
Provisioning capacity for far more users than the current base is a waste of money.
The need to scale arises because changes in the business can cause the size of a problem to swell or shrink dramatically.
Adding independent components to an architecture increases its complexity linearly, whereas adding components that other components depend on increases complexity exponentially.
Whenever a system is scaled, four outcomes are guaranteed: capital investment, increased complexity, increased maintenance cost, and time required to act.
Scaling an architecture up is fundamentally more difficult than scaling it down.
Over-utilizing infrastructure produces glaring usability effects, whereas under-utilizing it produces only subtle financial effects.
If scaling a solution back would save nothing, there is no reason to do it.

An application riddled with bad design decisions may be unable to run on an architecture substantially smaller than its large-scale original, blocking the cost reductions needed to survive a drop in demand.
An architecture's approach and final design are shaped as much by capital cost, complexity, maintenance cost, and time-to-act as by the technical challenge itself.

Smaller Internet businesses tend to prioritize low up-front investment and fast time-to-implementation, while large companies tend to prioritize minimizing risk and maximizing simplicity and maintainability.
Design architecture components to be as autonomous and as cost-effectively scalable as possible.
An architecture built from efficient, maintainable components scales better than an equally efficient and maintainable monolithic architecture.
Demand growth is usually non-uniform, so absorbing increased load often requires scaling only one or two components rather than the whole system.
Anticipating change is the defining skill of a good Internet architect.
No programming language inherently scales or fails to scale; solutions scale, so design should focus on the solution rather than a language-specific implementation.
High availability and load balancing are different concerns; decoupling their roles enables better architecture decisions.
Monitor both technical metrics (whether servers are up) and business-level metrics (whether the business is functioning).
Have the operations group participate regularly in business and technical-development meetings, because development's closeness to the business tends to cause operations' insights to be lost.
Educating the development and operations teams about the ramifications of failure is the first principle of avoiding failure.

Teams are used to run large systems for three reasons: the work exceeds one person's capacity, deep focused expertise is cheaper to find than broad expertise, and business continuity requires guarding against the 'key man' problem.
Uncontrolled change — feature creep, milestone hopping, sloppy version control, and premature implementation — is among the greatest risks to a large architecture.
Version control is the lowest-effort, highest-value control in a rapid-development environment and should always be used.
A 'push' is any controlled, planned action that changes the production architecture, including code pushes, schema changes, vendor upgrades, OS patches, and hardware or network changes.
A successful push plan has four parts: a plan from A to B, a plan from B back to A, a plan to restore A from bare metal, and a successful test of the first two plans.
Always maintain a tested back-out plan for reverting a change; in a rapid-development environment this is fundamental rather than optional.
condition: rapid-development environment

statement: Rapid development tends to reduce testing and quality assurance, which lets breakage reach production unnoticed.

Commodity (current- or previous-generation) hardware generally offers a better return on investment than the fastest, largest hardware, because of diminishing returns at the top of the performance curve.
Attempting to scale by buying a single large, fast, monolithic machine eventually saturates that machine and forces a hard lesson in the difference between scalability and performance.
Testing verifies only that a system reaches an expected outcome for the specific inputs provided; no form of testing can ensure correct behaviour under every possible condition.
Unit testing verifies that modules function correctly when used correctly, but it does not verify that they are used correctly.
Apply unit testing comprehensively across the whole system rather than to isolated modules, because partial coverage gives a false sense of confidence.
A full business-cycle testing infrastructure is usually more work to build than the systems it tests, which is why most systems lack it.
Subtle, intermittent bugs are the most damaging because they occur infrequently, can self-correct, and are hard to reproduce.
A version-control commit must be atomic: if it succeeds it must completely succeed, and if it fails it must be as if it never happened.

Select a version-control system by the properties that matter to a commercial Internet architecture — stability, durability, consistency, restorability, branching and tagging, usability on every platform you run, and changeset support — rather than by distributed disconnected-operation features.
The specific version-control system chosen is unimportant provided it has the features your architecture needs and is adopted consistently by everyone involved.
Leverage version control for deployment, not only development: promote tested code into a production branch and roll releases from tags.

Back up production configuration files into version control (for example, rsync /etc and key directories to a central host and commit) so that emergency, undocumented configuration changes are tracked.
Understanding how a server's configuration has changed over time is more valuable than the ability to restore it to a specific point in time.
A bare-metal recovery procedure remains necessary even though many disastrous failures do not require one.
No amount of careful planning or precisely followed procedure compensates for a poorly designed architecture.
A language's selection and a system's scalability have little to do with each other; architectural design and implementation strategy determine how scalable the final product is.
Design a large system first and hold coders to an architecturally-savvy standard, because a master architect cannot be involved in every aspect of organic, evolving development.
A good initial design is only a foundation; good design principles must be applied continually or the structures built on it will degrade.
Regular collaboration among the business, development, and operations teams is the most fundamental ingredient of good design.
Treat mission-critical as business-critical: each business defines which aspects — including policies and procedures, not just components — are vital to its operations.
The criticality of an environment is unrelated to its scale; load balancing concerns scale by combining resources for load, while high availability concerns resilience.
Guaranteeing 100% uptime is impossible, so most large production environments define high availability as the absence of unplanned outages.
Planned maintenance windows, even when unused, provide opportunities for proactive maintenance that reduces the risk of unexpected outages.
Machine-level failover is not the business goal of high availability; the goal is that the services the business provides remain functional and accessible.
Monitor the architecture both bottom-up with systems monitors and top-down with business monitors; business-level monitoring is as valuable as systems monitoring.
A monitoring infrastructure that does not adapt as the architecture, application, and business change becomes useless and even dangerous by creating a false sense of security.
SNMP dominates systems monitoring and most commercial components ship an SNMP agent, but many free and open tools — notably mail transport agents — do not.

For a component that does not expose a metric over SNMP, either fetch it through a simpler mechanism such as SSH or HTTP, or export it over SNMP for efficient integration at the cost of higher MIB-authoring overhead.
A capable monitoring system must provide flexible notifications with automatic escalation when failures are not resolved within a given time.

A capable monitoring system must support maintenance windows that suppress escalation, event acknowledgment that suspends notifications, and per-monitor scheduling so expensive or slow-changing metrics are polled less often.
A capable monitoring system must encode service dependencies so that an upstream failure such as a crashed switch suppresses redundant downstream alerts.
Maintain three environments — development, staging, and production — with staging kept as close to production as possible, ideally an exact replica down to hardware and software versions.
When staging and production are identical, a new release can be promoted by pointing production traffic at the staging environment and switching their roles, avoiding a push.
Production should be quiet, uneventful, and routine; investment in development and staging environments exists to buy that stability.
The best solution technically is not always the right solution for the business; infrastructure decisions are governed by cost versus benefit.

Under-investing in staging relative to production raises the push failure rate, yet can still be the correct business choice when the cost of those failures is below the cost of full staging infrastructure.
condition: when the cost of push failures is below the cost of building and maintaining full staging
exception: high-stakes environments such as banking where failures are very costly

statement: Emergency releases — security exploits or acutely crippling bugs — must be applied with extreme haste, outside the normal controlled release cycle.
Performance and scalability are orthogonal: scalability means a system can grow or shrink without fundamental change.
The performance of an individual component drastically affects how efficiently the whole system scales, so the performance of every introduced component must be scrutinized and judged.
The only way to increase the performance of a complex system is to reduce the resource consumption of one or more of its components, and a single slow component can capsize the entire architecture.
Speeding up code inside a bottleneck has a larger impact on performance than speeding up code outside it, and roughly 90% of execution time is spent in 10% of the code.

Optimize the most common execution path rather than the slowest component, because a 50% speedup of code that runs 5% of the time yields about 2.5% overall while the same speedup of code running 0.1% of the time yields only about 0.05%.
Performance review and tuning must be a perpetual cycle, with all infrastructure and application code open to review and revision.
Regularly change the resolution of performance analysis: reframing 'how do I make this faster?' as 'why am I doing this at all?' often exposes a better solution.
A mission-critical architecture must not depend on a single person; personnel are part of the architecture, so keep communication open and avoid isolating knowledge.
Fault tolerance is the capability of a system or component to continue normal operation despite hardware or software faults, measured by how many faults it can withstand before operation is impaired.
An architecture that survives a single component failure is 1 fault tolerant, while one that survives the failure of all but one component is N-1 fault tolerant — the strongest guarantee possible.
Hardware that is required to handle routine load cannot be counted as redundant hardware.

SMTP is intrinsically fault tolerant because senders try multiple advertised mail exchanges in ascending order of preference, whereas HTTP provides no such intrinsic fault tolerance and must be made highly available by design.

Well-designed distributed systems such as peer-to-peer networks provide controlled horizontal scalability: the network can grow arbitrarily large without requiring more powerful individual machines or sacrificing quality of service.
Once a three-node cluster works, scaling to n nodes is a repeatable process rather than an experiment; getting the machines to cooperate is the hardest part of distributed-systems design.
No enterprise-ready, horizontally scalable, N-1 fault-tolerant database exists, so because solving the three-node replication problem is expensive the accepted approach is to engineer around it.
condition: given the limitations of current replication protocols such as 2PC and 3PC

statement: High availability adds cost and disadvantages: more equipment to maintain, distributed-system troubleshooting that is dramatically harder than single-node, and application code that must handle content-synchronization issues across the cluster.

Load balancing is not high availability: it relocates the failure problem to another tier — often shifting responsibility from systems to network administrators — without giving the business any availability guarantee.

High availability is not load balancing: high availability implies only resilience, not efficient resource use, and in hot-standby configurations one node contributes 100% of its resources while the others contribute 0%.
A legitimate load balancer must include an intelligent resource-allocation mechanism; a device that distributes requests without one is merely a load distributor.
Building a provably optimal load-balancing system is impossible because it would require knowing all future requests and resource states; the goal is to run the business well, not to be optimal.
A single dedicated high-availability/load-balancing device is itself a single point of failure, so it must be deployed redundantly.
A vendor's selling points are not buying points; advertised advantages may simply not apply to your architecture.
VRRP (an IETF draft) and Cisco's proprietary HSRP are the two main router-failover protocols, both built on the concept of heartbeats.

Because web services are typically horizontally scalable and already run on every node, they usually need neither shared storage nor application failover; where shared storage is needed, network-attached storage such as NFS is often sufficient.
Databases are harder to make highly available; the classic path-of-least-resistance approach is shared attached storage with a heartbeat between two machines.
Traditional pairwise active/standby failover leaves one machine completely idle.

Choose a high-availability approach by how dynamic the business is: a fixed, well-understood workload can justify heavy dedicated infrastructure, whereas changing traffic patterns favour a more flexible solution.

In peer-based high availability the cluster, not any individual machine, owns a set of services, and each surviving machine negotiates to assume a subset; which machine holds which responsibility is irrelevant as long as at least one machine remains standing.
A cluster is a set of like machines united to provide a particular service, working in unison to keep that service running continuously and efficiently.
Peer-based high availability avoids expensive dedicated hardware, uses open-source implementations that can be modified for unique needs, and is simpler because it introduces no new network device.
Every new component introduced into an architecture brings new monitoring, more maintenance, more complex upgrades, specialized skills, and harder and costlier troubleshooting.
Pure peer-based high availability requires multiple IP addresses to keep more than one machine simultaneously active, which clashes with IP-unfriendly services.
condition: for IP-unfriendly services such as SSL

statement: A single IP address can serve at most one common name over SSL, so N distinctly named secure sites require at least N IP addresses.
Some services such as DNS and web serving are naturally conducive to concurrent operation across a cluster, whereas database services often force fundamental sacrifices.
Services that cannot exploit multi-IP peer high availability still benefit from N-way hot-standby, electing a new master on failure to serve over a single advertised IP address.
The most commonly ignored components in high-availability design are networking devices such as firewalls, switches, and routers.
When components of a system change, a previously adequate subsystem such as the network layer can become inadequate, so it must be re-reviewed rather than assumed still fit.
The high reliability of network equipment breeds a misconception that it needs no maintenance, yet plugging in a new device can leave a switch no longer optimally configured.
Systems administrators should learn enough network engineering to recognize when they need network review or assistance.

Commodity servers running free open-source operating systems are now viable production routers; the main remaining objection is high availability, which peer-based high availability with a free VRRP implementation resolves.
Load balancing does not mean balancing the system load average; system load is the average length of the run queue and is the wrong metric for web traffic.
Balancing on system load fails because of staleness: web requests are too short and the load average updates too slowly — every few seconds as a one-minute average — to reflect current workload.
The correct basis for load balancing is effective utilization of available resources, not total resources.
Round-robin load balancing suffers a queueing-theory problem in which overworked servers get no reprieve to recover.
Least-connections balancing is relatively sound with a good implementation but degrades when several load balancers make decisions in parallel.
Weighted balancing relies on arbitrary administrative constants and demands constant manual re-tweaking whenever servers are added or upgraded.
Combining a randomized algorithm with a resource-based one is an effective, probabilistically good answer to the load-metric staleness problem.

Multiple parallel load balancers must cooperate; uncooperative concurrent decisions double the intended effect of naive decisions, and a random distribution can beat the smartest uncooperative algorithm.
No single load-balancing model applies equally well to all practical situations.
Two machines cannot share a single IP address on the same Ethernet segment because of ARP, so without a virtual-IP device the rule is at least one distinct IP per machine.

Round-robin DNS exposes multiple IP addresses for one hostname and distributes traffic in practice, but the DNS specification guarantees no even distribution and the mechanism has no underlying intelligence.
The SSL handshake completes before any HTTP request is sent, so no Host header is available, which makes name-based virtual hosting infeasible for secure sites.
Running SSL on a non-standard port to conserve IP addresses is a poor workaround because many corporate firewalls permit SSL only over port 443.
Redirecting secure transactions to a shared delegate hostname conserves IP space but changes the visible URL and thereby diminishes user trust.
Web switches, also called black-box load balancers, are the most popular technology for scaling high-traffic websites and are sometimes the only viable solution given their raw performance.
A web switch behaves like a reverse network-address-translation router, exposing many private servers through a single routable IP address.
IP virtual servers provide the same load-balancing function as web switches but in software on commodity servers, with an identical network topology.
Application-layer load balancers run in user space, gaining features such as SSL-aware, per-transaction, and business-rule allocation at a substantial performance cost relative to layer-3/4 switches.
Operating at layer 3 lets a balancer avoid application-protocol knowledge, which enables hardware acceleration and versatility across many IP protocols such as SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DNS, FTP, and NNTP.
Packet translation merely manipulates packets and scales massively, whereas proxying must process and re-originate all data and is substantially more expensive.
Requirements, not convenience, dictate the load-balancing solution: if a web switch or IPVS cannot meet a functional requirement it is eliminated rather than merely deprioritized.

Linear scaling is a falsehood; horizontal scaling is sublinear because optimal request allocation would require knowledge of the future, so one machine reaches full utilization while added machines achieve less.
As a capacity-planning rule of thumb, expect about 70% per-server utilization on clusters of three or more servers.
condition: clusters of three or more nodes

statement: A load balancer should be a resource-allocation framework that lets the architect choose the allocation strategy, not merely a utilization equalizer.
Load balancing does not provide high availability, so load balancers are themselves a single point of failure and must be deployed in pairs with a high-availability solution between them.
Decentralizing an architecture across sites multiplies the cost of redundant load balancers per cluster, so beyond a couple of installations alternative approaches become more appropriate.
condition: when an architecture decentralizes across multiple geographic sites

statement: Session stickiness is not load balancing: assigning a request by anything other than load metrics is not balancing load.
Storing session state only on a local web server forces sticky sessions and creates a single point of failure for every user stuck to that server.
Splitting session data — rarely-changed parts in a central store and frequently-changed parts in a secure client cookie — can radically improve the load-balancing options available.
Most web content, by both volume and count, is static, and dynamic-serving techniques are inefficient when applied to static content.
Establish specific performance goals — peak requests per second derived from visitor counts, peak-hour share, and pages per visit — before evaluating a serving approach.
Browser caching reduces but does not eliminate static-object requests; rarely-changing sites benefit greatly, while news-style sites that add new objects per story benefit little.
An initial page load typically opens several concurrent TCP connections (about seven, held roughly four seconds) because of embedded page dependencies.
Apache's 1.3 process model dedicates one process per connection for that connection's entire lifetime, including idle lag and slow client delivery.
On a workstation a hundred 'running' processes feel instant only because a handful actually run at once, whereas on a busy web server all processes genuinely contend for CPU and disk.
A context switch — swapping one process off the CPU for another — is never free, so its cost must be budgeted on a high-traffic server.

Serving a web request takes far more than two context switches, because every network or disk interaction blocks the process and forces a switch; even the minimum path of accept, read, write, log, and close costs about ten context switches, a lower bound most environments never achieve.

At roughly 10 microseconds per context switch a server can perform about 100,000 per second, so serving 10,000 requests per second at about ten switches each would consume all CPU just switching, leaving nothing to run the actual work.
At a modest 1,000 requests per second a server spends about 10% of its time context switching, which an architect must account for when the CPU is also generating dynamic content.
Web-server models other than process-per-connection — thread-per-request, event-driven, or in-kernel serving — reduce context-switching cost.

Use the right tool for the job: one general-purpose web configuration can serve all traffic, but a specialized one is more effective, just as a claw hammer works everywhere yet is rarely the best tool.
Separating distinct kinds of work onto dedicated workers removes switching overhead and lets a cheaper, specialized resource handle each part.

A heavyweight Apache process embedding mod_perl or mod_php consumes far more memory (tens of megabytes) than a static-only worker (under one megabyte), and limited RAM caps how many can run before swapping causes disaster.
Serving heavyweight dynamic and lightweight static content from the same fat process wastes memory, so segregating static serving frees the dynamic servers to do their job.
Make each visit consume as few resources as possible so the same hardware supports many more visitors, which is what makes scaling up and down cost-effective.
Segregate static and dynamic content so the two can be scaled orthogonally, and design to allow this separation rather than require it.
Implement static/dynamic URL segregation through a function that generates static URLs, so the base can be changed or reverted in one place rather than hardcoded throughout the content.

Static content distribution is simpler than dynamic because control is deliberately forfeited: remote caches are allowed and objects are added and removed rather than changed in place, so no cluster-wide consistency semantics are needed.
Align the mechanisms used to distribute static and dynamic content so operators follow one mental model, because differing policies invite mistakes.
NFS-based content distribution places one copy on a file server that all web servers mount, which is simple but a single point of failure and weak over a wide-area network.
rsync-style differential synchronization is network-efficient but trades local resources for network savings, and its checksums plus the N-to-one fan-in heavily tax a busy master server.

Exporting content directly from revision control inherits version-control benefits — changesets, back-out, and diffs — and operator familiarity, but CVS's slow tagging and large-tree exports make it inefficient at scale.

Web caches are engineered for high throughput and concurrency and tend to outperform general-purpose web servers, so a reverse-proxy cache in front of a site both reduces origin traffic and offloads slow-client TCP handling.
A web cache fetches content from the authoritative source only on a miss and then serves subsequent requests from its local copy.
A simpler, single-purpose, per-connection-efficient web server outperforms a flexible, multipurpose one for caching, because flexibility costs resources on every connection.
Cache-on-demand is inherently less efficient than direct-serve because it must fetch misses and validate freshness, but the degradation is often acceptable.
A smaller cluster is cheaper to build, easier to manage, and simpler to troubleshoot, so reducing node count pays back beyond capital cost alone.
Open-source solutions gain a clear technical and financial advantage for geographically distributed sites, because commercial per-site costs multiply with each location.
Supporting infrastructure such as a static-content tier must meet the same or stricter availability requirements as the primary service it is a necessary part of.
Choose an operating system or platform for community support and the number of tested installations rather than ideology, since more tested installations mean lower failure likelihood.
Round-robin DNS distribution is uneven but adequate: a reference deployment showed about 30% machine-to-machine deviation second-to-second yet under 3% minute-to-minute.
When a virtual IP moves between machines, the new owner must refresh peers' and the router's ARP caches via gratuitous ARP, and some devices such as a Cisco PIX firewall refuse such ARP spoofing.
Place content geographically closer to users to reduce latency and increase throughput by traversing fewer potentially congested networks.
Optimize for a user's proximity on the network, not their physical location in the world; geographic targeting is the wrong frame.

The DNS round-trip-time method converges each local name server on the lowest-latency authoritative server, but suffers misdirection until convergence and becomes suboptimal after network-topology changes.

Anycast assigns one IP address to multiple servers and relies on shortest-path routing, but a route change mid-session breaks a TCP connection with a reset, so it suits connectionless protocols such as DNS rather than TCP sessions.
Combining Anycast DNS, answered by the closest name server, with per-cluster unique IP addresses delivers clients to the nearest cluster without breaking TCP sessions.
Caching dynamic content is harder than caching static content because the underlying data changes or varies by viewer, invalidating a simple cached copy.
A computer cache only speeds data acquisition; a cache miss costs only time, unlike the everyday sense of 'cache' that assumes the item persists.
Caching is a fundamental engineering technique found everywhere from CPU registers to name servers, not a web-specific trick.

No matter how fast an application is tuned, it is ultimately limited if it does not scale horizontally, and if doubling hardware yields only single-digit performance gains the architecture is in trouble.

Target a high horizontal-scaling efficiency well above half, where 100% means a perfectly horizontally scalable architecture and 0% means a vertical-only one whose sole recourse is performance tuning.

A transparent (layered) cache sits in front of the architecture, serves from its private cache, and repopulates on a miss from the authoritative source; it is ideal for static content because a commodity proxy can hold the whole store and approach a 100% hit rate.
Transparent caching requires no client configuration — deployed as a bridge or IP gateway — so clients are unaware of it.
An accelerating proxy cache spoon-feeds slow clients and frees the more expensive application servers, which must construct content, to move on to the next job.
Even when application pages are mostly unique and the cache hit rate is near zero, the accelerating effect of a proxy cache alone is often worth the investment.
An integrated (look-aside) cache is built into the application and is most similar to computational reuse, in contrast to a black-box transparent cache.

Computational reuse stores the result of an expensive computation when retrieving it later is cheaper than recomputing it; memoizing a naive recursive Fibonacci cut one example from about six seconds to under a hundredth of a second.

Computational reuse — storing an expensive result to retrieve later rather than recomputing it — yields a performance gain, not scalability; high performance does not ensure scalability, but low performance is fatal to it.
Integrated caching is a step toward horizontal scalability because it lets one architecture component use another less, though it is not always a good step to take.

Computational reuse assumes the answer will not change, so caching mutable data such as a database query result or user preferences requires either a cache-invalidation system or a timeout that accepts a margin of staleness.
Recursive DNS caching works well because every datum carries an explicit time-to-live that tells the cache exactly how long it may serve the answer before requerying.
Web-application queries usually carry no explicit TTL — the only implicit one is the life of the request — which makes caching beyond a single request hard to maintain and debug.

A data cache is computational reuse inside a core service: a database query cache such as MySQL's stores answers along with a reference to the data they depend on, so a change to that data efficiently invalidates the answer.
A data cache controlled by the database is simpler than an application-level integrated cache because one product owns both the cache and the authoritative data.
Most Internet data has a high read-to-write ratio, so caching read results pays off.

A write-back cache performs all modifications on the cache and writes them to the backing store lazily on eviction, which risks data loss or corruption on power failure and does not adapt well to distributed web systems.
A write-thru cache writes to both the cache and the backing store, exploiting temporal locality, since recently written data such as a new news article is the most-read data.
A collaborative distributed cache makes one node's stored result available to all nodes, with the data typically held on every node, so any single failure does not threaten availability.

A cache is not required for operation, only for performance and scalability, so it can be removed or reverted; but since most caches other than transparent layered ones have low operational cost, do not remove a working cache unless replacing it with something better.
The goal of caching in a scalable architecture is to reduce contention on a shared resource, not merely to gain performance.
Contention on a shared resource is the enemy of horizontal scalability.
The web tier scales horizontally easily because its work is parallelizable, whereas the database is a shared resource that is hard to scale horizontally and is stressed more as the web tier grows.
When analyzing scalability, the performance metrics that matter are those of the components that do not scale, such as database time, not the total request time.
Timeout-based cache invalidation is easy but incorrect, carrying a margin of error, and is fine for error-tolerant applications, but it wastes most purges when the read-to-write ratio is high.
Explicit cache invalidation is complicated but correct; integrate the invalidation trigger into the content-publishing process so data can be cached indefinitely and purged only on change.

memcached is a distributed caching daemon whose cluster shares keys across machines, and because it is only a cache, a node crash merely loses that partition while clients deterministically fail over with no harm.

memcached is not replicated, so an item is local only one in N times and remote lookups grow with cluster size; it relies on a remote cache fetch being cheaper than a database query, which is usually but not always true.
Artificially segmenting memcached clusters controls how many nodes each cache spans, which helps when clusters are separated by an expensive link or have too many concurrent clients.

Replicating a cache need not be atomic because a cache can be purged at will; active replication publishes cache operations as they happen, while passive replication stores a pulled item locally like cache-on-demand.
User data such as preferences and session state is small, often 100 to 500 bytes, and used mainly to shape or select other data, so it can be cached differently from bulk content.
A user's own machine, addressed through cookies, is a massively scalable, user-centric caching node, provided only information pertinent to that user is stored there.
Storing user-pertinent data in the client cookie yields a near-100% cache hit rate and offloads internal shared resources, at the cost of durability that a cache does not require anyway.
Cookie storage can be made tamper-proof with a secure message digest and private with symmetric encryption, and cookie theft can be mitigated with a refreshed timestamp that expires stale cookies.
Do not hardcode page content into HTML by hand; authors should not know where data resides and content is reused across pages, so let the system render shared content once.

Two-tier execution runs a page once to render slowly-changing shared content and then runs the result for per-viewer dynamic content, because a transparent whole-page cache that can only cache entire pages cannot achieve a good hit rate on mixed pages.
Script compilation is distributed and needs no shared resources, so caching compiled code via compiler caches or a persistent engine is a performance optimization rather than a scalability one.

Execution that pulls from a database or other shared resource costs time and context switches and should be avoided, whereas local execution such as an XSLT transform scales horizontally with the cluster.

In a file-based page cache replicated on every machine, invalidation means deleting files on all machines, and a machine that was down and missed a delete should have its cache blown before it rejoins the cluster.
The key to successful caching is understanding the true nature of the data: how frequently it changes and where it is used.
Caching techniques are largely language- and architecture-independent and applicable even outside the web, so treat them as methodologies rather than specific implementations.

Distributed database technology addresses several distinct problems — data resiliency, operational failover, increased query performance, complete reliability, and geographically distributed operation — that one-sentence explanations wrongly conflate.
Data resiliency keeps a complete, consistent, and current copy of the data elsewhere by shipping modifications in near real-time, to survive disaster or local hardware failure.
Operational failover adds to data resiliency the ability to assume operations: hot-standby fails over automatically, while warm-standby requires an engineer to act.
Read-only slave replicas that never become master and accept no modifications offload read queries to increase performance, which works because of the typically high read-to-write ratio.
True nonstop reliability requires synchronous commit: a transaction must not commit until a second server has agreed, or a transaction completed just before a failure may be lost.
Master-master (parallel-server) replication, common in financial institutions, trades speed for reliability because a commit becomes a collaborative decision that adds latency.
Geographically distributed databases run in an uncontrolled environment where latencies are orders of magnitude higher and peers can vanish for seconds to hours.

Replication is hard because of ACID: the techniques that enforce atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability efficiently on a single machine do not generalize to networked machines without a performance penalty.
Distributing a database forces a compromise on either performance or functionality, which people accustomed to single-instance RDBMS performance find hard to accept.
In multimaster replication every node can process transactions, which most systems do not actually need even though non-technical and many technical people assume this model.
Multimaster ACID is hard because atomicity requires an all-or-nothing commit across nodes and consistency requires a consistent global ordering of commits, whereas isolation is largely unaffected.

Tripling the number of replicas does not triple transactional throughput; read-only query performance can scale almost linearly, but transactional throughput falls when transactions touch the same data.

An almost-linear replication speedup is achievable only in the special case where operations on each location's dataset are disjoint, allowing atomicity and consistency to be enforced without collaboration.
condition: when operations on each location's dataset are disjoint (pure data aggregation)

statement: Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction by having peers prepare and signal readiness before commit; it is considered sufficient for banking and stock trading, but its lock-step progress means a single down node can halt the system, making it ill-suited to wide-area or hostile networks.
Two-phase commit is the only common correct multimaster technique, but due to its overhead it is not widely used for geographic replication.

Advancing data replication is held back by an organizational roadblock: group-communication experts know best how to coordinate distributed nodes, yet data is entrusted only to database experts, and the two must collaborate.
In a network partition each side can see only its own members and believes the others have crashed, leaving two ways forward: manual operator intervention or quorums.
Manual recovery from a network partition — stopping operations and having an operator redefine the consensus set — also requires hard resynchronization of the excluded nodes afterward.

A quorum is a subset of a group permitted to make decisions, and a correct quorum algorithm guarantees that at most one quorum exists at any time, so the system can keep making progress through arbitrary partitions and merges.
The simplest quorum is a majority of the configured nodes, but quorum rules can be weighted to favour business-critical nodes, such as always allowing a headquarters node to proceed.

Extended virtual synchrony provides reliable, ordered messaging with guaranteed knowledge of group membership at delivery time and without the cost of two-phase commit, which is enough to replicate ACID databases.
Multimaster replication is not ready for most environments because people want it for both availability and performance, and you cannot have both at once.

Master-master replication is the two-node special case of multimaster: a low-latency interconnect makes 2PC/3PC overhead reasonable, so for two nodes 2PC is simply how replication is done, though it adds no scalability.
Master-slave replication solves a different problem from multimaster and should not be treated as weaker — it is a different tool for a different job.
In master-slave replication only the master accepts modifications and the slaves serve read-only queries, which increases read-intensive performance almost linearly and sometimes super-linearly.
There are two ways to replicate a master to its slaves: ship the statement for the slave to re-plan and execute (DML replication) or ship the actual changed data (changeset or DML-log replication).

DML and changeset replication differ most for two query classes: cheap statements causing massive data change favour shipping the statement, while expensive statements causing small change favour shipping the changeset.
Massive data changes and expensive-yet-tiny-effect queries should both be rare in an OLTP system; if many of your queries fall into those classes, revisit the data model.
Changeset replication tends to be more reliable and adapts more easily to cross-vendor replication, whereas statement replication re-imposes the master's planning cost on every slave.

On a local-area network, network and I/O bandwidth are cheaper than CPU and memory, favouring changeset replication, whereas on a wide-area network where bandwidth is costly, statement replication makes more sense.

For horizontal scalability, master-slave replication is the only viable option, because master-master is limited to two nodes and multimaster 2PC collapses under the cost of each node coordinating with all the others.
Do not change what works if you can help it; a core product does not by itself enable the architecture, so switching it carries cost without proportionate benefit.
Replicate the data that is heavily queried but changes infrequently — data with a high read-to-write ratio — out to the clusters that read it.
Replicate by transaction ID, not by time, because in a database 'since' means since commit rather than since occurrence, so time-based replay creates a race condition that leaves slaves inconsistent.

Track database changes with triggers on insert, update, and delete; when only the latest view matters, it is sufficient to record the primary keys of modified rows rather than every transaction's full detail.
Change-log tables grow unbounded and require periodic automated cleanup of records already applied to all slaves.
For small, infrequently-changed tables, flipping-snapshot replication — truncate the idle copy, reload it, then repoint a view — avoids the complexity of change tracking at the cost of efficiency.
Use vendor-specific bulk-load mechanisms such as sqlldr, COPY, or LOAD DATA INFILE and database links for production data loading rather than generic row-by-row inserts.
Cross-vendor master-slave replication, implemented in an application external to both databases, lets a team genuinely pick the right database tool for each task.

When you already use a product at the core and need similar functionality elsewhere, prefer the same product, because fewer distinct products mean less required expertise and fewer release and life cycles to plan around.

'Similar functionality' is often poorly assessed: a replica is frequently needed precisely because of a different performance profile or usage pattern, so the new node's demands may genuinely differ from the master's.

Before adding a database for a new need, ask why the current one falls short, what specific features are missing, and whether the problem needs a database at all — and answer without a specific product in mind.
Logs are vital for monitoring, auditing, and troubleshooting, yet log infrastructure is one of the most neglected components of a large architecture.
Logs fall into two kinds — those that feed reports and those used to troubleshoot — and troubleshooting logs are often inadequate precisely because they are needed only when disaster strikes.
The two hard parts of logging at scale are volume and aggregation, since a large site can generate hundreds of millions of log events per day streaming from many servers.
For time-quantized reports, timestamp accuracy is overrated: a clock skew much smaller than the report's time granularity does not change the trends.
For distributed-system troubleshooting, relative timestamp accuracy is paramount: the events of a transaction must be logged cluster-wide in the order they actually executed.
Single-system troubleshooting is simple because one clock writes logs in order, whereas reconstructing cause and effect across a cluster of machines is hard.

Batch (periodic pull) log aggregation is simple but loses the logs written between the last fetch and a crash, offers no real-time analysis, and tempts you to retroactively alter already-published statistics.

Real-time unicast push logging, such as Syslog to a remote host, removes batch latency and enables real-time metrics and anomaly detection, but naive Syslog over UDP is unreliable and a redundant log host requires reconfiguring every publisher.

Passive sniffing aggregation manufactures logs from observed network traffic and needs no server reconfiguration, but it requires a single egress point, cannot read SSL traffic, and silently drops logs under load, making it a bad choice when logs are vital.
Reliable logging should capture all logs up to the moment of a crash and write them to more than one location, so log delivery must be both reliable and real-time.

Turn real-time log streams into business-level monitors that trigger immediately — such as upper bounds on 500 and 404 rates or requests-per-second versus trend — instead of discovering problems in 24-hour roll-ups after the damage is done.
Writing logs to multiple subscribers increases cost linearly unless a reliable IP-multicast substrate is used, which scales the number of subscribers without scaling the network infrastructure.

Separate logging into distinct roles — web servers that publish, log servers that journal, log monitors that analyze, and casual monitors — so each role can have its own uptime requirement, service level, and management.
A publish/subscribe log substrate instruments the whole architecture for performance assessment, debugging, monitoring, and auditing with little effort.
Fear of modifying code — of writing your own patch rather than reusing someone else's — is irrational inertia that leads teams to forfeit real advantages and adopt the wrong technology.
Real-time log streams let an engineer quickly build a custom analysis tool for a specific need, because the needed information is already at hand.
On large sites logs stream by so fast that automated tools are required to extract any useful real-time analysis.
Single hosts have real-time introspection tools such as iostat and vmstat, but web clusters lack analogous real-time tools, so build them on the log stream.

A load balancer's metrics are available only to those with access to it, cover only what it uses for its own decisions, and cannot include application-specific metrics because it operates above the application.
The best architects combine respect for the down-and-dirty details with a macroscopic view of the business and its technical metrics.

Technical staff should monitor technical business metrics such as registrations, orders, and marketing effects, because correlating business metrics with technical metrics in a healthy system reveals what is abnormal.
Set up metric collection before problems occur, as part of launching a service, so that historical data exists for comparison rather than only the data from the incident.
Choose a metric's collection period from how long it takes to fully understand its graph; collecting much more finely than that adds cost without adding value.
Retain metrics at progressively coarser granularity as they age — fine detail for days, coarse averages for years — since old data is rarely needed at fine resolution.
Metrics divide into those queryable over SNMP, easy to collect with established tools and well-known identifiers, and custom business metrics that require one-off collection scripts.
Place a custom marker in an unused log field, such as the remote-user field, so that it does not change the log format and break existing log processors.
The data behind most problems, when visualized correctly on a shared time axis, makes cause and effect obvious almost immediately.
Reconcile metric definitions across teams before trusting a discrepancy, because a mismatch such as counting all responses versus only HTTP 200s can masquerade as a business problem.
Centralized logging provides a single portal to audit day-to-day operations, and a brief review of a neglected server's logs almost always surfaces something out of line.
When a machine misbehaves badly you often cannot log in to it, but you can still read its logs if they are written to a remote host.
Most ongoing development is feature design — adding to an already-designed application — which is the most common source of mistakes.
A web application is ideally designed once and that initial design must be good because it underlies all later work, whereas feature-level design mistakes are smaller and easier to recover from.
Recognize when a feature is improperly designed and refactor it, because accumulated small bad decisions are a slow death.
Define the size and scope of a problem before building a solution, not after.
Choosing a tool merely because it was already there is a common and costly mistake; existing infrastructure is not automatically the right tool for a new problem.
When a feature does not need ACID guarantees — no durability, no isolation, no multi-row consistency — forcing it onto a relational database is the wrong tool.
Counting and top-N queries are expensive on most relational databases because they do not keep accurate cardinality and still fully sort despite an index and a LIMIT.

Instrumenting logging synchronously with content delivery is a recipe for disaster, because any slowdown in logging stalls the whole site; the desired behaviour is to serve slightly stale information while the back end catches up.
Processing events passively from the log stream gives near-real-time accuracy while ensuring that slowness in that processing can never slow the serving application.
'Too slow' is often really 'inappropriate': the tool is not slow, it is the wrong tool for the job.
For a problem that does not need persistence, prefer a solution that avoids touching storage and uses data structures that cheaply answer exactly the questions being asked.
Reuse existing infrastructure that already holds the needed data and supports extension, such as a log subscriber with a module API, as the platform for a new service.
Logs you are already publishing are effectively free to subscribe to, which is a crucial mental step in solving a problem with passive analysis.

Use a low-level language such as C for a performance-critical component when you need tight control over the data structures, for example to track millions of online users at thousands of requests per second.
Use a simple length-prefixed binary protocol in network byte order for a fast, efficient client-server service.
Non-blocking socket code must track partial-read progress across re-entries, returning on EAGAIN and resuming when more data arrives.
Eliminate expired entries from a data structure proactively rather than filtering them out at query time; with a time-ordered index, popping the oldest is an O(1) operation.

A low-level language such as C is verbose but gives cheap data management and granular control over data structures, justifying its use for a component that must sustain thousands of queries per second.
Performance-test against a representative dataset, not just a fast loop; a passive collector must be warmed with real production data before its numbers mean anything.
Because the tracking side sits outside the critical path, you can performance-test a passive service against a fresh instance fed by real production logs without building an elaborate test harness.

Profile to find the true bottleneck before optimizing: one client was capped at 43 queries per second almost entirely inside a big-integer library, and passing the 64-bit ID as two 32-bit halves raised it to roughly 2,800.

Run a load test in parallel from multiple nodes to build confidence in aggregate performance, account for the human error of tests not starting and stopping together, and stop once the goal is demonstrated.

Scalability is not performance: serving over ten thousand requests per second on one box is performance, while scalability means the implementation and use do not change as the problem's scope changes.
A service scales when it collects data outside the critical service path, works passively from log streams, and can be added to every node without loading any other component.
Know your tools: understanding a tool deeply is a key rule in solving any problem.
Do not pay for features you do not need; weigh the cost of unneeded capabilities rather than squashing a mosquito with a cannon.
The group-communication paradigm models participants as members of a group where any member can broadcast to and receive from the whole group, with open groups allowing non-members to send.

A group-communication system provides group-membership primitives that identify current members and notify the application when members join or leave, whether voluntarily, by network fault, or by crash.
Group message guarantees are defined along two axes: reliability — reliable messages reach all non-crashed members while unreliable ones may be lost — and ordering.
Common message ordering guarantees are FIFO, causal (an extension of FIFO), and total ordering, which is most useful when combined with at least FIFO.

Safe delivery, the extended-virtual-synchrony guarantee, delivers a message only once the local daemon knows all daemons hold it, signalling a transitional membership change on a partition; it is significantly slower than agreed or FIFO and should not be used casually.
In a group-communication network the daemons maintain their own membership, and a change in daemon membership from a crash or partition can induce changes in application group membership.

Reliable IP multicast suits a single sender broadcasting to many receivers whose identities do not matter, whereas group communication suits a small set of known participants that act as both senders and receivers.
Point-to-point communication among all participants, with no coordinating layer, is both expensive and chaotic.
Group-communication configuration files must be identical on every server, or daemons can silently fail to communicate while appearing healthy.
A multicast or broadcast group-communication system may silently fall back to unicast for two nodes but cannot for three or more, so a latent network fault only surfaces when the third node is added.
A group message lets a client trigger an action on every server in a group by sending one message, instead of having to know and connect to each server individually.
Even a reliable group message can be missed by a server that was crashed or partitioned when it was sent, leaving that server's state stale until it recovers.

For a cache, recovering from a missed invalidation by clearing the whole cache on restart is far simpler than guaranteeing delivery with safe messages and extra logic, and costs only on-demand repopulation.
Understanding the requirements and trade-offs of a distributed problem and choosing the appropriate tool and approach is essential to building smart distributed applications.
Guard against overly complex solutions during design, because complex solutions are costly to implement and carry excessive long-term costs.
condition: Applies to any project; especially for all large or complex systems or projects.

statement: Overengineering has two categories: building a product that exceeds its useful requirements, and building a product that is overly complex; the complexity category has the larger impact on scalability.
Overly complex systems limit how far a system can be scaled and reduce organizational productivity (slower onboarding, harder troubleshooting).

Test whether a design is too complex by having the responsible engineer present it to engineering cohorts of varying experience and tenure; if any cohort cannot understand and independently re-explain it, treat the system as possibly overly complex.
Do not implement or deploy scaling capabilities far ahead of need; scope creep added between product definition and launch is a form of overengineering.
Apply the Design-Implement-Deploy (D-I-D) approach: design for 20x capacity, implement (code) for 3x capacity, and deploy for roughly 1.5x capacity.
Discussing and designing how to scale is far cheaper than implementing it, so scale design (to the 20x-to-infinite range) should happen early and frequently and be written down for later reuse.
Defer high-cost engineering and asset spend to just before the capacity is needed (just-in-time scaling) to avoid idle assets that dilute shareholder value.
Provision roughly 1.5x peak capacity in production for a moderately high-growth company and around 5x peak for a hyper-growth company, and lean on cloud burst capacity for sudden demand increases.
condition: Multiplier depends on growth rate (moderate vs hyper-growth).

statement: Scale is elastic: it can both expand and contract, so solutions should be flexible enough to move capacity between systems as demand shifts.
Simplify a complex system in three separate passes: simplify the scope, then the design, then the implementation.
condition: When designing complex systems or products where engineering or computational resources are limited.

statement: Simplify scope by applying the Pareto Principle (80/20): deliver the ~20% of features that produce ~80% of the value and cut the rest.
Cutting unnecessary features reduces dependencies between functions, which lets the system scale more effectively and more cost-effectively.

Simplify implementation by reusing proven solutions: prefer a widely adopted open-source or third-party solution, then an internal proven solution, then a documented external approach you can legally copy, and only build your own when none exists.
The simplest implementation is almost always one that has already been implemented and proven scalable elsewhere.
Reduce the number of DNS lookups required to load a page, because DNS lookups add latency that can become a noticeable portion of the user experience.
condition: On web pages where performance matters.

statement: Every distinct domain that serves one or more objects for a page requires a DNS lookup (served from cache or from a name server).
As a general rule, fewer DNS lookups yield better page download performance, but reduction must be balanced against the browser's limit on simultaneous connections per domain.
exception: Combining all objects onto one domain to cut DNS lookups can hurt by defeating parallel per-domain connections.

statement: Reduce the number of objects on a page where performance matters, because fewer objects lower page download time and let each server serve more pages.
condition: On web pages where performance matters.

statement: Combine similar page objects (for example via CSS image sprites or combined CSS/JavaScript files) to reduce the number of distinct browser requests.
