exception: Do not over-combine: one very large combined object blocks all rendering until it fully downloads and wastes the browser's simultaneous-connection capacity.

statement: Browsers cap the maximum simultaneous persistent connections per domain; the HTTP/1.1 RFC recommends 2 but many browsers default to 6 or more.

Serve objects across multiple subdomains so the browser opens its per-domain connection maximum against each, increasing parallel downloads; one client cut average load time from 11 seconds to under 5 seconds using seven subdomains.
There is no absolute ideal object size or subdomain count; the only reliable way to tune page performance is to test pages across a variety of browsers and connection speeds.
Google reported that a 400-millisecond increase in search latency reduced their daily searches by almost 0.6%, evidence that slow page performance costs traffic.

Do not mix different vendors' routing and switching gear, because vendors interpret standard protocols differently and add proprietary protocols, causing intermittent interoperability and availability problems not worth the cost savings.
condition: When designing or expanding a network.
exception: Applies only to devices that must communicate to route traffic (routers, switches); for hubs, firewalls, load balancers, IDS, and DDoS appliances, choose best-of-breed instead.

statement: Heterogeneous networking gear (mixed router/switch vendors) tends to cause availability and scalability problems.
Dividing work across more workers increases throughput (work per unit time) and therefore scalability.

The AKF Scale Cube models scalability as three axes: X (horizontal duplication / cloning), Y (split by function, service, or resource), and Z (split by lookup or formulaic partition such as customer).
Three rules - cloning (X), splitting different things (Y), and splitting similar things (Z) - can scale nearly any system or database toward very high scale.
Apply X-axis scaling by cloning services or databases behind a load balancer to spread transaction load (horizontal duplication).
condition: Best for databases with a high read-to-write ratio (about 5:1 or greater) or any system where transaction growth exceeds data growth.

statement: X-axis cloning scales transactions but not data; its cost is duplicated data and functionality.
The database or persistent-storage tier is almost always the hardest part of a system to scale.
Most applications perform far more reads than writes, so scaling reads with read-only replicas is an effective database technique; one reservation system observed a 400:1 read-to-write ratio.

Perfectly in-sync replicated data is very expensive and often unnecessary; tolerate replication lag where the small chance of staleness is acceptable and handle the rare conflict in the application (for example, a final check before commit).
condition: Acceptable only where the application can tolerate a small probability of stale reads.

statement: Place an object cache (an open-source key-value store) in front of the database as a highly recommended first step for distributing reads before adding database replication.
Apply Y-axis scaling by splitting distinct functions and data by verbs (services) or nouns (resources), separating both the services and their data along those lines.
condition: Best for very large data sets where relations are not required, and for large complex systems where scaling engineering requires specialization.

statement: Y-axis splits scale both transactions and large data sets, raise cache hit ratios by isolating each function's data, and enable fault isolation.
Y-axis (service/resource) splits also scale engineering organizations, because teams can specialize in subsets of a complex system rather than understanding all of it.

Apply Z-axis scaling (sharding/podding) by partitioning one data set or service across pieces using something known about the customer or requestor (customer ID, name, geography, device, or a modulus/hash).
condition: Best for very large, similar, rapidly growing data sets (especially customer bases) or when fault isolation between customer groups is needed.

statement: Using unequal shard sizes lets you limit rollout risk by releasing first to a small customer segment and then to progressively larger segments.
Design systems to scale out (horizontally across many servers) rather than scale up (onto bigger hardware); 'scaling up is failing up'.
condition: For any system, service, or database expected to grow rapidly.

statement: The cost of ever-larger servers follows a power law: beyond a point, cost rises disproportionally to the processing gained, whereas the engineering cost of scaling out is roughly linear, so building to scale out is usually the better long-term investment.
Do not rely on Moore's Law to scale a hyper-growth system, because hyper-growth can outpace the doubling rate and the trend cannot hold indefinitely.
condition: Particularly for true hyper-growth companies whose customers or transactions grow faster than doubling every two years.

statement: For stateful applications, use load-balancer session affinity (session cookies) only as a fallback; prefer to eliminate the need to keep state on the application server.
Use small, inexpensive commodity systems rather than a few large high-end servers, especially in production during hyper-growth, to allow fast and cost-effective growth.
condition: In the production environment of a business going through hyper-growth.

statement: Large multi-processor servers carry the vendor's highest margins yet each added CPU does slightly less work (scheduling inefficiency, memory-bus contention, structural and data hazards), so you pay more per CPU and get less per CPU.

Do not trust a vendor's total-cost-of-ownership claim for the largest system; compute it yourself against an independent third-party utilization benchmark, comparing power cost and consumption to find the right commodity-range system.
Virtualizing one large system into N domains never yields more total processing power or throughput than N equivalent physical systems, because the virtualization software itself consumes CPU cycles.

Commodity systems are easier to negotiate, cheaper to maintain, allow more affordable redundancy, and fail less often per unit (fewer parts), so at scale treat them as disposable rather than investing time to repair them.
Design for three or more live data centers rather than two, to lower overall cost, increase availability, and provide disaster recovery.
condition: For a rapidly growing business considering adding disaster-recovery capacity.

statement: Three live sites need only about 150% of non-database capacity per type to survive any single-site failure, versus 200% for a two-site hot/cold configuration, although databases still require about 200% storage either way (total roughly 166% vs 200%).

Multiple live data centers require first segmenting data by the Y and Z axes (for fault isolation), cloning along the X axis (for availability and transaction growth), and eliminating or designing around state.
Slicing data along the Z axis lets you locate each customer's data in the data center nearest them, reducing dynamic-call response times.

A multiple-live-site model adds operational complexity, a small headcount increase, travel costs, and rising network interconnect costs, since a fully connected set of sites needs N additional connections for each new site.
Leverage the idle capacity reserved for disaster recovery to run test zones (load and performance tests) and to absorb unexpected demand spikes.
Use cloud and virtualization to scale on demand for temporary, spiky, and inconsistent demand.
condition: When demand is temporary, spiky, and inconsistent and response time is not a core product concern.

statement: Provisioning hardware in a cloud environment typically takes minutes, versus the days or weeks required to approve, order, rack, and load physical servers.

The cloud is cost-effective only for intermittent use: the break-even point versus buying a physical server is roughly 12 months of continuous (24x7) use, extended far longer when the server is used only part of each day.
condition: Break-even depends on hours of use per day.

statement: The components best suited to a cloud environment are batch processing, QA/test environments, and surge or burst capacity.
Use a relational database only when you need ACID transactional integrity or relationships between data; for other storage needs choose a more appropriate tool rather than defaulting to an RDBMS.
condition: When introducing new data or data structures into a system's architecture.

statement: An RDBMS provides strong transactional integrity and relational structure, but is harder to scale, costs more, and has lower availability than many alternative storage options.
Guaranteeing ACID consistency makes an RDBMS hard to distribute: synchronous replication or shared node ownership ultimately limits the number of nodes and their geographic spread.

Relational structure makes sharding or partitioning difficult: a single query joining two tables must be rewritten as two separate queries with the join performed in the application once the tables live in different databases.

A file system is a good storage choice for write-once-read-many data with few relationships and no expected read/write conflicts (for example, images), avoiding the transactional overhead of a database.
condition: When data is write-once-read-many, has few relationships, and has no read/write conflict.

statement: NoSQL stores (key-value, extensible-record, and document stores) deliberately limit relationships between entities, and it is this reduction in relationships that lets them distribute across many nodes for greater scalability, usually via asynchronous replication and eventual consistency.

There is a tradeoff between relationships and scale: more relationships increase flexibility but raise cost and reduce scalability, so choose a storage tool by degree of relationships needed, rate of growth, read/write ratio, and how well the data monetizes.
Use firewalls only where they significantly reduce risk, recognizing that each firewall lowers availability and creates a hard-to-scale chokepoint in network or transaction volume.

Decide where to firewall by weighing value-to-an-attacker against cost-to-firewall: firewall high-value data such as PII and PCI items (credit cards, social security numbers, password-reset data), but do not firewall low-value high-volume static content such as CSS, images, and JavaScript.
exception: Mid-value critical business functions are a case-by-case ('maybe') decision.

statement: In AKF's experience, failed firewalls are the second-largest driver of site downtime, behind failed databases.
Instead of firewalling low-value static content, deliver it from private IP addresses reachable only on ports 80 and 443 (and offload it to an edge cache or CDN).
Actively use application and web-server log files to diagnose and prevent problems, backed by a process that forces people to act on the issues the logs reveal.
Aggregate logs from all servers (using sampling or tiered log servers when volume is large) over an out-of-band network so that logging and aggregation do not impact production traffic.
Monitor aggregated logs with automated tools (custom grep scripts, Cricket, Cacti, or Splunk) that alert when error thresholds are exceeded, rather than collecting logs and then ignoring them.
Assign engineering and QA resources to identify and fix logged errors, and establish a process (for example periodic cleanup) so log errors do not accumulate unbounded or get ignored.

Logging carries a cost in both storage and transaction response time, so log asynchronously, summarize/archive/purge logs as their value declines, and make a cost-effective decision about how much to log and retain.

Avoid 'Maslow's hammer': teams reuse familiar tools and produce consistent but sometimes suboptimal solutions, so assemble diverse teams that can consider different tools, while not overspecializing past the point where you can support all the technologies you introduce.
exception: Each new technology adds a skill set to support; do not diversify so far that you lose depth of support.

statement: Never read back data you just wrote for the purpose of validating it; instead inspect and act on the error code returned by the write operation.
Reading after writing doubles transaction cost and halves throughput, and rarely returns risk-mitigation value commensurate with that cost.
On modern systems, write failures are caught during the write operation itself, so an immediate read-back to confirm a successful write essentially never detects a failure.

The appropriate protection against data corruption is high availability with multiple copies of data (standby database, replicated storage, and ideally multiple live sites), not read-after-write validation.

When recently written data will be needed again soon (as in a registration or purchase flow), keep it in a local or distributed cache rather than writing it and immediately fetching it back from the permanent store.

These rules are nomothetic (generally true) rather than idiographic (always true); when 'don't duplicate work' conflicts with staying stateless, resolve it by introducing state only in the limited set of operations where it actually decreases cost and increases scalability.
exception: Applies where local storage/affinity (state) genuinely lowers cost; otherwise prefer a stateless application.

statement: If a regulatory or legal requirement forces validation of a write, perform it asynchronously (write locally, recover failures from logs or a queue) and never block the user transaction pending a synchronous write to two data sources.
condition: Only when a genuine regulatory/legal requirement mandates verification.

statement: Avoid redirects wherever possible, because they delay the user from reaching the wanted resource, consume computational resources, and are prone to errors.

When a redirect is necessary, prefer a server-configuration redirect (such as an HTTP status code via Apache mod_alias or mod_rewrite) over an HTML meta-refresh or code-based redirect, because it avoids extra browser clicks and server HTML parsing or script interpretation.
On Apache, place redirect rules in the main httpd.conf rather than .htaccess files, because .htaccess is searched in every directory and reloaded on every document request, hurting performance.
condition: Applies to the Apache web server.

statement: Redirect mistakes such as loops, errors, overly long URLs, and empty redirects waste server resources and can hurt search-engine crawling and rankings.

Replace some redirects with lighter techniques; for example, track clicks with an onClick handler that requests a 1x1 pixel, so the browser is not sent through an extra page or header round-trip before loading the desired page.

Relax temporal constraints (requirements that an object hold a particular state between a user's actions) wherever possible, because such constraints are significantly harder and more expensive to scale under RDBMS ACID consistency.
condition: Any time you consider adding a constraint that an item maintains a certain state between a user's actions.

statement: The CAP (Brewer) Theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee all three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.
A BASE architecture (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) relaxes ACID consistency to gain flexibility in scaling, accepting that data becomes consistent only eventually.

Do not lock inventory when a user merely views an item; lock it only when the item is added to the cart, performing that lock on the master (write) database so the purchasing user is guaranteed the reservation while other viewers may or may not see it as available.
Do not require instantaneous consistency for user-to-user transfers of money, messages, or items; a delay of a few seconds before the recipient sees it is usually acceptable.
exception: Genuinely synchronous communication such as chat does require instant transfer.

statement: Compensating for the rare edge case where a user is disappointed is usually far easier than being unable to scale the system.
Use a content delivery network (CDN) to offload traffic from your site, gaining faster delivery, higher availability, and absorption of traffic spikes.
A CDN caches content on edge servers and only queries the origin server to check for updates, so it absorbs most user requests and reduces the servers, power, bandwidth, and staff you must provide.

Justify a CDN by a full cost-benefit analysis (response-time reduction, resulting activity increase, availability gain, and infrastructure savings) rather than cost alone, and monitor its usage; AKF found clients with greater than about $10M revenue are usually better served by a CDN.
condition: Cost-benefit varies by traffic volume and revenue scale.

statement: Even dynamic pages contain cacheable static content (images, JavaScript, CSS), and the dynamically generated text is usually the smallest part of a page, so a CDN benefits dynamic sites too.
Use HTTP Expires and Cache-Control headers, choosing a cacheable lifetime per object type (image, HTML, CSS, etc.), to reduce object requests and improve performance and scalability.
condition: Consider every object type.

statement: HTML meta tags (Pragma, Expires, Cache-Control) are unreliable for controlling caching because many browsers ignore them and proxy caches do not inspect HTML at all; real HTTP response headers must be used instead.
When an HTTP response includes both an Expires header and a Cache-Control max-age directive, max-age overrides Expires even if the Expires header is more restrictive.
Enable HTTP keep-alives (persistent connections), which Apache reports cut HTML page latency by about 50%, but tune the keep-alive timeout to balance connection reuse against tying up server threads.
Make Ajax calls cacheable using the Last-Modified, Cache-Control, and Expires headers, to cut user-perceived response time and server load.
exception: Except Ajax calls that genuinely require real-time data likely to have just been updated.

statement: Ajax improves interactivity by avoiding round-trips, but mishandled it can sharply increase the number of server requests, and a large burst over a short period can flood and fail server farms even though the calls are asynchronous to the browser.
Where data is not private, set Cache-Control: public (and avoid no-store) so intermediate proxies and CDNs can cache and reuse result sets for other users.
exception: Never mark genuinely private data as public.

statement: Request specific objects by stable atomic IDs (for example id=124556) rather than relative offsets (for example page=3&item=2), because relative names change and cause cache coherency and consistency problems.

Deploy a page cache (reverse proxy cache) in front of web servers to offload static and dynamic requests, recognizing the scalability benefit is much greater for dynamic content than for static content.
Use ETags (entity tags) with If-None-Match conditional GET requests to maximize cacheability across page caches and other proxy caches in the network path.
Employ application-level caching to scale cost-effectively, and design it from a systems-architecture perspective rather than ad hoc so it remains effective long term.

Maximize cacheability by combining the Pareto Principle with AKF Scale Cube Y-axis (functional) and Z-axis (customer) splits, so the heavily hit ~20% of objects or users are concentrated where cache hit rates stay high.

Treat caching architecture as iterative: hypothesize likely usage, split to maximize cacheability, evaluate effectiveness in production, then refine the splits using real production data, repeating the cycle.
A learning organization continuously analyzes production traffic, cost per transaction, and user-perceived response times to detect bottlenecks early and feed that data to the architecture team.

Implement an object cache (an in-memory key-to-hashed-value store) wherever queries or computations are performed repeatedly, primarily between the application and database tiers, to save computational resources.
condition: Any time you have repetitive queries or computations.

statement: Use the database's Top SQL report (the most frequent and most resource-intensive queries) to decide when an object cache is needed and which queries to eliminate from the database by caching.

Do not build a home-grown object cache; many production-grade solutions exist (for example Memcached, which Facebook ran across more than 800 servers and 28 TB of memory), so a build decision should be highly scrutinized.
Monitor the object-cache hit ratio, aiming for about 85% or better (misses 15% or less), and add object-cache servers when the ratio drops.

Place object caches on their own tier of servers (between application and database, or between web and application tiers) rather than co-locating them on the web or application servers, so the cache can be sized and scaled independently.
condition: Any time object caches have been implemented.

statement: Object caches are memory-heavy but require relatively little CPU, so sizing a dedicated cache tier to that profile saves money and lets added capacity be used entirely by the cache.
Learn aggressively from both mistakes and successes at every opportunity; the companies that learn best, fastest, and most often are the ones that grow fastest and scale best.

Do not fully trust what customers say (focus groups are limited by social construction); launch quickly and watch actual customer behavior, ideally using A/B testing on chosen metrics such as abandonment, time on site, and conversion.

Never let an incident pass without a postmortem that reaches the real root cause and feeds the learning back into the organization; mistakes are unavoidable, but making the same mistake twice is unacceptable.

The root cause of a production failure includes the process and people that allowed it, so add controls such as peer code review, DBA review of all queries, and load/performance testing to keep defects like poorly performing queries out of production.
You cannot test quality into a system; use QA to lower the cost of delivered products, increase engineering throughput, surface quality trends, and cut repeated defects, not to create quality.

Hire a QA person whenever doing so recovers at least one engineer's worth of productivity (for example 11 engineers each spending ~10% of their time testing), typically at a lower per-head cost than an engineer.

In hyper-growth organizations (engineering doubling annually), QA's most important role is to surface the recurring, systemic engineering failures the organization keeps repeating, because QA is often the only team positioned to see them.
condition: Especially where engineering teams are doubling or more year over year.

statement: Always design every release with the ability to roll back, and reject 'the application is too complex' or 'we release too often' as excuses for being unable to roll back.

Make database changes additive only: add columns or tables and deprecate dependencies in a later release, and never change the semantic meaning of existing data within a release that still depends on it.
Script and test the release's DDL/DML changes and their rollback scripts ahead of time in QA or staging and under load, rather than applying changes by hand.

Add a 'wire on / wire off' feature-flag framework (config-driven, supporting role-based and random-percentage access) so a buggy feature can be disabled without rolling back the entire codebase and to enable limited beta testing.
To make rollback safe, disambiguate SQL in the application by removing SELECT * queries and adding explicit column names to all UPDATE statements.

Run a lightweight three-phase postmortem for every major issue: phase 1 build only the timeline, phase 2 identify issues from the timeline without proposing fixes, phase 3 state SMART actions each with a single named owner.

No postmortem is complete until it addresses the people, process, and technology causes; a single failure such as 'a server died' is never the true root cause, so ask 'why' about five times to uncover the holistic systemic causes.

There is a reliability paradox: the best-built systems fail least and therefore give the organization the fewest chances to learn, and the complexity of tightly coupled modern systems makes some accidents inevitable (Normal Accident Theory).

For reliable, rarely-failing systems, practice organizational mindfulness (High Reliability Organization strategies): preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify interpretations, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, and deference to expertise during crises.
condition: Most valuable where a well-designed system fails infrequently even under extreme scale.

statement: Plan the data model carefully up front (entities, relationships, normalization, and likely future database splits), because fixing a broken data model after implementation can cost on the order of 100 times what it costs to fix during the design phase.
condition: When designing the data model, adding tables/columns, or writing queries.

statement: A database is considered normalized when it satisfies at least third normal form ('the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key'), which reduces data redundancy and the risk of integrity problems.

Higher normal form increases data integrity but adds relationships that raise cost and constrain how the database can be split, so normalization level is a tradeoff rather than an absolute good; to increase scale, teams often deliberately reduce normal forms.

Entity relationships determine how a database can be split or sharded, so extensive relationships (for example an order entity tied to many others) make a Y-axis split difficult to perform after the fact.
Have a competent DBA familiar with the data model review new queries and analyze their performance characteristics before they enter production.

When join-heavy SQL performs poorly, try in order: tune the query; create a view, materialized view, or summary table to preprocess the join; pull the data sets into the application and join in memory to move load to the easier-to-scale application tier; or push back on the business requirement.
Be cognizant of explicit locks and monitor implicit locks whenever using a relational database, in order to maximize concurrency and transaction throughput.
condition: Anytime you employ relational databases.

statement: Lock granularity trades off throughput: too-fine locks (many row locks) incur acquisition and contention cost, while too-coarse locks (a whole page for a few rows) block other transactions, so match lock granularity to the size of the write.
Initially let the database optimizer choose the lock size, since it has more knowledge at operation time, but monitor production and override the lock type or DML when the optimizer chooses poorly.
Reduce database lock contention by changing entity relationships and applying AKF Scale Cube splits: X-axis read replicas, Y-axis table splits, and Z-axis customer-specific table splits.

Choose a database and storage engine that supports multiple lock types and granularities; some engines (for example MySQL's MyISAM) limit you to table-level locks and thereby cap transaction throughput.

Do not use a multiphase commit protocol (such as two-phase or three-phase commit) to store or process transactions as a way to extend a monolithic database; split data storage and processing with Y- or Z-axis splits instead.

Multiphase commit is a blocking protocol that holds the application-server thread and locks all involved database rows for the entire protocol duration; AKF saw two-phase commit on under 2% of calls lock up a database that had previously handled thousands of reads and writes per second.

Minimize the FOR UPDATE clause in SELECT cursors and question every use in review, because the row locks it holds for an uncontrolled duration can block other transactions and create near-deadlock slowdowns in high-transaction systems.
The ANSI SQL standard defaults a cursor to FOR UPDATE unless FOR READ ONLY is declared, so consult the database documentation and declare read-only cursors to minimize locks.
condition: Behavior and the read-only keyword vary by database.

statement: Never use SELECT * (or an INSERT without an explicit column list); always declare the specific columns being selected or inserted.
SELECT * breaks column-to-variable mapping when the table structure changes and transfers unneeded data, which adds up at high query rates; naming columns also preserves the ability to roll back.

Design fault-isolation domains called swimlanes when splitting databases or services to scale: a swimlane shares nothing and permits no synchronous calls across its boundary, so a failure inside one swimlane does not affect the others.
condition: Whenever you are beginning to split up databases to scale.

statement: Swimlanes follow four principles: share nothing (never share databases or servers, though some border routers, load balancers, or a SAN may be shared), allow no synchronous calls across boundaries, limit asynchronous calls across boundaries, and implement any cross-swimlane asynchronous call with timeouts and wire-on/wire-off control.

Fault-isolative swimlanes increase availability, speed incident and problem detection (fewer components to investigate), improve scalability through independent horizontal growth, and lower development cost and time to market.

When fault isolation requires an otherwise-shared synchronous dependency, duplicate the service into each swimlane (for example N payment gateways) or place a per-swimlane read replica or cache for shared read-only data such as login credentials.

When using virtualization, keep swimlane boundaries on physical-server boundaries; do not mix virtual servers from different swimlanes on the same physical host, because doing so removes most of the fault-isolation benefit.
exception: Where virtualization is used to flex capacity across product offerings, flex whole physical servers in and out of a swimlane rather than mixing swimlanes on one server.

statement: Never implement, and always eliminate, single points of failure, striving for active/active configurations and using load balancers to spread traffic across multiple instances of a service.
condition: During architecture reviews and new designs.

statement: Everything fails - servers, storage systems, network devices, and even data centers - so design on the assumption that any named component can and will fail.

The database is the most common single point of failure because it is the hardest to scale across nodes and so is often left as a singleton; a database SPOF is especially damaging because every service pool making synchronous calls to it fails when it does.

When code cannot be changed in time, quick fixes for a single point of failure include active/passive (hot/cold) configuration, using another component such as database locks or a master-slave split to control access, or load-balancer session affinity; the best long-term fix is code that can run on many hosts.
Reduce the number of components connected in series, because components in series have a multiplicative effect on the risk of failure.
condition: Anytime you are considering adding components.

statement: Each additional component placed in series multiplies down total availability; adding one more 99.9%-available component in series adds about 43 minutes of downtime per month, and adding components in parallel mitigates this.

Teams commonly parallelize the web and application tiers but overlook the database and network layers (especially firewalls), which remain in series; split the database and scale it horizontally to remove that single in-series component.

Create a framework to disable and enable (wire on / wire off) product features so that risky, very-high-use, or shared services can be turned off to fail gracefully rather than bringing down the site.
condition: For risky, very high use, or shared services that might cause site failures when slow or unavailable.

statement: Implement wire-on/wire-off only where the implementation cost is less than the risk (likelihood times impact) of failure; good candidates are high-throughput shared services such as payment gateways and features undergoing significant change.
exception: Do not make everything toggleable; universal wire-on/wire-off is costly and ill-advised.

statement: Reduce the cost of wire-on/wire-off by building reusable shared libraries that future features can adopt, lowering the per-feature implementation cost over time.
Design and implement stateless systems, because state and session data limit scalability and increase cost in memory, processing power, and the number of servers required.
condition: During design of new systems and redesign of existing systems.

statement: Always push back on the need for state, and implement it only where a clear competitive advantage is demonstrated in key operating metrics through A/B or multivariate testing.

State distribution (moving state to the browser or a distributed state cache) is not the same as being stateless; prefer truly stateless designs and use browser or distributed-cache state only when state is genuinely justified.

Relying on load-balancer affinity to handle session and state is adequate only where growth has slowed or availability requirements are relaxed, because affinity complicates capacity planning and loses a customer's session when their bound application server fails.
condition: Acceptable mainly for products with slowed growth or relaxed availability needs.

statement: When session data is required, prefer storing it in the user's browser via cookies, so any web server in the pool can serve the request and the system avoids the storage and retrieval overhead.
condition: Anytime you need session data for the best user experience and cannot avoid it.

statement: Keep browser cookie data as small as possible, because cookie data transfers with every request and large cookies slow both page loads and the web servers (browsers support roughly 4KB and 20 cookies per domain).

Protect session cookies from sidejacking on open WiFi by transmitting at least the authorization cookie over HTTPS (for example via a per-page HTTPS JavaScript authentication call) even when the bulk of the page is served over unsecured HTTP.
When state must be stored within the system and cannot be pushed to the user's browser, use a distributed cache rather than server-local session storage.
condition: Anytime you need to store session data and cannot do so in the user's browser.

statement: Three things to avoid when caching session or state: do not require user affinity to a specific server, do not use state or session replication that duplicates data across nodes, and do not locate the session cache on the same server doing the work.

Choose a state store by trading persistence against cost: a database-only store is most costly but durable and handles conflicts well, a nonpersistent object cache is fast and cheap but loses data on failure, and a hybrid database-plus-cache gives durability with cost-effective scale.
Do not build your own caching solution for session or state; use an existing distributed object cache or database given the many available options.

Favor asynchronous over synchronous communication wherever possible for calls between services and tiers, so each service and tier is as independent as possible and a slowdown or failure in one does not cascade.
condition: Consider for all calls between services and tiers.

statement: Synchronous call chains have a multiplicative effect on both availability and bug risk (chained 99.99% components multiply down) and make a fault harder to localize, because a failure in one synchronously called component propagates to all callers.

Asynchronous calls are harder to implement than synchronous ones (they need callbacks or coordination unless fire-and-forget), so apply them selectively to the calls that most need decoupling rather than to every call.

The best candidates to make asynchronous are calls to external or third-party APIs (always), notoriously long-running or computationally heavy processes, frequently changed or error-prone methods, and calls with no temporal constraint (fire-and-forget, such as a welcome email).
Calls that remain synchronous should have timeouts and exception handling so the system gracefully handles a synchronously called method or service that fails or is slow.
Treat the message bus like any other critical component and scale it ahead of demand, because a message bus can fail under load just like any other physical or logical system.
condition: Anytime a message bus is part of your architecture.

statement: An enterprise service bus or message bus is a commonly overlooked giant single point of failure; its asynchronous nature does not exempt it from high-demand bottlenecks or port-exhaustion failures.

Scale a message bus using the AKF Y axis (split by message or service attribute such as temporal, service, quality-of-service, or resource) and the Z axis (split by customer); the X axis (cloning the bus) does not help much because all applications would still need to listen to all buses.

Scale the message bus consistently with the rest of the architecture (a bus per Y-axis function or per Z-axis customer pod), and when both apply prefer the Z-axis split so the bus stays within swimlane fault-isolation boundaries.
Do not publish everything on a message bus; limit bus traffic to items whose value exceeds the cost to handle them, because message traffic is not free and adds costly demand on the system.
condition: On any message bus.

statement: Decide message-bus publishing by a value/cost quadrant: publish 100% of high-value/low-cost data, do not publish low-value/high-cost data, and sample the remaining quadrants to align cost with value.

On a message bus the per-message cost is roughly constant while data value varies, so statistically significant sampling of lower-value high-volume data can retain nearly all of its value at a fraction of the cost.

Scale your own system rather than relying on vendor or proprietary solutions to achieve scalability, for three reasons: own your destiny, keep your architecture simple, and reduce total cost of ownership.
condition: When considering whether to adopt a new feature or product from a vendor.

statement: Vendor proprietary scaling features such as database clustering create lock-in: once you scale on one vendor's solution you cannot easily switch, and the vendor can then raise prices dramatically with few alternatives for you.
Treat the ability to split up and scale your application as a core competency, and use vendors only for things outside your core competency, operating their products in the simplest manner possible.
exception: This does not mean building everything yourself, such as writing your own database or firewall.

statement: Match storage cost to data value and purge or archive data whose value is lower than its storage cost; because data value changes over time, storage tiering must be a living, ongoing process rather than a one-time analysis.
condition: Apply during design and throughout the data's lifecycle.
exception: Data required for regulatory or legal reasons should be kept on the cheapest compliant storage rather than purged.

statement: Use recency, frequency, and monetization (RFM) analysis to value data, then place high-value, frequently-accessed, recent data on fast costly storage (such as striped/mirrored SSDs), tier aging data down to cheaper slower media, and purge never-accessed, no-value data where regulation allows.

Storage is never free: it costs the purchase price of the media, the space it occupies (an opportunity cost), and the power and HVAC to run and cool the drives, with per-unit power and cooling cost rising even as media gets cheaper and denser.

Keep like transactions together and separate unlike ones: remove business and product intelligence from the database (move stored procedures into application logic) so the expensive database can focus on relational transactions.
exception: Stored procedures are not inherently bad; the concern is their overuse on the scale-governing database.

statement: The database is usually the most expensive compute resource and often the governor of scale, so spending its cycles on business logic both raises the cost per transaction and steals capacity needed for scaling.

Do not tie corporate or back-office systems (ERP, data warehouse, CRM) synchronously to the product platform; move data between them asynchronously (batch ETL, or a message bus when temporal constraints require) so each scales independently and product availability is not reduced by another in-series system.

Adopt 'design to be monitored' as an architectural principle: when adding or changing modules, build in hooks (for example asynchronous start/end timestamps around transactions such as SQL, API, RPC, or method calls) so execution can be watched.
condition: Anytime you add or change modules of the code base.

statement: Monitor first from business metrics to answer 'Is there a problem?' (broad scope, little data), then use application monitoring for 'Where is the problem?', then system tools such as Nagios or Cacti for 'What is the problem?'; high server CPU or memory alone does not tell you whether customers are actually affected.

Detect customer-affecting problems by plotting business metrics against the same period one week earlier (week-over-week) and alerting when the value falls out of statistical significance; more advanced monitoring can later answer 'Why is there a problem?' and 'Will there be a problem?'.

Be competent in, or buy competency for, every component of your architecture; the build-versus-buy and core-versus-context decision is separate from the requirement to understand, operate, troubleshoot, and promptly restore whatever you use.
condition: For any Internet service or commerce solution.

statement: You are in the service business, not the software business: to the customer every problem is your problem and cannot be blamed on suppliers, so availability and response time matter more than any single feature.

Match in-house expertise to team size and component importance: a larger team or a more heavily relied-upon component argues for in-house expertise, while a smaller team or less important component can be outsourced, but any partner relied upon must have 'skin in the game' and feel the pain when service fails.

Prioritize scalability rework by risk reduction minus cost (R - C = P): rate each initiative's risk reduction and cost on a High/Medium/Low scale, where risk equals the probability of a problem times its impact, and impact decomposes into percentage of customers affected, percentage of functionality affected, downtime, data loss, and response-time degradation.

Measure system availability by actual lost revenue rather than wall-clock time, because traffic and revenue-producing transactions are unevenly distributed across the day so every hour is not equivalent.

The highest-priority ('very high') scalability rework items are those rated high risk-reduction at low cost; in AKF's rating these were relaxing temporal constraints, object caches, designing for rollback, learning from failures, using the right database lock, avoiding SELECT *, avoiding vendor scaling lock-in, and being competent.
condition: AKF's ratings target smaller action-oriented companies reworking an existing solution; your own risk/cost may vary.

statement: Applying these rules when building from scratch costs significantly less than reworking an existing system for the same benefit, so include as many of the rules as make sense up front rather than retrofitting later.
The 50 rules were chosen as the changes AKF most frequently recommends to clients, and none ranks 'Very Low' priority because lower-value candidate rules did not make the cut for inclusion.

For reworking an existing system, the lowest-priority ('Low - 4') items - those whose cost is high relative to their risk reduction - are designing to leverage the cloud, not checking your work, and wiring functions on and off.
condition: Ratings are for reworking an existing system; building from scratch changes the cost calculus.

statement: Codify a selected subset of these rules as your organization's architectural principles and use complete adherence to that set as the exit criteria for software and infrastructure design and architecture reviews.

These rules have exceptions and not all apply to every system (for example the database rules do not apply if you use no relational database), and the priority model is an average that will be wrong for specific cases, so adapt and prioritize the rules to your business rather than applying all of them blindly.
exception: Skip rules whose domain you do not use, or whose cost is unjustified given your business's stage and uncertainty.
